course: INFO 7375: Prompt Engineering for Generative AI

scoring.rule: Five statements, each true or false, 1 point each. The student checks the statements they believe are true. A statement scores 1 point if it is checked and true, or unchecked and false; otherwise 0.

chapters.6: Chapter 6: Claude Code and diff review

questions.stem: Check each statement that is historically accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: McCulloch and Pitts published a mathematical model of an artificial neuron in 1943.
statements.explanation: The artificial neuron model is from 1943.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The term "artificial intelligence" comes from the proposal for the 1956 Dartmouth workshop.
statements.explanation: McCarthy coined it in the 1955 proposal for the 1956 workshop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: AI was founded as a field in 1942.
statements.explanation: The neuron model is 1943 and the field was named in 1956; nothing founded it in 1942.

statements.label: D
statements.text: AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result is widely seen as the start of the modern deep learning boom.
statements.explanation: That is the standard marker for the boom.

statements.label: E
statements.text: ChatGPT was released to the public in 2015.
statements.explanation: ChatGPT launched in November 2022.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is historically accurate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Transformer was introduced in 2017 in "Attention Is All You Need".
statements.explanation: Correct.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (1950) was published before Rosenblatt's Perceptron (1958).
statements.explanation: 1950 comes before 1958.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Backpropagation was popularized in 1986 for training multi-layer networks.
statements.explanation: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The LSTM (1997) was introduced before AlexNet (2012).
statements.explanation: 1997 comes before 2012.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Perceptron (1958) was introduced after backpropagation was popularized (1986).
statements.explanation: Reversed: the Perceptron came first.

questions.section: 2. What is a model? What is a language model?
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model is a function from inputs to outputs whose parameters are learned from data.
statements.explanation: output = f(input; θ).

statements.label: B
statements.text: A language model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens given the preceding tokens.
statements.explanation: That is P(next token | previous tokens).

statements.label: C
statements.text: A language model answers by looking up stored answers in a database of facts.
statements.explanation: It computes a distribution; it does not retrieve stored answers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Text generation is autoregressive: each chosen token is fed back as input for the next step.
statements.explanation: Predict, sample, append, repeat.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model's weights are updated every time you send it a new prompt.
statements.explanation: Inference does not update weights.

questions.section: 2. What is a model? What is a language model?
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how an LLM turns a prompt into output.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The logits are one raw score per token in the vocabulary.
statements.explanation: Logits have length vocab_size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Softmax is applied to the logits to produce probabilities.
statements.explanation: Softmax turns scores into a distribution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Embeddings are produced after the softmax step.
statements.explanation: Embeddings come right after tokenization, before the Transformer layers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Changing a prompt, its context, or a setting is the same thing as training the model.
statements.explanation: None of these change the weights.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After a token is sampled it is appended to the input and the process repeats.
statements.explanation: That is autoregressive generation.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about feedforward neural networks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each neuron computes an activation function applied to w · x + b.
statements.explanation: Weights, bias, then nonlinear activation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Without nonlinear activations, a stack of layers collapses into a single linear transformation.
statements.explanation: Linear composed with linear is linear.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Backpropagation computes the gradients of the loss used to update the weights.
statements.explanation: Forward pass, loss, backprop, gradient descent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A feedforward network contains a compiler that translates the network into English.
statements.explanation: No such component.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In training, the loss is computed before the forward pass.
statements.explanation: The forward pass comes first; the loss measures its output.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about RNNs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An RNN carries a hidden state from one time step to the next.
statements.explanation: h_t depends on h_(t-1).

statements.label: B
statements.text: An RNN processes a sequence step by step, which limits parallel training.
statements.explanation: Tokens are handled in order.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because of vanishing or exploding gradients.
statements.explanation: Early information fades.

statements.label: D
statements.text: LSTM and GRU gating eliminates the vanishing-gradient problem entirely.
statements.explanation: Gating reduces it; it does not eliminate it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: RNNs compute attention over all positions at once, exactly like Transformers.
statements.explanation: That describes Transformers.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a character, or punctuation.
statements.explanation: It depends on the tokenizer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One word always equals exactly one token.
statements.explanation: Rare or long words are split into several tokens.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Before the model sees text, it is converted into an array of integer token IDs.
statements.explanation: The array length is the number of tokens.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The context window limits how many tokens the model can process at once.
statements.explanation: It is the maximum length of the token array.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "0.75 words per token" holds exactly for every language and tokenizer.
statements.explanation: It is an approximation for English and varies.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The logits vector for next-token prediction has one entry per token in the vocabulary.
statements.explanation: Length vocab_size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The embedding matrix has shape vocab_size × d_model.
statements.explanation: Each ID selects one row.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prompt of n tokens becomes an n × d_model matrix after embedding.
statements.explanation: One embedding row per token.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pricing, rate limits and context limits are measured in words.
statements.explanation: They are measured in tokens.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The logits vector has length equal to the number of tokens in the prompt.
statements.explanation: Its length is the vocabulary size, regardless of prompt length.

questions.stem: For logits [1, 2, 3] at T = 1, softmax gives about [0.090, 0.245, 0.665]. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The three probabilities sum to 1.
statements.explanation: Softmax outputs sum to 1.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding 100 to every logit changes the probabilities.
statements.explanation: Softmax is shift-invariant.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiating is for numerical stability and does not change the result.
statements.explanation: It prevents overflow.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Lowering the temperature to 0.5 increases the probability of token 3.
statements.explanation: About 0.867 at T = 0.5.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing the (positive) temperature can change which token has the highest probability.
statements.explanation: A positive T preserves order.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about temperature and sampling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Temperature must be greater than zero in the softmax formula.
statements.explanation: T divides the logits.

statements.label: B
statements.text: As temperature grows very large, the distribution approaches uniform.
statements.explanation: Flatter as T increases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lowering temperature can fix an answer when the highest logit belongs to a wrong label.
statements.explanation: Lower T only concentrates more on the wrong label.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Higher temperature generally produces more varied outputs across runs.
statements.explanation: A flatter distribution samples more variety.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A token probability of 0.665 means there is a 66.5% chance the generated claim is factually correct.
statements.explanation: It is a sampling probability, not a truth probability.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about softmax.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Every softmax output is between 0 and 1.
statements.explanation: By construction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Softmax preserves order: the largest logit gets the largest probability.
statements.explanation: Exponentiation is monotonic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The raw logits [1, 2, 3] are already a probability distribution.
statements.explanation: They sum to 6.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With a fixed seed, sampled draws are reproducible.
statements.explanation: The seed fixes the random stream.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a finite number of samples, observed counts match the expected counts exactly.
statements.explanation: Counts drift from expectation.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about self-attention.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Queries, keys and values are learned linear projections of token representations.
statements.explanation: Q, K and V are projections.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Attention scores are computed as Q·Kᵀ divided by √d_k.
statements.explanation: Scaled dot-product attention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Softmax over each query's scores produces weights that sum to 1.
statements.explanation: Each row is normalized.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Attention on its own encodes word order, so positional information is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Attention is order-agnostic; positional encoding is added.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In a decoder-only language model, a causal mask prevents tokens from attending to future tokens.
statements.explanation: Tokens see only earlier tokens.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The output for each token is a weighted sum of value vectors.
statements.explanation: Weights times V.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Multi-head attention lets the model attend to different kinds of relationships in parallel.
statements.explanation: Several heads run at once.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The vector for "bank" changing when "river" is nearby shows the model has understood the meaning of "bank".
statements.explanation: A changed vector is not evidence of understanding.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Surrounding tokens can influence a token's representation through attention.
statements.explanation: That is how context changes it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attention was introduced so that the whole input must be squeezed into one fixed vector.
statements.explanation: Attention removes that bottleneck by letting the model look back at all positions.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Code in a programming language follows a formal grammar and is interpreted unambiguously.
statements.explanation: Formal grammar.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Invalid syntax in a program produces an explicit error.
statements.explanation: Syntax errors and exceptions are explicit.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A language model accepts ambiguous natural language and still produces an output.
statements.explanation: It always produces something.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A language model runs outside the computer's normal instruction execution.
statements.explanation: It is ordinary arithmetic on CPUs and GPUs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The same prompt can produce different outputs when sampling at temperature above 0.
statements.explanation: Outputs are sampled.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A language model's wrong answer can look as fluent as a right one.
statements.explanation: Errors are silent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A program executes your instruction exactly, while a language model treats your prompt as context for predicting tokens.
statements.explanation: That is the key difference.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A deterministic program gives the same output for the same code and input.
statements.explanation: Deterministic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A language model's mistakes are reliably flagged as errors.
statements.explanation: They are not flagged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At temperature above 0, a language model's output is deterministic.
statements.explanation: Sampling makes it probabilistic.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is a strength of a well-written pure function compared with a language model.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Same input gives the same output.
statements.explanation: Deterministic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Behavior can be checked with unit tests.
statements.explanation: Testable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It can be composed with other functions and reused.
statements.explanation: Composable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It interprets vague, ambiguous instructions gracefully.
statements.explanation: That is the language model's strength.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It performs exact arithmetic and comparisons.
statements.explanation: Exact.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A function's failures surface as explicit, inspectable errors.
statements.explanation: An exception says what broke and where.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The course's design rule is to let the model generate and let functions check.
statements.explanation: Validators, schema checks, softmax, path policies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Chapter 1 probabilities() and sample() functions and the Chapter 2 JSON contract validator are examples of functions that check.
statements.explanation: Course examples.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The course builds mechanisms as Python functions so that Claude is not used at all.
statements.explanation: Claude is used for the fuzzy parts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pure function may return different outputs for the same input.
statements.explanation: Same input gives the same output by definition.

questions.section: 9. Chapter 1: Division of Labor and The Gate
questions.stem: Under the course's division of labor, check each statement describing a task that belongs to the human.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Predicting the effect of temperature before running the code.
statements.explanation: The human predicts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Building the first version of the implementation.
statements.explanation: The human builds the first version.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deciding what the experimental result does and does not support.
statements.explanation: The human decides.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Organizing the observed sampling results into a table.
statements.explanation: AI can organize the observed results.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Explaining one failure case without Claude supplying the answer.
statements.explanation: The human explains it.

questions.section: 9. Chapter 1: Division of Labor and The Gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a working "gate".

statements.label: A
statements.text: A gate is capable of rejecting an output.
statements.explanation: A check that cannot reject is not a gate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A gate can rely on the model's stated confidence.
statements.explanation: Model confidence is not a gate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A gate can stop a consistently repeated false answer.
statements.explanation: That is Chapter 1's design question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A gate is a check or a human decision placed before acceptance or action.
statements.explanation: Definition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A check that passes every output is a useful gate.
statements.explanation: It cannot reject anything.

questions.section: 9. Chapter 1: Division of Labor and The Gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Chapter 1.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A repeatable answer can still be wrong.
statements.explanation: Consistency is not correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lowering the temperature gets a consistently false answer through a real gate.
statements.explanation: A real gate still rejects it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: AI should help diagnose Python errors after your first attempt.
statements.explanation: Part of the AI side of the split.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You should record what you delegated and what you did with the time saved.
statements.explanation: Record the split.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Training that rewards human approval cannot favor confident-sounding answers over correct ones.
statements.explanation: It can.

questions.section: 10. Chapter 2: The three-response experiment and what the green cannot distinguish
questions.stem: A JSON schema validator passes (green). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The green cannot distinguish a true claim from a false claim in a correctly structured response.
statements.explanation: It checks structure, not truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The green cannot distinguish a source ID that supports the claim from a valid source ID that does not.
statements.explanation: It checks the ID is valid, not that it supports the claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The green cannot distinguish malformed JSON from well-formed JSON.
statements.explanation: That is exactly what it catches.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The green cannot distinguish a response with an extra unexpected field from one without.
statements.explanation: Schema validity catches extra fields.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A green result tells you the claim is factually valid.
statements.explanation: Factual validity is a separate check.

questions.section: 10. Chapter 2: The three-response experiment and what the green cannot distinguish
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three-response experiment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Three identical responses prove the answer is correct.
statements.explanation: Consistency is not verification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Variation in wording is not automatically a failure.
statements.explanation: Three different wordings can all be correct.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You should record the exact prompt, all outputs, model label, date and interface.
statements.explanation: Needed for reproducibility.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Factual correctness should be judged separately from surface variation.
statements.explanation: Two different questions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Temperature can be set in every Claude interface.
statements.explanation: Settings differ by model and interface.

questions.section: 10. Chapter 2: The three-response experiment and what the green cannot distinguish
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A format-pass rate measures how often the answers are factually correct.
statements.explanation: A format-pass rate is not an accuracy score.

statements.label: B
statements.text: JSON validity, schema validity and factual validity are different checks.
statements.explanation: Parses, right fields and types, true and supported.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing test suite establishes only the behavior it tests.
statements.explanation: Not universal reliability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Held-out cases should be kept separate from the cases used to revise the prompt.
statements.explanation: Do not change the test after inspecting results.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When treating a prompt as an experimental intervention, you should change one feature at a time.
statements.explanation: Isolate the effect.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about an agentic loop.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each action produces an observation that updates the state for the next step.
statements.explanation: State, action, observation, update.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The policy and the controller are different pieces.
statements.explanation: The policy proposes; the controller runs the loop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The loop should have a turn or budget limit.
statements.explanation: Bound the loop.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the loop stops, the task has succeeded.
statements.explanation: It may have exhausted its budget.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Repeating the same search several times counts as progress.
statements.explanation: Repeating the same action is not progress.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether a system is an agent depends on the actions it can take, not on its product name.
statements.explanation: Judge by capabilities and consequences.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The policy proposes the next action and the controller executes it and enforces limits.
statements.explanation: Different roles.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A bounded loop cannot take an unauthorized action.
statements.explanation: It can still do one unauthorized thing, hence permissions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The loop stops when the goal is met or the budget runs out.
statements.explanation: Two stopping conditions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The difference between a chat system and an agent is the action surface.
statements.explanation: What it can actually do.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about solve-verify asymmetry.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking a completed Sudoku is easier than solving one.
statements.explanation: Classic example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It suggests generating with a model and verifying with a cheap independent check.
statements.explanation: Tests, validators, source lookup.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The asymmetry holds equally for every task.
statements.explanation: It disappears when verifying is as hard as solving.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the same model to confirm its own answer is an independent verification.
statements.explanation: It is not independent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When verifying is as hard as solving, the advantage disappears.
statements.explanation: E.g. judging a long novel argument with no ground truth.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about fluency.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fluent answer is not necessarily a correct one.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence of correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Training that rewards human approval can favor confident-sounding answers.
statements.explanation: Confidence can beat correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confident tone is a calibrated measure of how likely the answer is to be true.
statements.explanation: It is not calibrated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A wrong answer can be just as fluent as a right one.
statements.explanation: Smooth, grammatical, confident either way.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fluency is evidence that an answer is correct.
statements.explanation: It is not.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "This function returns a sorted list for every input in test set X" is falsifiable as stated.
statements.explanation: A failing input would refute it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The model is intelligent in its own way" is falsifiable as stated.
statements.explanation: No observation could show it wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "For logits [1, 2, 3], lowering temperature to 0.5 raises token 3's probability above 0.8" is falsifiable as stated.
statements.explanation: And true: about 0.867.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The new prompt is better" is falsifiable as stated.
statements.explanation: Better at what, measured how, on which cases?

statements.label: E
statements.text: A claim is falsifiable if you can say what observation would show it is wrong.
statements.explanation: Popper.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's opening scenario, in which the same question put to Claude twice produces two different answers.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude can write a fluent, confident account of why the answers differed, and that account may even be right.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the account "may even be right."

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two different answers show that a difference has been observed, but not yet that its cause has been isolated.
statements.explanation: "You have observed a difference. You have not yet isolated its cause."

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The prompt was vague," "the model was creative," and "the system was unreliable" are explanations that each identify the moving part.
statements.explanation: None of those descriptions identifies the moving part.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude cannot know which moving part you needed to isolate.
statements.explanation: Knowing what you needed isolated is on the human side of the division of labor.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can check its own account against the machinery and put its name on the result.
statements.explanation: It cannot check its account against the machinery or sign the result.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's argument in brief.

statements.label: A
statements.text: One of the three jobs is to out-produce Claude at generating plausible candidates.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to compete with Claude on candidates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude has a stake in whether its output is true.
statements.explanation: It "has no stake in whether any of it is true."

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can tell you whether its output is the thing you needed.
statements.explanation: It has no way to tell you whether the output is what you needed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The three jobs that stay with you are conduct, check, and drive.
statements.explanation: Decide before it runs (conduct), check what comes back (check), sign what you keep (drive).

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude is far better than you at producing fluent text, working code, and long lists of plausible candidates, so the chapter says not to compete with it there.
statements.explanation: Speed and volume are Claude's strength; the chapter says not to compete there.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the distinction that both parts of the chapter serve.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A score is not a probability.
statements.explanation: Scores are not yet probabilities; they must be transformed first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A probability is not an observed frequency.
statements.explanation: Assigned chance and appearing share are different quantities.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making a run repeatable makes its answer true.
statements.explanation: Repeatability does not make an answer true.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making one outcome increasingly likely adds evidence that it is correct.
statements.explanation: The chapter says an outcome can be made more likely "without adding any evidence that it is correct."

statements.label: E
statements.text: An observed frequency is not a correctness judgment.
statements.explanation: A count of selections says nothing about correctness.

questions.source: Opening (before "What you will be able to do")
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the chapter's Part 2 experiment is set up.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Part 2 shrinks the machine to three outcomes and three numbers so that every intermediate value can be inspected.
statements.explanation: Nowhere for an unexplained operation to hide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter's Python experiment needs an API key.
statements.explanation: It needs no API key.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The toy reproduces Claude closely enough to stand in for it.
statements.explanation: "The toy will not reproduce Claude, and that is its advantage."

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter's Python experiment spends direct API credits.
statements.explanation: It spends no direct API credits.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Public readers are told to begin with the university's Claude portal.
statements.explanation: Enrolled Northeastern students use the portal; public readers need their own Claude Code-enabled account.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the table of the three jobs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Conduct comes from the companion book Computational Skepticism for AI.
statements.explanation: Conduct pairs with Conducting AI.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Check has the driver's seat as its device.
statements.explanation: Check's device is the sign-off; the driver's seat belongs to Drive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Drive comes from the companion book Irreducibly Human.
statements.explanation: Drive pairs with Irreducibly Human.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Check comes from the companion book Conducting AI.
statements.explanation: Check pairs with Computational Skepticism for AI.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Conduct adds the question "What did I decide before Claude started, and what must be true before this output goes downstream?" and its device is the gate.
statements.explanation: Conduct maps to the gate.

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Conduct job.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A gate is a general preference about quality that does not need to be testable.
statements.explanation: A gate is "a specific, testable condition that must hold before an output moves on."

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Conducting AI the human's job is "not to type less" but "to decide more precisely."
statements.explanation: This is the quoted formulation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude implements well from a complete specification and badly from an incomplete one.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: As used here, a gate is a few lines written after Claude has produced code, describing what the code happens to do.
statements.explanation: A gate is written before asking Claude for anything.

statements.label: E

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours

questions.source: Three jobs that stay yours

questions.source: The unfinished script

questions.source: One question, asked over and over

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

questions.source: One question, asked over and over
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what happens inside a prediction step.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

questions.source: Where the numbers come from

statements.label: B

questions.source: Inside one prediction step
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the transformer and the two jobs inside a prediction step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A feed-forward network takes each token's context-informed vector and moves it toward scores for the next token.

statements.label: B

statements.explanation: Both are fitted together by the single next-token objective.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Self-attention is the learned part that gives each token its context.
statements.explanation: Attention decides which other tokens to read from.

statements.explanation: Parallelism is the relevant property here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Someone wrote down what attention should look for.
statements.explanation: Those weights came out of the fit, like every other parameter.

questions.source: Inside one prediction step
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's caution on Figure 1.4a ("Two learned parts on one stream").

statements.text: PaLM uses what its authors call parallel layers.

statements.label: B

statements.explanation: Read it as two learned components sharing one stream, not simultaneous computation.

statements.explanation: Each sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection, so its output is added to its input.

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about queries, keys, and values.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The token's new vector is the weighted mix of the keys.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every token produces a query, a key, and a value.
statements.explanation: This is the paper's formulation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dividing by the square root of the key length keeps the scores from growing so large that the softmax saturates.
statements.explanation: That is the role of the scaling term.

statements.label: D

statements.label: E

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the `bank` attention table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The weights in the table were measured from a real model.

statements.label: B

statements.explanation: Highlighted weight in the first row.

statements.explanation: Highlighted weight in the second row.

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three precise points the chapter makes on attention.

statements.text: What is learned is the set of projections that produce queries, keys, and values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The attention weights in the table are stored in the model.

statements.label: C

statements.explanation: The masking applies in the decoder, not the encoder.

statements.label: D

questions.source: Self-attention: each token chooses what to read from
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about direct access in attention and what an attention weight shows.

statements.label: A

statements.explanation: A weight shows where one head read, not why the model answered.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Direct access is what let the paper's model do without recurrence and convolution.
statements.explanation: The chapter cites the paper (section 3.5).

statements.label: C
statements.text: A heat map of attention is a hypothesis to test, not an explanation.
statements.explanation: The chapter's warning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The first token and the hundredth are one comparison apart.

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: Distance does not weaken the link in the same way.

questions.source: The feed-forward network: an ordinary neural network
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the feed-forward network.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is applied to each token's vector separately and identically.
statements.explanation: It is position-wise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In the paper's base model, the vector has 512 numbers and the hidden layer has 2,048.
statements.explanation: Those are the base-model sizes given.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ReLU sets every positive value to zero.
statements.explanation: It sets every negative value to zero.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It lets tokens exchange information with each other.
statements.explanation: Attention already did that; this layer never lets tokens talk.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It is two linear transformations with a ReLU between them.
statements.explanation: FFN(x) = max(0, xW1 + b1)W2 + b2.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's toy feed-forward example.

statements.label: A

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about putting the pieces together.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The vector for `bank` after `river` ends up somewhere different from the vector for `bank` after `savings`.

questions.source: Stochastic parrots
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the stochastic parrot argument.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter settles the dispute in favor of the critics.

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: That is the conceptual half; the empirical half concerns consequences such as training costs, unauditable corpora, and unearned trust.

statements.text: Critics cite probing work suggesting that internal representations track non-linguistic structure.
statements.explanation: The critics' evidence.

statements.explanation: "These are my choices; no model produced them."

statements.label: C
statements.text: A failure sentence written after reading the output describes the output rather than testing your understanding.

statements.label: D

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: Those are the stated choices.

questions.source: The gate: write the experiment before you run it
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the contract in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal scores get equal probabilities.
statements.explanation: The contract says equal scores get equal probabilities.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The function accepts a temperature of zero.
statements.explanation: The function refuses an empty list, a nonfinite score, and a zero, negative, or nonfinite temperature.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sampling with the same seed repeats.
statements.explanation: The contract ends with: sampling with the same seed repeats.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A larger score never gets a smaller probability at positive temperature.
statements.explanation: Ordering is preserved.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one.
statements.explanation: The contract begins: probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one.

questions.source: The gate: write the experiment before you run it
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong versions your tests must catch and about Claude's role in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If your tests cannot tell the wrong versions from the right program, the gate is nonetheless finished.
statements.explanation: If your tests cannot tell the wrong versions from the right program, "the gate is not finished."

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude can write the gate for you without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: The gate is where your understanding goes on the record.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If you pair the probabilities with the wrong labels, the sum is still one.
statements.explanation: A sum check alone does not catch mislabeled probabilities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can sharpen the gate.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you reinitialize the generator on every draw, one repeatability test might still pass.
statements.explanation: A fresh generator each draw can still repeat.

questions.source: Three scores are not yet three chances
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why [1, 2, 3] is not yet three chances.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The list expresses an ordering in which the third entry is largest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dividing scores by their sum would fail on negative scores.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The scores sum to six.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Dividing each score by six is the transformation implemented in the lesson.
statements.explanation: That would be a different transformation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The list already expresses chances.
statements.explanation: "It does not yet express chances."

questions.source: Three scores are not yet three chances
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the softmax formula and what it guarantees.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing a positive temperature can make a smaller score the largest probability.
statements.explanation: It changes concentration but cannot do that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The probability of outcome i is the exponential of z_i divided by T, divided by the sum of the same quantity over all outcomes.
statements.explanation: This is the displayed formula.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For positive T, the ordering of the scores survives the transformation.
statements.explanation: Dividing by T and exponentiating preserve order; the total is shared.

statements.label: D

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probabilities summing to one shows that the inputs were sensible and the outcome labels true.
statements.explanation: It is a statement about the transformation, not about the inputs or labels.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the shifted scores for [1, 2, 3] at temperature one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The weights are approximately 0.135335, 0.367879, and 1.

statements.text: The weights sum to approximately 1.503215.

statements.label: E

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why subtracting the maximum is allowed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test file proves that every numeric input is handled.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The large shared offset carries information about relative preference.

statements.label: C

statements.label: D

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: "The computer does not need large intermediate exponentials to express a ratio."

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the input checks and the sum check.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker

statements.label: B
statements.text: A larger T brings the ratio closer to one.

statements.label: D

statements.label: E
statements.text: Temperature changes the ordering of the outcomes.
statements.explanation: The transformation changes relative concentration, not ordering.

statements.text: At T = 0.5, outcome 2 receives about 0.867.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see

statements.label: B

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up

questions.source: Opening section (untitled introduction)

statements.explanation: They need no direct API credits.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running the validator and the constructed response set requires direct API credits.
statements.explanation: They run offline with no credits.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the contract you should be able to write before any prompt is tried.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It includes the evidence criterion you will apply.
statements.explanation: The criterion is fixed up front.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It states what the consuming program refuses.
statements.explanation: The refusals are part of the contract.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is written after the prompt has been tuned, so that it matches the output you observed.
statements.explanation: A contract written after tuning just describes the output.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It includes an evaluation set split into development and held-out cases.
statements.explanation: The split is part of the contract.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It states the object the consuming program accepts.
statements.explanation: The object is the first element.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the contract comes before the prompt.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When a specification is incomplete, Claude can be relied on to flag the gap.
statements.explanation: It may quietly fill the gap with something plausible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you write the prompt first and tune until the output looks right, the contract becomes whatever the output happened to look like.
statements.explanation: The criterion then follows the output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude implements well against a complete specification.
statements.explanation: Completeness is what makes it work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The prompt should be written first and the contract derived from it.
statements.explanation: The prompt is derived from the contract.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After prompt-first tuning, every later pass rate measures agreement with your own habituation.
statements.explanation: The criterion drifted to match the output.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the consumer's needs in the teaching contract.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A response containing answer, sources, and confidence fails the validator even if all three values look reasonable.
statements.explanation: Extra keys are rejected.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The consumer needs a nonblank answer.
statements.explanation: One of the stated needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The consumer accepts a response whose sources list is empty, if the answer is nonblank.
statements.explanation: It needs at least one source identifier.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The contract accepts the two required keys plus arbitrary extra keys.
statements.explanation: It accepts exactly two keys.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The consumer needs the source identifiers to belong to a supplied set.
statements.explanation: One of the stated needs.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the exact-keys rule.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A consumer that assumes a fixed shape finds the rule protective, because unexpected additions become visible instead of silently ignored.
statements.explanation: Visibility is the benefit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You should choose the contract for your consumer, not because a short teaching function happened to choose one.
statements.explanation: The consumer decides.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether to allow extra keys is a trade-off between strict predictability and accepting some useful objects.
statements.explanation: The chapter frames the choice as that trade-off.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The rule is plainly correct no matter what the downstream job is.
statements.explanation: You cannot call it good or bad without naming the downstream job.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An exploratory analysis that wants extensible metadata may find the same rule an obstacle.
statements.explanation: The same rule can be a cost.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about requests versus checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding "always obey the schema" to a prompt is equivalent to checking the schema after the response arrives.
statements.explanation: The two are not equivalent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter's contrast between requests and checks is unrelated to Chapter 1's point about the system prompt.
statements.explanation: It is the same point one level up.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The prompt requests behavior from the producer, while the validator checks the returned object against executable conditions.
statements.explanation: Request versus check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A request can be ignored or misunderstood, whereas the local check has a definite acceptance rule.
statements.explanation: Only the check is definite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A prompt that asks for a schema guarantees that the returned object satisfies it.
statements.explanation: A request can be ignored or misunderstood.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Consider the constructed response {"answer":"The sources do not say.","sources":["s1"]}. Check each statement that is true about it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference contract includes a field for insufficient evidence.
statements.explanation: It has no such field.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding a status field to the object would solve the problem within the current validator.
statements.explanation: The validator rejects the extra key.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reference validator accepts it.
statements.explanation: It is a nonblank answer with a known source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing "be accurate" in the prompt supplies a refusal state.
statements.explanation: It does not supply one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The validator accepts it because it recognizes the answer as an honest refusal.
statements.explanation: It cannot tell a refusal from an assertion.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what happens when a finding reopens an earlier design decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether a refusal is an acceptable answer is a decision about the interface.
statements.explanation: The chapter frames it as an interface decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out case that guided the redesign stays held-out.
statements.explanation: Any case that guided the redesign counts as development evidence from then on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The record should include a new contract version and new tests.
statements.explanation: Both are named in the chapter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If you redesign the contract, you should record the redesign and test it as a different version.
statements.explanation: A new version needs its own tests.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A finding like the refusal limit can reopen an earlier decision without making the design waterfall.
statements.explanation: The chapter says none of this makes the design waterfall.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the evaluation set in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The held-out list is not shown to Claude and is not used to revise the prompt until the revision is frozen.
statements.explanation: The list is sealed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate specifies five development questions and five held-out questions.
statements.explanation: The sizes are stated in the gate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The held-out list may be listed and dated after the responses are inspected, since it is sealed anyway.
statements.explanation: Both lists are dated before any response is inspected.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The held-out list may be shown to Claude while drafting, as long as the final prompt is unchanged.
statements.explanation: It is sealed until the revision is frozen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The evaluation set is what defines what "supported" means for each question.
statements.explanation: The evidence criterion does that.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the evidence criterion in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For each question, the criterion gives one sentence saying what "supported" means for it.
statements.explanation: That is the criterion's content.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Computational Skepticism for AI suggests recording pass or fail, with unknown folded into fail.
statements.explanation: It records pass, fail, or unknown against a criterion fixed before you read the output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Supported and contradicted are the only two outcomes the criterion needs.
statements.explanation: A third outcome is recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Cannot be reviewed" is recorded as a third outcome beside supported and contradicted.
statements.explanation: Three outcomes are recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The criterion is best written after you know which prompt wins, so that it reflects the winning prompt's strengths.
statements.explanation: Write it before you know which prompt wins.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong versions the gate says your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A validator that accepts a source list when any entry is known, where the contract says every entry, is a wrong version your tests must catch.
statements.explanation: One of the three named.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The well-formed but wrong color-fixture response is one that your validator tests will catch.
statements.explanation: No validator test will catch it; your evidence column must.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A validator that checks only that the keys exist is one of the wrong versions the gate says your tests must catch.
statements.explanation: One of the three named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The color-fixture response must be caught by your evidence column, not by a validator test.
statements.explanation: It is well formed and wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A validator that skips the nonblank check is a wrong version your tests must catch.
statements.explanation: One of the three named.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about failure sentences, the pass condition, and what the experiment may claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you cannot write the failure sentence for a held-out question, you may proceed because the validator will catch the problem.
statements.explanation: Then you do not yet know what you are checking for.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate is finished when the validator accepts or rejects each of the three fixture responses as predicted.
statements.explanation: It needs a named test for every contract line that fails if the line is deleted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For each held-out question, the gate asks for one sentence describing an answer that would pass the validator and fail the evidence criterion.
statements.explanation: That is the failure sentence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The experiment may claim that any answer the validator accepted is correct.
statements.explanation: It cannot say any answer is correct beyond the reviewed claims.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the failure sentence after seeing the responses is equivalent, since it still describes a failure.
statements.explanation: Afterward you have described the output, not tested your understanding.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the order of checks in validate().

statements.label: A
statements.text: A successfully parsed value is automatically the kind of value the contract wants.
statements.explanation: The dictionary check comes next for that reason.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After parsing, the field values are checked first and the exact key set last.
statements.explanation: The order is dictionary check, exact key set, then field values.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For "not json", the key-set check runs and fails.
statements.explanation: None of the dictionary-field checks runs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: json.loads runs first and can fail before any field rule is relevant.
statements.explanation: Parsing is first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The string "not json" is rejected at the parsing step.
statements.explanation: The exception path returns False.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the answer and sources checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A whitespace-only answer passes the nonblank check because it is still a string.
statements.explanation: strip() removes surrounding whitespace, so it fails.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sources field may be a bare string such as "s1" instead of a list.
statements.explanation: It must be a list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The answer field may hold any JSON value, provided the key set is exactly right.
statements.explanation: The answer must be a string.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The integer 1 fails as an answer even though a human could display it as text.
statements.explanation: The function does not coerce.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sources list may contain a non-string entry as long as at least one entry is a known identifier.
statements.explanation: Every entry must be a string in the allowed set.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how validate() treats the sources list.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The expression computes the fraction of acceptable references and accepts when most are known.
statements.explanation: It does not compute a fraction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One valid identifier cannot compensate for another invalid entry.
statements.explanation: The word "every" matters.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Every entry in sources must be a string.
statements.explanation: The check includes isinstance for each entry.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With allowed identifiers {"s1"}, a sources list of ["s1", "missing"] is rejected.
statements.explanation: One invalid entry sinks the list.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The nonempty requirement is a condition separate from the requirement that every entry belongs to the allowed set.
statements.explanation: Deleting the nonempty check is a separate edit.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Boolean return value of validate().

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Boolean is convenient for a pass rate and easy to test.
statements.explanation: That is the upside.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reference collapses every rejection into False.
statements.explanation: This is an intentional simplification.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Boolean tells a reviewer how to repair a response.
statements.explanation: It tells the reviewer nothing about repair.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A richer result naming the parse failure, key mismatch, wrong type, or unknown source is behavior the reference already has.
statements.explanation: It is an extension to your own version.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The absence of a message is not the absence of a reason.
statements.explanation: For each failing fixture you stop at the first relevant boundary and name it.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the six lesson tests.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The six lesson tests include a test of the empty-experiment rule in the rate function.
statements.explanation: The sixth test covers it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: They exercise a valid object, invalid JSON, a wrong-typed answer, an unknown source, an extra key, and the empty-experiment rule.
statements.explanation: That is the stated list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You are asked to predict the result before editing a scratch copy and rerunning the tests.
statements.explanation: Predict, then check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The tests pass" means every promised behavior of the function is defended.
statements.explanation: Tests pass for the behaviors they exercise.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Each test is evidence for one behavior, not for the function as a whole.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three behaviors the chapter says the six lesson tests never defend.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing all to any leaves all six tests passing.
statements.explanation: The every-entry rule is undefended.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deleting the nonempty-source check leaves all six tests passing.
statements.explanation: The nonempty rule is undefended.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The extra-key rule is one of the three behaviors the lesson's tests never defend.
statements.explanation: One of the six tests exercises an extra key.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Deleting the nonblank check leaves all six tests passing.
statements.explanation: The nonblank rule is undefended.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rejection of invalid JSON is one of the three behaviors the lesson's tests never defend.
statements.explanation: One of the six tests exercises invalid JSON.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what validate() receives and can decide.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The validator receives the allowed identifier set, not the source sentence.
statements.explanation: It gets {"s1"}, not the text.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If someone says validate() verifies source support, you can point them to the final all(...) condition as the comparison of source content with answer content.
statements.explanation: That condition checks identifier membership, not content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One of the compact lines of validate() compares the source content with the answer content.
statements.explanation: The source_ids argument supplies identifiers, not passages.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The validator can decide whether the words attached to s1 support the answer.
statements.explanation: It cannot, since it lacks the words.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The validator can reject an invented address such as missing.
statements.explanation: Membership is checkable.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about membership and support.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A known citation entails support for the claim attached to it.
statements.explanation: Figure 2.1's point is that it does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Membership in a registry and support for a proposition are different relations.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An address is useless once the accompanying summary misstates its source.
statements.explanation: It still gives the reviewer somewhere to look.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing the source-existence question also answers the support question.
statements.explanation: It makes the support question possible; it does not answer it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An address can point to a real document while the accompanying summary misstates it.
statements.explanation: The address stays useful as somewhere to look.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the accepted red response {"answer":"The fixture says red","sources":["s1"]}.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The red response's acceptance exposes an exotic model behavior.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the failure is not hidden in an exotic model behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: To explain why the red response passes, we have to speculate about model internals.
statements.explanation: We can trace it to the missing check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The red response satisfies every implemented condition.
statements.explanation: Keys, answer, sources, and membership all pass.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The red response's acceptance shows that the validator is broken.
statements.explanation: The validator enforces its stated contract.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fact that the source sentence says blue enters the calculation.
statements.explanation: It does not enter the calculation.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who answers the support question.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Asking for a brief explanation with cited evidence makes an answer easier to inspect.
statements.explanation: The explanation is still output to evaluate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You should request hidden chain-of-thought so you can read the model's real reasoning.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to request it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An articulate rationale is access to an authenticated internal process.
statements.explanation: Do not treat it as one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the generator is also the only reviewer of its support, you have the first opinion run twice.
statements.explanation: That is not independent review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can be asked to set the claim and the source sentence side by side.
statements.explanation: For this small case you can verify the comparison at a glance.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the three responses are decided by validate().

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the second response, parsing and shape checks succeed, but missing is not in the supplied identifier set.
statements.explanation: It returns False at membership.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For "not json", parsing fails and the exception path returns False.
statements.explanation: The first response.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The observed acceptance sequence in the saved execution is false, true, false.
statements.explanation: It is false, false, true.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For the third response, all implemented checks succeed and the result is True.
statements.explanation: The color fixture.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For "not json", none of the dictionary-field checks runs.
statements.explanation: Parsing failed first.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the pass_rate function and its result for the fixture.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function knows how the responses were selected.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each accepted response contributes one and each rejected response contributes zero.
statements.explanation: It sums the Boolean decisions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The numerator is 2, because two of the three responses parse as JSON.
statements.explanation: Only one response is accepted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The denominator is the number of supplied responses.
statements.explanation: It divides by len(responses).

statements.label: E
statements.text: The result is 1/3, saved in the JSON as 0.3333333333333333.
statements.explanation: One acceptance among three.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the one-third result describes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result describes the share of the answers that are factually correct.
statements.explanation: It is a format rate, not accuracy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The three cases are a random sample of Claude's production behavior.
statements.explanation: They are not a random sample.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The three cases were constructed to expose three boundaries.
statements.explanation: They are test cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The one-third result estimates how often a real service will make these mistakes.
statements.explanation: It estimates nothing about a real service.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model was called to generate the three cases.
statements.explanation: They are constructed strings; no model was called.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about pass_rate on an empty list of responses.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Returning zero could be mistaken for a tested system that failed every case.
statements.explanation: Zero looks like a result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The error is a bug the chapter recommends replacing with a return value of zero.
statements.explanation: The refusal is a design choice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reference refuses to assign a pass rate to an experiment with no denominator.
statements.explanation: There is nothing to divide by.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The function raises an error.
statements.explanation: It raises ValueError.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Returning one could be mistaken for perfect performance.
statements.explanation: One looks like a result.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's table comparing validate() with the support review.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the missing-identifier response, the support review is "cannot be reviewed" because the cited address resolves to nothing.
statements.explanation: No source to read.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A validate() result of True beside a review result of contradicted is the expected report for the third row.
statements.explanation: It is not an inconsistent report.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For the red response, the support review is "contradicted" by s1, "The color is blue."
statements.explanation: The source says blue.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The missing-identifier response fails at parsing.
statements.explanation: It parses and is shaped correctly; it fails source membership.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For "not json", the support review is "cannot be reviewed" because there is no claim to compare.
statements.explanation: No claim to review.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the fluency trap and the cost of checking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fluency trap is that the more fluently an output presents, the more confident you become in it and then in your own evaluation of it.
statements.explanation: The chapter's definition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Form and content are linked, so a more fluent output is more likely to be correct.
statements.explanation: They are independent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If verification is not budgeted, it still happens informally.
statements.explanation: If it is not budgeted it does not happen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Form and content are independent.
statements.explanation: Fluent form says little about content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The support review is the cheap check and the validator is the expensive one.
statements.explanation: The validator is the cheap check.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the classroom comparison of a baseline prompt and a revision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ten questions establish broad reliability.
statements.explanation: They define a manageable classroom experiment only.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Five additional questions are held out.
statements.explanation: The held-out set is reserved.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Without a fixed evaluation set, "better" is a feeling.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The lesson compares a baseline prompt and a few-shot revision on five development questions.
statements.explanation: Five dev questions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A fixed evaluation set is what makes an improvement measurable.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about treating a revision as a hypothesis.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hypothesizing that examples will help the output shape is a testable proposal.
statements.explanation: It is a proposal, not a result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A controlled comparison requires pretending the rest of the world is fixed.
statements.explanation: It requires recording what you changed and limiting the explanation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You should predict a specific failure that the revision might address.
statements.explanation: State the target failure first.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding examples counts as an improvement because it sounds like established practice.
statements.explanation: That is a proposal, not a result.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you change examples, task, source material, persona, and questions at once, any observed difference becomes hard to attribute.
statements.explanation: Change something you can describe.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about development and held-out questions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you need another untouched check, you can relabel the old held-out set as independent.
statements.explanation: Design a new evaluation instead.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out case that guided a choice is a moral failing that voids the experiment.
statements.explanation: It is bookkeeping.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Showing only the final success is enough, since development failures can be discarded.
statements.explanation: Preserve the failures too.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once a held-out case has guided a choice, it is development evidence.
statements.explanation: Its role has changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Development questions are available while you revise.
statements.explanation: They guide revision.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about personas.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A persona is a hypothesis to test.
statements.explanation: It is not a certificate of support.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "You are an expert" changes none of the validator's checks.
statements.explanation: The checks are fixed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a persona helps on your cases, the role label can certify the answer before the evidence review.
statements.explanation: Describe the observed difference and its conditions instead.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a persona helps on your cases, you should describe the observed difference and the conditions.
statements.explanation: Describe the difference; do not let the label certify the answer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "You are an expert" adds a supporting passage to the source collection.
statements.explanation: It adds none.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about running the experiment with Claude Code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you have not run the comparison, your artifact should say proposed experiment.
statements.explanation: Honest labeling.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keep the proposed prompt, the actual returned text, the executable acceptance result, and your evidence judgment visibly separate.
statements.explanation: Four things.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude Code can organize the experiment, run your local validator, draft candidate prompts, and challenge your interpretation.
statements.explanation: Its stated role.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The actual returned text can be folded into the proposed prompt in the record.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the pass rate compresses or ignores.

statements.label: B

statements.label: B

statements.explanation: In a chat window they arrive as one voice saying done.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One job is proposing the next action.
statements.explanation: Proposing is the first job.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One job is deciding whether the final result is any good.
statements.explanation: Judging the result is the third job.

statements.label: E
