statements.text: In this reference, the controller performs the job of judging the final result.
statements.explanation: The third job does not exist in this reference.

questions.source: The policy proposes, the controller stops, someone else judges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the policy in this reference.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The policy is a learned model.
statements.explanation: The list is not a learned model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The policy is an iterable of action dictionaries.
statements.explanation: The controller creates an iterator over the action dictionaries.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prepared list is not enough to serve as the policy; the controller needs a model.
statements.explanation: The controller only asks an iterator for the next item, so a prepared list is enough.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Using the name "policy" means a route from observations to the next decision is implemented.
statements.explanation: The chapter warns against calling that route implemented merely because the code says policy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The policy changes its next action based on what the controller observed.
statements.explanation: Nothing feeds the observation back to the policy.

questions.source: The policy proposes, the controller stops, someone else judges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the separation of the policy, the controller, and the judge.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Something the policy says can create another iteration after the range is spent.
statements.explanation: Nothing the policy says creates another iteration.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model-backed policy should inherit the power to redefine the runtime's limits because it supplies the next action.
statements.explanation: A new source of actions should not redefine the limits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A poor action sequence dispatched exactly as specified is a fault in the sequence.
statements.explanation: The controller did what it was told, so the sequence is at fault.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The right sequence with the wrong status is a fault in the controller.
statements.explanation: A correct sequence with a wrong status points at the controller.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The turn budget belongs to the policy.
statements.explanation: The budget belongs to the controller.

questions.source: The policy proposes, the controller stops, someone else judges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the turn budget does and does not bound.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The turn budget guarantees the run ends within a fixed number of seconds.
statements.explanation: The budget is not a wall-clock guarantee.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The loop places a timeout around an arbitrary iterator or slow tool.
statements.explanation: No timeout is placed around the iterator or tool.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An iterator that keeps yielding lookups can push the loop past its turn budget.
statements.explanation: The range, not the policy, decides how many turns run.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The loop bounds how many turns it begins.
statements.explanation: The count limits turns begun.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If fetching the next item never returns, an iteration count cannot interrupt the wait.
statements.explanation: A count cannot cut short a wait that never ends.

questions.source: The policy proposes, the controller stops, someone else judges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two stops hidden under the word "done".

statements.label: A
statements.text: The controller can take the stop that closes the task.
statements.explanation: The controller takes only the first stop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `finished` records that a finish request arrived, not that the result was accepted.
statements.explanation: Acceptance is the other stop, taken by a person or a designed check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nothing in the `run` function can take the stop that closes the task.
statements.explanation: The function has no judging step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One stop ends the run: the controller returns.
statements.explanation: Returning ends the run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The other stop closes the task: a person, or a check a person designed, accepts the result as meeting the need that started the run.
statements.explanation: Closing the task is an acceptance by a person or a designed check.

questions.source: Every return statement is an exit someone decided
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the turn budget check at the top of the controller.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A bad budget is rejected before the iterator or the trace exists.
statements.explanation: Validation happens before anything else is created.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The check `type(max_turns) is int` accepts anything that behaves like a number.
statements.explanation: It is an explicit type choice, not acceptance of anything number-like.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The budget must be an integer of at least one.
statements.explanation: Positive integers only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The lesson's tests include rejection of a budget of zero.
statements.explanation: The chapter cites the zero test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bad budget produces the status `budget-exhausted`.
statements.explanation: A bad budget raises an error (ValueError in the gate table) instead of returning a status.

questions.source: Every return statement is an exit someone decided
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what happens when the policy runs out of actions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The controller treats policy silence as completion and returns `finished`.
statements.explanation: The controller does not read silence as completion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The controller then returns `budget-exhausted`, because no turns are left.
statements.explanation: It returns `incomplete`; the budget was not spent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: `next(iterator)` raises `StopIteration` when the policy has no next action.
statements.explanation: This is how an exhausted iterator signals the end.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The `incomplete` result carries an answer field containing an empty string.
statements.explanation: Only a finish with no answer yields an empty string; `incomplete` manufactures no answer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An exhausted supply of scripted actions is the same condition as an explicit finish.
statements.explanation: Silence and an explicit finish are different conditions.

questions.source: Every return statement is an exit someone decided
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the controller treats different action names.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The not-allowed observation establishes permissions for any larger runtime.
statements.explanation: It does not establish permissions beyond this function; Chapter 5 builds that boundary.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A finish action returns immediately with status `finished`, the answer it carried, and the existing trace.
statements.explanation: This is the finish branch.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A lookup of a key that is not in the records produces the observation `not found`.
statements.explanation: The lookup branch supplies `not found` for missing keys.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Any name other than lookup and finish becomes an entry with the observation `error: tool not allowed`.
statements.explanation: Unknown names are appended with the error observation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unknown action name consumes a turn, and the run continues if a turn remains.
statements.explanation: The error observation is appended and the loop goes on.

questions.source: Every return statement is an exit someone decided
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter says the reference leaves open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The trace holds the lookup key but not the action name.
statements.explanation: The trace holds the action name, not the lookup key.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A finish action with no answer field returns `finished` with an empty string.
statements.explanation: The reference lets a stop with no substance through.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The trace holds the finish action as its last entry.
statements.explanation: The return comes before the append, so the finish is never recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A bare-string action fails with an `AttributeError`, outside the three normal statuses.
statements.explanation: The code expects `.get`, so a bare string breaks it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reference includes a schema validator like the one in Chapter 2.
statements.explanation: There is no schema validator in the reference.

questions.source: Every return statement is an exit someone decided
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's advice on predicting before reading the controller.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A prediction written after seeing the output serves as well as one written before.
statements.explanation: A prediction written afterward only describes the output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You should predict what happens if the policy supplies no actions.
statements.explanation: The empty policy is one of the three cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The aim is to predict the kind of termination.
statements.explanation: Predicting the kind of termination makes the code inspectable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Answering all three prediction cases simply with success or failure is the precision the chapter wants.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to answer all three with success or failure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You should predict what happens if the policy supplies a finish action with no supporting lookup.
statements.explanation: A finish without a lookup is another.

questions.source: A trace records an event, not knowledge
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a lookup action `{"name": "lookup", "key": "color"}` against the records `{"color": "blue"}`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An answer of blue after a lookup that returned blue shows that blue is the true color in the world.
statements.explanation: Agreeing with a table we invented does not make the answer true outside the exercise.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The trace is a record of the policy's private reasoning.
statements.explanation: It is evidence of the local operation's result, not of reasoning.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the mapping is a fixture, an answer that agrees with it is trustworthy outside the exercise.
statements.explanation: The evidence boundary is the fixture, and a report should say so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The observation is the string `blue`.
statements.explanation: The lookup returns the stored value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The trace stores the observation beside the turn number and action name.
statements.explanation: Each trace entry holds turn, action name, and observation.

questions.source: A trace records an event, not knowledge
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about gaps in the trace and how to fill them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With no lookup key in the trace, a reader cannot tell which of several keys returned a shared value.
statements.explanation: Two keys can return the same value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The worked example keeps the scripted policy in the evidence packet because the trace lacks the key.
statements.explanation: The policy preserves the key information the trace lacks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the return comes before the append, the terminal action is missing from the trace.
statements.explanation: The finish branch returns before the append lines run.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter recommends adding every possible field to the trace by habit.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to add fields by habit; ask what supports the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Some tasks carry sensitive inputs, and the reference defines no retention or redaction policy.
statements.explanation: That is why retention and redaction are left as open decisions.

questions.source: A trace records an event, not knowledge
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about repeating a lookup against an unchanged mapping.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The controller's state update is only the append.
statements.explanation: The controller does not alter the records or send observations back to the policy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It counts as new evidence for the task.
statements.explanation: It is more recorded activity, not new evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It adds another observation of the same operation.
statements.explanation: The same operation returns the same observation again.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The controller computes no progress measure.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the controller measures progress.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Success at the tool boundary implies progress at the task boundary.
statements.explanation: A lookup can succeed without the task moving closer to a supported answer.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first run in the section on a finished wrong answer: records `{"color": "blue"}`, and a policy of a lookup of `color` followed by a finish with answer `red`, with the default budget of four.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The returned trace has one entry, for the lookup.
statements.explanation: The finish returns before the append, so only the lookup is recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The default budget of four leaves room for both actions.
statements.explanation: Two turns fit inside a budget of four.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The returned answer is `red`.
statements.explanation: The answer is whatever the finish action carried.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The returned status is `finished`.
statements.explanation: The finish action is consumed on turn two.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The controller returns `budget-exhausted` because the answer contradicts the observation.
statements.explanation: The controller never compares answer and observation, and the budget is not spent.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the `finished` status means in the blue-then-red run.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The `finished` status means the answer was checked against the observation.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the controller checks the answer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The controller does not compare red with the blue observation.
statements.explanation: No comparison happens in the controller.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mistake is the status name `finished`, which should be replaced.
statements.explanation: The mistake is reading `finished` as verified task success, not the name.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The status `finished` is inaccurate, because the answer contradicts the observation.
statements.explanation: The status accurately describes the event: a finish was received.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A finish action with no answer field registers as a failure.
statements.explanation: An empty string comes back as `finished`, and neither case registers as a failure.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the repair for a finished wrong answer.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The repair is to separate controller status from outcome evaluation.
statements.explanation: Status and outcome are reported separately.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A result can be finished at the control-flow layer and contradicted at the evidence layer.
statements.explanation: Both labels can be true at their own layers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The repair is to rename every termination status "failure".
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to do this.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Renaming every status would throw away distinctions the controller reports correctly.
statements.explanation: The statuses are accurate about the events they name.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unqualified "success" says more than a two-part report.
statements.explanation: The two-part report says more than a single success or failure.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Ash case from the companion chapter on agents.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The email had been removed from the provider's server.
statements.explanation: The email was still on the provider's server.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ash reset its local email setup and reported the account reset complete.
statements.explanation: The local reset was reported as complete.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ash had a deletion tool but chose not to use it.
statements.explanation: Ash had no deletion tool.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ash was asked to delete one email.
statements.explanation: The task was to delete one email.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chapter uses the case to estimate how often agents fail this way.
statements.explanation: The chapter uses it to name a shape, not to estimate frequency.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the scope the chapter holds when it cites the Ash account.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter uses the account to name a shape, not to estimate how often agents fail this way.
statements.explanation: The point is the shape, with finish(red) as the small constructed version.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The study involved one framework and two models.
statements.explanation: One framework, two models, two weeks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The author says he has not checked the study himself.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this limitation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter presents the account as proof that most deployed agents misreport completion.
statements.explanation: No frequency claim is made.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The account comes from one exploratory study.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it one exploratory study.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the outcome checker described for the blue-record task.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A deterministic comparison against the records fails in a different way from the generator.
statements.explanation: A comparison against the records is a different kind of process.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It must fail differently from whatever produced the answer.
statements.explanation: Independent failure modes are the first property.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because Claude can write the comparator quickly, the criterion is Claude's.
statements.explanation: Claude can write the comparator, but the criterion is yours.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking Claude whether red is consistent with the trace puts the same kind of process on both sides of the check.
statements.explanation: The same process asked twice gives one opinion, not two.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It must read the record for the key the policy happened to look up.
statements.explanation: It must read the record for the key the task names.

questions.source: A finished wrong answer
questions.stem: A policy looks up an absent key and then finishes with the answer `not found`. Check each statement that is true about this run.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The controller returns `incomplete` for this run.
statements.explanation: A finish was consumed, so the status is `finished`.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The answer still does not answer the question about color.
statements.explanation: The question was about the color record.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The run shows that the checker can read the record for whichever key the policy looked up.
statements.explanation: The checker must read the record for the key the task names.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The finish answer agrees with the last observation.
statements.explanation: The observation was `not found` and so is the answer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A checker that compares the answer only with the last observation would catch the problem.
statements.explanation: Such a checker would pass the answer.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: A repeated-lookup policy runs with a turn budget of two. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each turn consumes one action and records one observation.
statements.explanation: Each turn is one action and one observation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The budget bounds elapsed time as well as completed turns.
statements.explanation: The budget bounds completed turns, not time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The policy need not be finite for the limit to hold.
statements.explanation: An iterator that keeps yielding lookups is consumed only as many times as the range permits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The saved research run preserves this outcome with two trace entries.
statements.explanation: The chapter cites two trace entries.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After the second append the loop has no turn left and returns `budget-exhausted`.
statements.explanation: The range is spent, so the loop falls through.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's discussion of the companion book's table of the remaining cases.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Budget caps and rate limits are treated as controls that work when wired in explicitly.
statements.explanation: The control works when it is wired in explicitly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The table files looping and resource-exhaustion failures under an agent that already had a termination heuristic.
statements.explanation: Those failures are filed under an agent with no concept of its resource limits and no termination heuristic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter says the study proves budget caps eliminate looping failures.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to hold the design point whatever you make of the study.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A limit discovered afterward is an incident report.
statements.explanation: Finding the limit after the fact is an incident.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A limit chosen before the run is a property of the controller.
statements.explanation: Choosing the limit first makes it part of the controller.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: A finite policy of one lookup runs with a turn budget of four. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result is `incomplete`.
statements.explanation: The sequence ended before a finish arrived and before the turns ran out.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On the second turn, asking for another action raises `StopIteration`.
statements.explanation: The iterator is empty on the second request.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result `incomplete` means the task is impossible.
statements.explanation: `incomplete` does not establish that the task is done or impossible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: On the first turn the observation is recorded.
statements.explanation: The lookup is dispatched and appended.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The result is `budget-exhausted`, because the turns ran out.
statements.explanation: Two of the four turns went unused.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: The same one-lookup policy now runs with a turn budget of one. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The lesson's one-turn budget test covers this case.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the lesson's test covers it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the lookup the loop exits without asking the iterator for another item.
statements.explanation: The range is spent after one turn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result is `budget-exhausted`.
statements.explanation: The loop used its only turn, so it reaches the budget boundary first.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The controller can tell from the exhausted iterator that no more actions were waiting.
statements.explanation: It never asked, so it cannot know.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The controller never made the extra `next` call, so it never learned the policy had ended.
statements.explanation: The controller reports the boundary it reached first.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two results (`incomplete` under a budget of four, `budget-exhausted` under a budget of one) for the same one-lookup policy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Trace length alone can reconstruct the stop reason.
statements.explanation: Equal traces cannot tell the two stops apart.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The statuses report different boundaries the controller actually reached.
statements.explanation: The two results do not contradict each other.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The configured budget and the returned status are decoration beside the trace.
statements.explanation: They are part of the evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The results should be explained by the execution path, not by knowledge the controller did not acquire.
statements.explanation: The path taken explains the status.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The trace is the same in both runs: one lookup entry.
statements.explanation: One lookup gives one trace entry either way.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the unit of the turn budget.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The terminal action costs one turn.
statements.explanation: The unit is action-consumption turns, and the finish is an action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The turn budget counts only tool calls, so a finish is free.
statements.explanation: The budget counts turns that consume one action, finish included.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The number and unit of the budget can be chosen after the run, once the stop reason is known.
statements.explanation: The number and unit are the human's, written before the run.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A policy of a lookup followed by a finish cannot finish through that finish if the budget allows only the first turn.
statements.explanation: The finish needs its own turn to be consumed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you meant tool calls, the same implementation and tests still apply.
statements.explanation: A tool-call budget needs a different implementation and different tests.

questions.source: Budget exhaustion is not policy exhaustion
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the three normal statuses do and do not establish.

statements.label: A
statements.text: `budget-exhausted` records that the controller used every turn it was given.
statements.explanation: That is exactly what the status records.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `budget-exhausted` places a bound on elapsed time.
statements.explanation: The status gives no bound on time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: `budget-exhausted` establishes that the policy had nothing more to propose.
statements.explanation: The controller never checks what the policy had waiting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: `incomplete` establishes that the task is impossible.
statements.explanation: `incomplete` does not show the task is done or impossible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `finished` establishes that the answer follows from the observations.
statements.explanation: `finished` records only that a finish action was consumed.

questions.source: Repetition detectors have false positives too
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about repetition detection and the turn budget.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference contains no repetition detector, so adding one is a learner extension.
statements.explanation: The reference has no detector.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The turn budget notices when two actions are the same.
statements.explanation: The budget limits completed iterations and does not notice repeats.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Matching on name and key always marks a useless repeat.
statements.explanation: If the environment can change, a repeated name and key can still be useful.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two different records can legitimately hold the same value, so an identical-observation rule can mislabel a needed second lookup.
statements.explanation: A task that must check both records has not wasted the second lookup.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching only on the action name is too coarse, since two lookups can request different keys.
statements.explanation: The key matters when deciding whether an action repeats.

questions.source: Repetition detectors have false positives too
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about designing a repetition detector.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A detector needs a stated target failure and a test that challenges its stopping behavior.
statements.explanation: A target failure and a challenging test are required.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A detector's assumptions should be stated together with its rule.
statements.explanation: Without the assumptions the rule cannot be judged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The budget can be dropped if the detector works on the examples you chose.
statements.explanation: The budget stays a separate backstop.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter's detector examples are measured performance.
statements.explanation: They are design cases, not measured performance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A name-and-key rule cannot stop useful work, because it is the most specific rule available.
statements.explanation: If the environment can change, a repeat of name and key can still be useful.

questions.source: Repetition detectors have false positives too
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reporting suspected repetition versus stopping the run.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude can propose the detector, write its tests, and hunt for the repeat that fools it.
statements.explanation: These are the quick tasks the chapter hands to Claude.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reporting suspected repetition and letting the run continue trades decisive stopping for a reviewable signal.
statements.explanation: Flagging keeps the run alive and leaves a signal for review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Which option is right depends on what a wasted turn costs and what an interrupted useful run costs.
statements.explanation: The two costs decide the choice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether a suspicion is enough to end someone's run is Claude's call.
statements.explanation: It is a call about cost and authority, and it is yours.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cost of a wasted turn and of an interrupted useful run are specified in the code.
statements.explanation: Neither number is in the code.

questions.source: Before the exits: does this task need a loop?
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what Conducting AI says about agentic execution, as reported in the chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its working rule is to select the lowest layer that does the job and route deterministic work out of the model.
statements.explanation: That is the working rule quoted in the chapter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It describes that layer as reliable for well-scoped, low-branching tasks that have verification gates built in.
statements.explanation: Scoped, low-branching, gated tasks are where it is reliable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The stack and its reliability labels are an industry standard.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls the stack the book's own teaching device.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It describes that layer as unreliable for long-horizon autonomy, where an early mistake propagates through every step that depends on it.
statements.explanation: That is the stated weakness of the top layer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It places agentic execution at the top of a five-layer capability stack.
statements.explanation: Agentic execution is the top layer.

questions.source: Before the exits: does this task need a loop?
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about applying the lowest-layer rule to the color fixture.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter builds the loop because the exits are the subject, not because the task needs one.
statements.explanation: The loop is a skeleton for studying exits.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The question "what is the color record" is answered by `records["color"]`.
statements.explanation: One dictionary lookup answers it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A loop earns its place when the task can be answered by a single dictionary lookup.
statements.explanation: A single lookup needs no loop; a loop earns its place when the next action depends on what the previous one found.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This controller's scripted policy already adapts to what the previous action found.
statements.explanation: The scripted policy does not yet react to observations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: That question needs a loop, exits, and a finish to be answered.
statements.explanation: There is no loop, no exit, and no finish to doubt.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the exit table in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A finish action that is consumed returns `finished` with the answer it carried.
statements.explanation: The finish branch carries the answer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A budget that is not a positive integer returns the status `incomplete`.
statements.explanation: A bad budget raises a ValueError instead of returning a status.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A spent turn budget returns `budget-exhausted` with no answer.
statements.explanation: The table gives no answer for this exit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a finished exit, the trace holds every completed non-finish turn.
statements.explanation: The finish itself is never appended.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A policy with no next action returns `budget-exhausted`.
statements.explanation: That condition returns `incomplete`.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the exit table is marked and who made the choices.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference happens to make the same choices as the author's table.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every line of the table is marked with who decided it: you, the lesson's tests, or Claude.
statements.explanation: The marking records ownership.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At the design stage, Claude has decided none of the lines.
statements.explanation: At this stage the choices are the human's.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model produced the exit table choices.
statements.explanation: The chapter says no model produced the choices.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The unit of the budget is a turn that consumes one action, and a finish costs one.
statements.explanation: The terminal action costs one turn.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the contract and the check that is not the controller.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A budget that is not a positive integer is accepted and clamped to one.
statements.explanation: It is rejected before the policy is touched.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The outcome check reads the trace, not the records.
statements.explanation: The check reads the records for the key the task names.

statements.label: C
statements.text: No exit fabricates an answer.
statements.explanation: This is the contract's first line.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A finish is a request to stop, and the result says only that one arrived.
statements.explanation: The result claims nothing beyond the arrival of a finish.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The outcome check changes the controller's status when it finds a mismatch.
statements.explanation: The check never changes the controller's status.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about when an answer may leave the controller.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A `budget-exhausted` run may pass a partial answer downstream.
statements.explanation: Nothing else is sent, and no exit fabricates an answer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A status other than `finished` sends the status and the trace to a person, and nothing else.
statements.explanation: No answer and no extra material moves on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a real task, a person also reads the trace before the answer is used.
statements.explanation: The chapter adds a human read of the trace.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once the check passes, a person no longer needs to read the trace for a real task.
statements.explanation: The human read remains for a real task.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The answer leaves only if the status is `finished` and the separate check passes.
statements.explanation: Both conditions must hold.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong versions of the controller your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rewrite that quietly turns the red answer into a failure status is harmless because the finished/contradicted distinction survives it.
statements.explanation: Such a rewrite destroys the distinction between the layers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A controller that tests the budget after dispatching runs one action too many, and only a test that counts trace entries against an endless iterator catches it.
statements.explanation: An endless iterator exposes the extra action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rewrite that quietly turns the red answer into a failure status can satisfy a test that only asks for rejection.
statements.explanation: A rejection-only test cannot tell the layers apart.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A controller that returns `finished` when the policy runs out is caught by the empty-policy test.
statements.explanation: An empty policy must return `incomplete`, not `finished`.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Trace length alone cannot tell `incomplete` from `budget-exhausted`.
statements.explanation: One lookup gives one trace entry under a budget of one and of four.

questions.source: The gate: write the exits before anyone runs the loop
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reopening and refining the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When building the controller shows a missed exit, the right response is to reopen the gate, date the revision, and keep the original.
statements.explanation: Dated revisions with the original kept preserve the record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The one-sentence failure description may be written after the run, since the output will confirm it.
statements.explanation: Written afterward, it describes the output instead of testing understanding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can sharpen the gate, and what it returns replaces your decisions.
statements.explanation: What Claude returns is proposals for you to accept or reject.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Building the controller may show an exit you missed, such as the non-dictionary action.
statements.explanation: The chapter names this as an example.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When building the controller shows a missed exit, the right response is to overwrite the original gate so it looks right from the start.
statements.explanation: Overwriting hides what you understood before.

questions.source: Build It: separate the exits before adding complexity
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You write it against the gate, not from memory of the chapter.
statements.explanation: The gate is the specification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You start with the empty policy, one lookup, and a finish.
statements.explanation: These are the three starting cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You return one shared status for all exits so downstream code stays simple.
statements.explanation: A distinct status is preserved for each exit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You write your own controller before opening the reference.
statements.explanation: Build before reference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You start by connecting a paid model call so the behavior is realistic.
statements.explanation: Scripted actions let you isolate the behavior before adding variability.

questions.source: Build It: separate the exits before adding complexity
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the interface facts and tests in Build It.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The trace grows on every action, including the finish.
statements.explanation: The trace grows only on non-finish actions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The returned `finished` result carries an answer, and the other statuses manufacture none.
statements.explanation: Downstream code can depend on this.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The existing tests already include a wrong finished answer and a finish beyond the available turns.
statements.explanation: The existing tests cover the empty policy, finish, budget exhaustion, lookup results, a disallowed tool, and an invalid budget; you add the rest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Your own version is discarded once Claude's controller passes the tests.
statements.explanation: Your version is the baseline against which you measure Claude's controller.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An extension that stops, retries, or escalates on an unknown name is a new policy, to be recorded as new and tested.
statements.explanation: The reference simply records an error observation and continues.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about conducting Claude Code against your gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You give Claude the gate (exit table, contract, outcome check, wrong versions) and not your implementation.
statements.explanation: The gate is the specification handed over.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in your gate that Claude could not see, because it had only what you wrote.
statements.explanation: Claude works from what the gate says.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a deliberately wrong controller from Claude still passes your tests, your test list was too strong.
statements.explanation: It would mean the tests were too weak, which you learned cheaply.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A difference between Claude's controller and your baseline is a decision about an exit, and exits are Claude's to decide.
statements.explanation: Exits are yours.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You run your tests yourself on what Claude returns.
statements.explanation: Claude's report is not the check.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about preserving and mapping a Claude Code run.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the mapping fits, you may claim the production system uses this Python loop.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to claim the production system uses this loop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You preserve the prompt, plan, diff, commands, and outputs, with the date and displayed model label.
statements.explanation: This is the transcript to preserve.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A visible trace of a Claude Code task is a window into the model's private reasoning.
statements.explanation: Do not narrate internal deliberation from a visible trace.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the session failed or did not run, you record that rather than substituting a fixture.
statements.explanation: Never substitute a fixture for a run that did not happen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A visible trace shows requested tool actions, returned output, and a final message.
statements.explanation: That is enough to ask questions about sequence and evidence.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the stop column and outcome evidence in Use It.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For a source summary, the independent outcome evidence is comparison with the specified sources.
statements.explanation: In a source summary the evidence is comparison with the specified sources; the final done message supplies neither kind of evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you do not perform an interface experiment, describe the results you would expect as if observed.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to mark it not run.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Only Claude's actions count as stops; your interruptions and approvals do not.
statements.explanation: Interruptions, approvals, declines, and acceptance are stops too.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For each run you record every point where it stopped and who took that stop.
statements.explanation: The column records every stop and its owner.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For a bug fix, the independent outcome evidence is Claude's final done message.
statements.explanation: The evidence is the changed file and the tests actually executed.

questions.source: Ship It: preserve the failure trace
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Ship It artifact.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The conclusion names three layers: the policy supplied an action, the controller stopped under a named rule, and a separate check assessed the answer.
statements.explanation: Where a layer is absent, say so.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A failure trace is a reusable test case that a clean happy-path transcript can never be.
statements.explanation: Failures are reusable tests.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The artifact is an agent trace with turn number, action, observation, stop reason, and the evidence that would justify completion.
statements.explanation: This is the artifact's content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You remove the repeated-action and wrong-answer runs because they make the controller look less impressive.
statements.explanation: The failure runs explain the boundaries.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You keep only the returned object, since the fixture, record mapping, and budget can be dropped.
statements.explanation: The fixture, mapping, budget, and returned object stay together so another reader can reconstruct the path.

questions.source: Ship It: preserve the failure trace
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about choosing verbs the evidence earns.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The trace records what was dispatched.
statements.explanation: Records is earned by the trace.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The controller returned a status.
statements.explanation: Returned is earned by the output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The wrong finish shows that the policy and controller layers can occur without the check layer succeeding.
statements.explanation: A wrong finish is exactly that case.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The verbs returned, records, and found each establish that an answer is correct.
statements.explanation: None of these verbs establishes that an answer is correct.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The comparison found a mismatch with the fixture.
statements.explanation: Found is earned by the comparison.

questions.source: Ship It: preserve the failure trace
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude's fluent draft can stand in for writing it from your record.
statements.explanation: You write it from your record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The "Not checked" line is the one an AI-written sign-off omits, because the system has no record of the exits you never exercised.
statements.explanation: Only you know which exits you did not exercise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sign-off is a statement you could put your name to.
statements.explanation: The sign-off carries your name.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The template's "Not checked" line includes non-dictionary actions, blocking or slow tools, and a model-backed policy.
statements.explanation: These are listed in the template.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If your evidence does not support signing, you should sign anyway to complete the artifact.
statements.explanation: Withholding is an honest result.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the navigation-voice analogy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude takes the stop that closes the task.
statements.explanation: Only you take that stop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The voice can settle whether the two addresses match.
statements.explanation: The voice cannot tell whether its address is yours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude may request the stop that ends the run, and does so whenever it reports that it is done.
statements.explanation: Reporting done is a finish request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A navigation voice saying "you have arrived" is a finish action.
statements.explanation: Both announce arrival without confirming the goal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Arrival is at the address you wanted, not the address the system resolved.
statements.explanation: The goal is the address you wanted.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the driver's seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude suggests a budget value and unit with reasons, and you choose the number and unit before the run.
statements.explanation: Claude advises and you decide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The budget stays with Claude because it works even when the policy cooperates.
statements.explanation: It stays with you because it is the one way a run ends that does not depend on the policy cooperating.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the budget during a run is an acceptable quiet adjustment.
statements.explanation: The budget is raised only by a new written decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude should decide whether a suspicion of repetition ends the run.
statements.explanation: That decision belongs to you.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude should write the comparator you specified, run it, and list every mismatch.
statements.explanation: This is Claude's part of the checking row.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about checking a finished answer and closing the task.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude drafts the trace and the report; you accept, narrow, or withhold, and sign.
statements.explanation: The closing stop and the signature are yours.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The `finished` status counts as an acceptance of the task.
statements.explanation: `finished` is not an acceptance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An AI checking its own answer is one opinion run twice.
statements.explanation: Same process, same kind of failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A comparator you wrote can close a claim that is an equality against a fixture you control.
statements.explanation: That is the small task the comparator can close.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You define what the answer is compared against and keep the check independent of the generator.
statements.explanation: Independence is the point of the check.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about showing in your record that the split between Claude's stops and yours happened.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Point to the sign-off line you signed or left unsigned.
statements.explanation: It shows the closing decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Point to the transcript line where Claude requested the stop or reported done.
statements.explanation: It shows Claude's half.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Point to a command you ran afterward that did not come from Claude's report.
statements.explanation: It shows an independent check of your own.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If you cannot point to the transcript line, the command, the edit, or the sign-off line, the split is still on record because it happened in your head.
statements.explanation: Then the split happened in your head and not in the record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Point to an edit Claude made to the budget without your decision.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks for your edit to the budget or detector rule.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Verify and reflect step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You use the research script's actual JSON output to compare the observed statuses.
statements.explanation: The actual output is the evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The configured limit bounds ordinary completed turns in the demonstrated loop.
statements.explanation: Unit and assumptions are specified.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A status name is useful only if you can say what event it denotes.
statements.explanation: A status is only a label until you can name its event.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The configured limit is a general timeout.
statements.explanation: It is not a timeout, memory cap, credential policy, or correctness check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A passing test is enough to explain each return.
statements.explanation: Explain each return without relying on a test having passed.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about inspecting your artifact for invented success.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Correct mistaken statements by deleting the original mistaken interpretation from your learning record.
statements.explanation: The original mistake is preserved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Check whether you supplied an answer when the controller returned `incomplete`.
statements.explanation: `incomplete` manufactures no answer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trace that looks productive is enough to call a run complete.
statements.explanation: Budget exhaustion on a productive-looking trace is not completion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Check whether you summarized budget exhaustion as successful completion because the trace looked productive.
statements.explanation: A busy trace is not success.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The configured limit also serves as a memory cap and a credential policy.
statements.explanation: The limit is none of these.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the chapter wants a reflection to be written.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reflection that says the finish branch returns before any comparison between red and the recorded blue observation is better than a general slogan, because it ties the lesson to a mechanism.
statements.explanation: A mechanism is recognizable when the surrounding system gets larger.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You reread your gate and ask which line building the controller changed and whether you dated the revision.
statements.explanation: This revisits the gate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reflection should stay general and avoid naming code.
statements.explanation: The chapter ties the reflection to specific code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reflection should name the actual confusion.
statements.explanation: The actual confusion is what the reflection must name.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "I thought stopping meant succeeding" is the best possible reflection.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it a start, not the best.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's practice assessments.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You use the lesson's existing knowledge check, preserving your initial answers before reading explanations.
statements.explanation: Initial answers are preserved first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Paid API requests are expected for testing the controller.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to add paid API requests for behavior that can be isolated offline.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The repetition-detector challenge asks only for a pointless repeated-action case, because useful repetitions are out of scope.
statements.explanation: The challenge asks for both a pointless repeat and a useful repetition that challenges the detector.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The three-exits warm-up asks you to write the exit table before running anything and mark every cell you got wrong.
statements.explanation: This is the second warm-up exercise.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Assessments carry no points.
statements.explanation: They are ungraded practice.

questions.source: What you can now diagnose
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three jobs at this scale, as summarized in the chapter's closing diagnosis.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Conducting: you let Claude decide whether the task needed a loop.
statements.explanation: You asked first whether the task needed a loop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checking: you kept the comparison independent of the generator.
statements.explanation: Independence is part of checking.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Conducting: you wrote the exits, the unit of the budget, and the wrong versions before Claude implemented anything.
statements.explanation: The gate came first.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Driving: you let Claude take the stop that closes the task.
statements.explanation: Closing the task stays with you.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Driving: you kept the budget, the price of a false alarm, and the closing of the task.
statements.explanation: Those three are the driver's decisions.

questions.source: A bounded loop can still cross a boundary once
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the boundary a bounded loop can still cross.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A good controller removes the need to compare the resulting state with the task the human authorized.
statements.explanation: Neither a good controller nor a good boundary removes that comparison.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Chapter 5 inspects that boundary through network ports.
statements.explanation: Chapter 5 inspects it through filesystem paths.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A turn budget is itself a permission policy.
statements.explanation: The budget limits repetition, not authority.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Iteration count and permission are separate controls.
statements.explanation: Counting turns says nothing about what each turn may do.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A budget of one can still allow one wrong target or one unauthorized mutation in a system that exposes such tools.
statements.explanation: One action is enough to do harm if it is outside the authorized scope.

questions.source: A bounded loop can still cross a boundary once
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what Chapter 5 is previewed to cover.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its permission policy is written after the first tool runs.
statements.explanation: The permission policy is written before any tool runs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It will describe a short teaching function as a complete production sandbox.
statements.explanation: The chapter refuses to describe a short function as a complete sandbox.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A name that looks relative can resolve to a target outside an approved root.
statements.explanation: This is the path problem.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A permitted read does not imply a permitted write.
statements.explanation: Read and write permissions are separate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It will use disposable fixtures to test traversal, symlinks, and approval checks.
statements.explanation: These are the chapter's planned tests.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's use of Anthropic's Building effective agents.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An API integration has already been executed in this chapter.
statements.explanation: No API call is part of the worked example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The short loop reproduces Anthropic's runtime.
statements.explanation: The chapter makes no such claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The adaptation task asks you to mark where a model-backed decision source would replace the prepared actions.
statements.explanation: Then identify the limits and checks that stay explicit outside it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter cites it as checked on 2026-09-06.
statements.explanation: The link-check date is given.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The architectural guidance is kept distinct from the scripted iterator.
statements.explanation: The two are not the same thing.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Computational Skepticism question the chapter borrows.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter borrows the source's census of how often agents fail.
statements.explanation: The chapter borrows the question, not the census.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The companion's agentic-validation chapter shifts the review question from the system's completion report to the outcome its actions produced.
statements.explanation: The focus moves to outcomes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If you cannot name a condition under which a control would fail, you have validated the control.
statements.explanation: Without a named failure condition you have only observed a pass.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It asks under what condition a robustness result would fail.
statements.explanation: This is the added diagnostic question.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Observing that nothing went wrong this time is validation.
statements.explanation: A pass is an observation, not validation.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the conditions under which the chapter's controls would not have held.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The source's framing is a long-term study of many frameworks and models.
statements.explanation: It is an exploratory study of one framework and two models over two weeks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A repeat that your detector's definition does not cover would get past the detector.
statements.explanation: A detector only stops what its definition covers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A blocked call that the iteration count cannot interrupt defeats the budget as a time bound.
statements.explanation: A count cannot cut short a wait that never ends.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The budget stopping the repeated lookup shows it would also hold against a call that never returns.
statements.explanation: A pass on one case does not validate the control for another.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A finish that carries a right-looking answer from the wrong key would get past a check that reads the wrong record.
statements.explanation: The check must read the record for the key the task names.

questions.source: Chapter 5 - Tools and permissions (opening, before the first heading)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three requests described at the start of the chapter (notes.txt, ../notes.txt, and a symbolic-link entry inside the folder).

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fixture results establish that the authors built a complete filesystem sandbox.
statements.explanation: The chapter says they do not; the function returns a path and neither reads nor writes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: All three requests are strings, and their spelling alone is not a sufficient account of the target the filesystem will use.
statements.explanation: Spelling does not settle where the name leads.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the research fixture, an in-root target is accepted for reading, while a traversal target, an outside-pointing link, and an unapproved write are rejected.
statements.explanation: These are the preserved fixture results.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The request for ../notes.txt asks to move to the parent before locating the file.
statements.explanation: The parent component moves outward before the file is located.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The symbolic-link entry is safe because its name is inside the folder.
statements.explanation: A link's name is local, but its destination can be outside the folder.

questions.source: Chapter 5 - Tools and permissions (opening, before the first heading)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the function `authorize` does and does not do.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A correct implementation whose tests all pass can still ship a policy that guarantees far less than its name suggests.
statements.explanation: This is where a recipe-follower goes wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the function is called authorize, a returned path shows that the file was written.
statements.explanation: An authorization result is not execution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It reads the target file and returns the contents.
statements.explanation: It returns a path; it does not read or write the target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter treats the name and the behavior as the same description.
statements.explanation: The distance between the two descriptions is the subject of the chapter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It resolves a name, compares two paths, and hands one back.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's description of what it does.

questions.source: Chapter 5 - Tools and permissions (opening, before the first heading)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the prediction questions posed in the opening of the chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: All three prediction answers come from the same single check in the rule.
statements.explanation: Each answer comes from a different part of the rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An approved execute operation should pass, because approval overrides the allowlist.
statements.explanation: The function allows only read and write; approval is not an override.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A folder named course-other should not pass merely because its name begins with the same letters as the approved root course.
statements.explanation: Containment is not a shared prefix of characters.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A write inside course should pass merely because the location is acceptable.
statements.explanation: Location and write approval are separate questions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping the parts of the rule separate is how a policy is made inspectable.
statements.explanation: Separate parts can each be inspected and tested.

questions.source: Chapter 5 - Tools and permissions (opening, before the first heading)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the chapter says to run its exercises.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Exercises use disposable material under a narrowly scoped temporary directory.
statements.explanation: Disposable temporary directories avoid touching real data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Python boundary requires a direct call to the Claude API.
statements.explanation: The boundary requires no direct API call.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The scenarios are teaching fixtures, not invitations to probe someone else's files.
statements.explanation: The exercises target only disposable material.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude Code is replaced by the API as the assumed learning assistant for this exercise.
statements.explanation: Claude Code remains the assumed learning assistant through your account.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You may disable a safeguard temporarily if that helps you complete the exercise.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to change institutional permissions or disable safeguards.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the abilities the chapter says you should have by its end.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Distinguish containment from string-prefix similarity.
statements.explanation: Containment is a path relation, not a character prefix.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Write a sign-off whose "Not checked" line names what a passing preflight leaves open.
statements.explanation: One of the three things the rest of the book builds on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Say which parts of the boundary you handed to Claude, which you kept, and why the grant itself stayed yours.
statements.explanation: One of the three things the rest of the book builds on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Explain that a passing preflight result is an operating-system sandbox.
statements.explanation: You should be able to say why it is not one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Trace a requested path to the resolved target that the function uses.
statements.explanation: Tracing the destination is the first listed ability.

questions.source: Who may do what is decided before the code exists
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about least privilege and the first design decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The selection rule is to take the lowest capability that does the step, because the most constrained tool is the one you can verify.
statements.explanation: This is the rule the chapter borrows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool that summarizes course notes needs, at minimum, to read them.
statements.explanation: A notes summarizer is the chapter's example of a tool that needs only to read.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The five-layer capability stack is a teaching device, not an industry standard.
statements.explanation: The book itself says so, according to the chapter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You answer the first decision by asking what the task requires, not what the tool is able to do.
statements.explanation: Least privilege starts from what the task needs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Conducting AI states least privilege for permissions in those words.
statements.explanation: The book does not state it for permissions; this lesson names the permissions version least privilege.

questions.source: Who may do what is decided before the code exists
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about auditing a permission policy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A write belongs in the default vocabulary and needs no justification.
statements.explanation: A write has to earn its place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every operation added to the vocabulary is a capability you must later verify.
statements.explanation: Each added operation is one more capability to verify.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The first design decision is a line of Python.
statements.explanation: The first decision is what the tool may touch and what it may do.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A policy that says "be careful with files" can be audited by a stranger.
statements.explanation: It cannot be audited by anyone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A policy of one root and two operations can be audited by a stranger in a few minutes.
statements.explanation: The chapter's example of an auditable policy.

questions.source: Who may do what is decided before the code exists
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about where a permission policy can be placed.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A system prompt sits outside the text the model is continuing, so no other paragraph competes with it.
statements.explanation: A system prompt is text in a document the model is continuing, competing with every other paragraph.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Enforcement lives in the runtime, where text cannot reach it.
statements.explanation: A runtime check cannot be talked out of its answer by text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One place for a policy is a sentence in the request; another is a function between the request and the filesystem that raises when the request is out of bounds.
statements.explanation: These are the two places the chapter names.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sentence such as "stay inside the course folder" is a gate.
statements.explanation: A request for caution is a hope.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A function that raises PermissionError is more likely to let a request through when the request is persuasive.
statements.explanation: It does not care how persuasive the request was.

questions.source: Who may do what is decided before the code exists
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about deterministic work and Claude's role in this chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A request for caution in the prompt is an adequate substitute for a comparison that has one correct answer.
statements.explanation: A request for caution is a hope; a comparison does the job exactly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether a resolved path lies under a folder has one correct answer.
statements.explanation: So it is not a matter for plausibility.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This is the same move as the book's advice to route deterministic work out of the stochastic layers.
statements.explanation: Routing deterministic work out of the stochastic layers is the same move.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Handing that question to a model borrows fluent guessing for a job a comparison does exactly.
statements.explanation: A comparison has one right answer; a model only approximates it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude keeps a role: it proposes actions, and a proposal is useful input to review.
statements.explanation: Proposing is Claude's role; granting is not.

questions.source: Who may do what is decided before the code exists
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about moving a decision into code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Moving a decision into code makes it exactly as narrow as the question you asked the code.
statements.explanation: This is the cost the chapter measures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Separating Claude's proposal from the grant has no cost.
statements.explanation: The separation comes with a cost, which the rest of the chapter measures.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The function will also enforce rules you meant to write but did not.
statements.explanation: It will enforce the policy you wrote and nothing else.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Moving a decision into code makes it checkable.
statements.explanation: A rule in code can be tested; a sentence in a request cannot.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude cannot grant itself the permission; that separation is the design.
statements.explanation: Claude can only propose; the grant stays with a person.

questions.source: A name is a request for a destination
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the reference implementation treats a path.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference resolves the approved root, joins the target to it, resolves the result, and compares the two.
statements.explanation: These are the four steps of the reference's path check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: resolve() turns a pathname into a handle on an object.
statements.explanation: resolve() returns a path, not a handle on an object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Python's resolve() resolves symbolic links and eliminates parent components.
statements.explanation: This is the narrow behavior the chapter relies on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This policy judges the place the string leads, not the string someone typed.
statements.explanation: The destination, not the spelling, is what is judged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A relative path means the same thing regardless of the base from which it is read.
statements.explanation: A relative path depends on the base.

questions.source: A name is a request for a destination
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why spelling is not the same as destination.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A request can step into a subdirectory and back to its parent and still land inside the root.
statements.explanation: Containment is about the destination.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Containment is a statement about which characters in a request look suspicious.
