statements.explanation: It is a statement about the destination.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Parent components in a path can move outward from the directory it is read from.
statements.explanation: That is what a .. component does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A request with no visible parent component cannot lead out of the root.
statements.explanation: A link can lead out without any parent component.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A symbolic link can only redirect a name to another entry inside the same root.
statements.explanation: A link can redirect a name toward another location, including one outside the root.

questions.source: A name is a request for a destination
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about resolving a path that may not exist.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference calls resolve() with strict checking, so a target that does not exist is rejected.
statements.explanation: It calls resolve() without strict checking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A returned Path is evidence that something was opened.
statements.explanation: A returned Path does not show that anything was opened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Acceptance of a write creates the file and shows that its contents are valid.
statements.explanation: Acceptance neither creates the file nor validates its contents.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a write, the preflight can accept a location it cannot inspect, because the file about to be created does not exist yet.
statements.explanation: A file about to be created cannot be inspected yet.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether the target exists is the same question as whether the operation succeeded.
statements.explanation: Existence, object type, access at the moment of use, and success are separate questions.

questions.source: A name is a request for a destination
questions.stem: A student runs the lesson's demo on macOS with root /tmp/course and target notes.txt, and it prints /private/tmp/course/notes.txt. Check each statement that is true about this output.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function reports where the name leads, not how it was spelled.
statements.explanation: Resolution replaces the spelling with the destination.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The printed path proves that notes.txt exists and was read.
statements.explanation: The demo says no file is read or written.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On macOS /tmp is a link to /private/tmp, so a resolved path starts with /private/tmp.
statements.explanation: The resolved path starts from the real location.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The root was never resolved, because the printed path differs from the typed root.
statements.explanation: The function resolves the root first; that is why the printed path differs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The differing spelling shows the function failed or was bypassed.
statements.explanation: The printed path is where the name leads, which is the intended output.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter's gate block fixes in advance.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gate says execute should be accepted when approval is present.
statements.explanation: Execute is refused even with approval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate lets you claim a file was read or written once a proposal passes the preflight.
statements.explanation: You may claim only that a proposal passes a preflight.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A write needs a human approval you can name; in tests it is a simulated fixture, labeled as one.
statements.explanation: Tests use a labeled, simulated approval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Root: one disposable directory, named in the gate.
statements.explanation: The gate names the one disposable directory first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Operations: read and write, and no other operation.
statements.explanation: The gate allows no operation beyond read and write.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the gate says the function must accept.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A contained read must be accepted.
statements.explanation: Contained reads are on the must-accept list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Execute must be accepted when approval is present.
statements.explanation: Execute is refused even with approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Traversal out of the root must be accepted if the operation is a read.
statements.explanation: Traversal is listed under Must refuse.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approval value that is truthy but not exactly True must be accepted for a write.
statements.explanation: Only exactly True passes; anything else is refused.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A contained write without approval must be accepted, since the location is acceptable.
statements.explanation: It is listed under Must refuse.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who owns the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A refusal you accept from Claude should be marked as Claude's proposal.
statements.explanation: Marking provenance keeps the policy honest about who proposed what.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude is not permitted to propose a refusal you missed.
statements.explanation: Claude may propose one; you accept or reject it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The finished policy should be kept in Claude's words.
statements.explanation: It should be kept in your words.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Every line of the gate is yours, including lines that look arbitrary, such as why exactly True and why execute is refused even with approval.
statements.explanation: The gate records the human's decisions, even arbitrary-looking ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can write the whole gate for you without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: It cannot write it for you without defeating its purpose.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four wrong versions your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Returning base / target instead of the resolved path is one of them.
statements.explanation: Returning the unresolved join hands the caller an unchecked path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every one of the four variants fails at least one of the six lesson tests.
statements.explanation: Only the prefix variant fails; the other three pass all six.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Containment by string prefix, using str(path).startswith(str(base)), is one of them.
statements.explanation: Prefix testing is the first listed wrong version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Truthy approval, replacing approved is not True with not approved, is one of them.
statements.explanation: not approved accepts any truthy value, not only True.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Textual cleanup of .. with os.path.normpath instead of resolve() is one of them.
statements.explanation: normpath cleans text but never follows links.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the six lesson tests handle the four wrong versions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The other three variants pass all six lesson tests.
statements.explanation: Only the prefix variant is caught by any of the six tests.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One of the six lesson tests passes an approval value that is neither True nor absent.
statements.explanation: No lesson test passes a non-Boolean approval value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The lesson's success tests compare the full resolved path.
statements.explanation: They check only the final name of the returned path.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sibling test fails the string-prefix variant.
statements.explanation: A sibling like course-other starts with the same characters as course.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At least one of the six lesson tests builds a symbolic link.
statements.explanation: No lesson test creates a link.

questions.source: The gate: write the policy before the function
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about extending the test list and the dated sentence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test list that cannot tell the wrong variants from the right program is not a gate yet.
statements.explanation: A gate that cannot reject the wrong programs proves nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Writing that sentence after running the code is better, because it records the real output.
statements.explanation: Written afterward, it describes the output instead of testing your understanding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The six lesson tests are enough to serve as the whole test list.
statements.explanation: The gaps are why the list is longer than six.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You should write one sentence about what you would see if your function were wrong, and date it before you run anything.
statements.explanation: A prediction written beforehand tests understanding.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Added tests the chapter names include a symlink case, a non-Boolean approval case, and a check that the returned path is the resolved one.
statements.explanation: These cover the gaps the six lesson tests leave.

questions.source: Three decisions in eleven lines
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three decisions the reference function makes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The first decision the function makes is the operation vocabulary.
statements.explanation: Decisions are read in order of the function.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Execute is refused even with approval true, before the path is resolved at all.
statements.explanation: The allowlist check comes first and needs no path.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The second decision resolves the root and the joined path and requires the result to be relative to the base in the path sense.
statements.explanation: Containment is a relation between resolved paths.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Approval is a universal override of the operation allowlist.
statements.explanation: Approval does not override the operation allowlist.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The third decision concerns writes and compares the approval value with True.
statements.explanation: Only the write branch consults the approval value.

questions.source: Three decisions in eleven lines
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the write condition approved is True.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing approval check shows the approval was issued before the call and matches the request.
statements.explanation: A Boolean carries neither fact.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A passing approval check shows that a human reviewed the request that produced the value.
statements.explanation: It does not prove a human reviewed anything.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It asks for any arbitrary truthy object, not specifically the Boolean True.
statements.explanation: It asks for the Boolean True and not any arbitrary truthy object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The approved is True check is applied to reads as well as to writes.
statements.explanation: It applies only when the operation is write.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It is an exact identity comparison.
statements.explanation: "is" tests identity, so only the object True matches.

questions.source: Three decisions in eleven lines
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the return value and what the function claims.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function authenticates where the root and approval inputs came from.
statements.explanation: It does not authenticate them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: There is no open, read_text, or write_text in the listed code.
statements.explanation: No file is opened, read, or written by these lines.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The function performs the operation after authorizing it.
statements.explanation: It does not perform the operation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The name authorize accurately describes a complete approval system.
statements.explanation: The name must not inflate what the lines implement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The return value is the resolved path.
statements.explanation: The function hands back a path and nothing else.

questions.source: Three decisions in eleven lines
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about seams in the function.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a multi-step workflow, risk sits less inside any one tool than at the seam where one step's output is handed to the next on trust.
statements.explanation: Conducting AI's point, as the chapter reports it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The root and the approval value are inputs that come in to this function.
statements.explanation: Root and approval are accepted on trust, not verified.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For each seam you state what is passed, what it is trusted to be, and how that trust was earned.
statements.explanation: These three questions make trust at a seam inspectable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The returned path is a seam, because it goes out to whatever uses it.
statements.explanation: The caller decides what to do with the returned path.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the caller supplies an overly broad root, the containment check will reject it.
statements.explanation: It will enforce that broad root faithfully.

questions.source: Containment is not a shared prefix
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about containment and absolute targets.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Placing a root variable before a target expression forces the target inside the root.
statements.explanation: An absolute target discards the root.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reference decides containment by comparing the characters of the two path strings.
statements.explanation: It asks about a relation between resolved paths.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A string test asking whether the target starts with the text naming course confuses the two directories.
statements.explanation: course-other begins with the letters of course but is not inside it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A target inside course-other must not be accepted under a policy that allows only course.
statements.explanation: A sibling directory is outside the approved root.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When the second operand of a pathlib join is absolute, it is treated as relative to the first operand.
statements.explanation: The first operand is discarded.

questions.source: The symlink that leaves the folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the symbolic-link fixture.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The symlink result is only a description, because no fixture with a link was actually executed.
statements.explanation: It is an executed fixture, preserved in the research script and its output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The link is rejected because its name looks suspicious.
statements.explanation: It is rejected because its resolved destination fails containment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A policy written in terms of visible names would catch the outside-pointing link.
statements.explanation: Names alone would not reveal the outside destination.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The research script creates a symbolic link inside a temporary root that points outside it.
statements.explanation: The fixture builds a link whose destination is outside the root.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Showing the rejection required reading the outside file to see where the link points.
statements.explanation: No read of the outside file is needed.

questions.source: The symlink that leaves the folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about testing the parent-component route and the link route.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A directory listing can show a local entry whose destination is elsewhere.
statements.explanation: A listing shows names, not where links lead.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because both routes end at the same containment question, one test of either route is enough.
statements.explanation: They should be tested separately.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The parent-component route and the link route should be tested separately.
statements.explanation: The mechanisms differ, so one test cannot stand in for the other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A string pattern that catches .. also catches an outside-pointing link.
statements.explanation: Neither string pattern covers the other.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two routes differ in mechanism but end at the same containment question.
statements.explanation: Both routes are decided by the same containment relation.

questions.source: The symlink that leaves the folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the time boundary between the check and a later use.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the caller uses the returned resolved path, replacing the original link entry need not redirect it.
statements.explanation: The resolved path is a different name from the link entry.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The function checks and returns; a later caller may open a file.
statements.explanation: The check and a later open are separate events.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reference binds the check and the operation into one indivisible act.
statements.explanation: The check and a later open are separate acts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The research run attempts to prove resistance to changes by another process.
statements.explanation: The run tests a stable fixture, not concurrent changes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Every swap of the link entry defeats this function.
statements.explanation: It would be wrong to claim that.

questions.source: The symlink that leaves the folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the returned path as the second seam.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A careless caller can check one path and then open the original, unchecked target.
statements.explanation: Nothing forces the caller to open the checked path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The teaching function can force callers to use its result.
statements.explanation: The function only returns a path; callers decide what to open.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A call named authorize earlier in a program shows that a later open is covered.
statements.explanation: Follow the value that reaches the open call, not the presence of the word.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the laundering shape, something unverified takes on the look of something verified because it passed near a reassuring step.
statements.explanation: A reassuring-looking call makes an unchecked value look checked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The failure at the returned-path seam needs a race between the check and the open.
statements.explanation: A careless caller can fail without any timing change.

questions.source: The symlink that leaves the folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the limits on the symlink result mean.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a constructed, stable fixture the function rejected an outside-pointing destination, and that is a result you can report.
statements.explanation: The result is bounded to the stable fixture that was run.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rejection shows the function resists replacement of the link by another process.
statements.explanation: The chapter says that is not shown.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the result has limits, the test accomplished nothing.
statements.explanation: The limits locate the rejection; they do not erase it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The honest gap is that this is a preflight pathname check that returns a pathname and establishes nothing about the later access.
statements.explanation: The check says nothing about what happens at open time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Protection against every later mutation is a separate item to document.
statements.explanation: Resistance to later changes was not tested and is documented separately.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reads and writes in this policy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In this policy a contained read does not need a separate approval flag, and a contained write does.
statements.explanation: This is the exercise's deliberate rule about consequences.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Which operations need a human is a judgment about consequences that is yours to make for each task.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls this a judgment about consequences.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The approved root must already reflect the task's data boundary.
statements.explanation: If the root is too broad, correct code enforces a wrong policy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An in-root read passing is a statement that every file under any root is appropriate to read, upload, or disclose.
statements.explanation: It is a deliberate rule for the exercise, not that statement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A read changes nothing in the filesystem, but what it exposes cannot be un-exposed once it has left the folder.
statements.explanation: A read cannot be taken back once data leaves the folder.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the delegation chapter and the approved root.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the root holds material the workflow should not touch, the policy is wrong for that task however correct the code.
statements.explanation: The code can be right while the policy is wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The score should be used as a number rather than a question.
statements.explanation: Use it as a question, not as a number.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Computational Skepticism delegation chapter asks of each sub-task whether the action can be undone.
statements.explanation: Undoability matters for deciding what to delegate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The approved root is chosen after the code is written, because the code reveals what it should hold.
statements.explanation: The root is part of the policy, decided before the code exists.

statements.label: E
statements.text: That chapter's five-question score has external validation.
statements.explanation: It is the author's own instrument with no external validation.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the write condition and containment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A report that says a test wrote x because the returned path ends in x confuses an authorization result with execution.
statements.explanation: A returned path is an authorization result, not an operation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A contained write is rejected unless the approval value is exactly True.
statements.explanation: The write condition is checked after containment passes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The same target can be accepted for reading and rejected for writing without inconsistency.
statements.explanation: Location and write approval are separate questions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A write proposal that is accepted should be reported as a completed write.
statements.explanation: Accepted proposal is the right phrase.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Passing the containment check can substitute for the write condition.
statements.explanation: Passing containment cannot substitute for the second.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the approval flag represents in this model.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The flag is a signature.
statements.explanation: It is a supplied Boolean, not a signature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you place True in a fixture, you should label it a simulated approval input and not attribute it to a person.
statements.explanation: A fixture True is simulated and should be labeled so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The flag is an identity check on the approver.
statements.explanation: It checks nothing about who approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The flag is a record that someone saw the precise change.
statements.explanation: It does not show that anyone saw the precise change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The flag is a decision supplied from outside the function.
statements.explanation: The function consumes the flag; it does not produce the decision.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the standard a handoff condition must meet.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Boolean fails that standard the way "the human reviews it" does.
statements.explanation: A reader can see the value but cannot tell whether anyone decided anything.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Challenge item 11 asks you to build a richer approval record.
statements.explanation: Item 11 is the exercise on richer approval records.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A handoff condition is worth having only if a stranger can read it, observe the system, and decide whether it was met.
statements.explanation: The companion book's standard, as the chapter states it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A richer approval record authenticates its own contents.
statements.explanation: Nothing here authenticates its contents.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A richer condition names the operation, the target, and the approver, was issued before the call, and has a target that matches the request.
statements.explanation: These features let a stranger test whether the condition was met.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the scope of an approval.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approval for a disposable draft is not approval to overwrite an original.
statements.explanation: Approval attaches to a specific operation and target.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Approval for one target is not a license over a directory.
statements.explanation: A directory is a much wider scope than one file.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The surrounding process must bind its decision to the actual operation and target.
statements.explanation: Otherwise one approval could be stretched over other changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A model can produce its own independent human approval by writing the word approved.
statements.explanation: A model writing the word approved is not an independent human approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The source of an approval value matters as much as its type.
statements.explanation: A True from the wrong source is still only a Boolean.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a human in the loop.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Applying this to grants is the companion book's own claim.
statements.explanation: The chapter marks it as the author's reading.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The companion chapter calls this drift a character flaw.
statements.explanation: It calls it economics acting on attention, not a character flaw.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If approval is requested for every small step, the answer can drift toward yes.
statements.explanation: Frequent requests wear down careful checking.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A human in the loop is automatically a control.
statements.explanation: Costly checking pushes supervisors toward accepting, so a human is not automatically a control.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When checking is expensive, the cost structure pushes a supervisor toward accepting.
statements.explanation: Checking costs effort, so approving becomes the easy default.

questions.source: Read and write are different authority questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the operation allowlist.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You should let write stand for anything a tool might execute.
statements.explanation: Do not stretch write to mean anything a tool might execute.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The policy refuses operations outside its allowlist even with approval set.
statements.explanation: Approval cannot override the vocabulary.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If your task needs another operation, you should change the policy deliberately and review the new risk and tests.
statements.explanation: A new operation means new risks and new tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approved execute is allowed because execute is a kind of write.
statements.explanation: Execute is outside the allowlist.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A small vocabulary is useful only while its entries stay specific enough to enforce.
statements.explanation: Vague entries cannot be enforced.

questions.source: Work through the boundary matrix
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the rows of the boundary matrix.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An escaping traversal raises PermissionError because the resolved target fails containment.
statements.explanation: Traversal fails the containment relation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A contained write without approval raises PermissionError, showing containment does not waive write approval.
statements.explanation: Containment does not substitute for write approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A contained read returns a path, which shows the proposal passes the displayed preflight.
statements.explanation: The contained read passes every check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A contained write with a True fixture returning a path shows that a person approved it.
statements.explanation: It shows a simulated approval input satisfies the check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Execute raises PermissionError because the resolved path fails containment.
statements.explanation: Execute fails on the operation allowlist, before any path is resolved.

questions.source: Work through the boundary matrix
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reading the matrix rows as branches.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the traversal row the containment branch fires because the operation vocabulary is violated.
statements.explanation: The operation vocabulary is satisfied; the resolved target escapes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The execute row fails after the path has been resolved.
statements.explanation: It fails first, without resolving anything.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The link row ends in a different branch from the traversal row.
statements.explanation: Both end in the containment branch, by different routes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The contained read shows that the target exists and was read.
statements.explanation: It shows only that the proposal passed preflight.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The contained read passes all three checks.
statements.explanation: Operation allowed, containment holds, and no write condition applies.

questions.source: Work through the boundary matrix
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the unapproved write case and the status of the matrix.

statements.label: A
statements.text: That case proves location and operation authority are separate.
statements.explanation: The same location passes for reading and fails for writing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The lesson tests, rather than the research fixture, add the Boolean-approved write and the rejection of execute.
statements.explanation: The research fixture covers the first four rows of behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The matrix maps implemented conditions to observed or directly tested results.
statements.explanation: Each row ties a condition to a result that was actually observed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The matrix is a security certification.
statements.explanation: It maps conditions to tested results and certifies nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The unapproved contained write passes the first two checks and fails the third.
statements.explanation: Operation and location are fine; only the approval is missing.

questions.source: Build It: make denials explainable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how to build your own version.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You start by giving a tool broad filesystem access to see whether it behaves politely.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to begin that way.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You read the six lesson tests before the reference and predict which rule produces each result, not just accept or reject.
statements.explanation: Predicting the rule, not just the outcome, shows understanding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Your own version is the baseline: the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
statements.explanation: Your baseline is what you measure Claude's version against.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If an unapproved write passes in your version, check that your write condition is independent of containment.
statements.explanation: Write approval must not be implied by containment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You implement the allowlist, path resolution, containment check, and write condition against a disposable fixture.
statements.explanation: These are the four parts of the preflight.

questions.source: Build It: make denials explainable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about designing the tests for your own version.

statements.label: A
statements.text: To test a later check, you let the earlier checks pass.
statements.explanation: Otherwise an earlier failure hides the later check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A suite of denial cases alone is enough to show that the policy works.
statements.explanation: A policy that rejects everything passes a denial-only suite and fails the authorized task.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A single proposal combining an unknown operation, an escaping path, and missing approval is the best test, since it exercises every check.
statements.explanation: It does not say which boundary you meant to test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each test should be narrow enough to explain.
statements.explanation: A narrow test points to the rule it exercises.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fixture cleanup should use broad deletion commands.
statements.explanation: Cleanup goes through the temporary-directory lifecycle.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about handing the gate to Claude Code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude Code is opened on real production files so the results are realistic.
statements.explanation: It is opened on disposable fixtures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You ask for an implementation that may use whichever third-party libraries are convenient.
statements.explanation: The request is for the standard library only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A statement from Claude that the tests passed is your evidence.
statements.explanation: It is Claude's report, not your evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You hand Claude Code your own implementation and ask it to confirm that it is correct.
statements.explanation: You give it the policy and the tests, not the implementation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You give Claude Code your policy block and your test list, not your implementation.
statements.explanation: The policy and tests are the specification; the implementation is Claude's job.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three things to do with what Claude returns.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in the gate, which Claude cannot see because it has only what you wrote.
statements.explanation: Claude sees only the gate you wrote, so gate gaps are invisible to it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every variant that survives your test list is a gap in the list.
statements.explanation: The list failed to distinguish a wrong version from the right one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can see gaps in your gate because it reads your whole project.
statements.explanation: Claude has only what you wrote down.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You apply the variants from your gate to its function one at a time.
statements.explanation: A variant that survives is a wrong program your tests cannot detect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You compare its function with your baseline and name one difference in behavior, not in line count or style.
statements.explanation: Behavior differences can reveal a missed boundary or a missed case.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the independence of checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A checker that fails the same way as the first adds verification.
statements.explanation: It adds agreement, not verification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A second checker reduces error only to the degree that it fails differently from the first.
statements.explanation: Independent failure modes are what make a second check useful.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A generated assurance that the code is secure can be accepted as stated if all of Claude's tests pass.
statements.explanation: It should be narrowed to the conditions the tests demonstrate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tests Claude writes for the function Claude wrote share its reading of your policy.
statements.explanation: Same author, same reading, same blind spots.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cases Claude adds should be treated as proposals: read each, run it, decide.
statements.explanation: A proposal is not evidence until you have run and judged it.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the transcript and the comparison with a real permission system.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You preserve the transcript: prompt, plan, diff, commands, and outputs, with the date and displayed model label.
statements.explanation: The transcript is the record of what actually happened.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Inspecting the permission configuration in your Claude Code environment is authorization to change university settings.
statements.explanation: Inspection is for comparison, not for changing settings.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the session failed or did not run, you record that rather than substituting a fixture.
statements.explanation: Substituting a fixture would misreport what ran.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Product details change, so the chapter's Boolean should not be substituted for a current product policy.
statements.explanation: The Boolean models a small preflight, not a product's rules.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Anthropic's Claude Code permissions documentation describes runtime permission rules.
statements.explanation: It is the primary source the chapter compares against.

questions.source: What the toy boundary cannot guarantee
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the five limits the chapter lists.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Time and filesystem state: the function makes a later open atomic with the check.
statements.explanation: The check and the open are not made atomic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Meaning: the function inspects the diff of an approved write.
statements.explanation: It never looks at the content of a diff.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Data policy: the preflight includes a destination-channel policy and content classification.
statements.explanation: The preflight has no such data policy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Authentication: the function has no independent account of who supplied the root or the approval value.
statements.explanation: The root and approval value are trusted inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Coverage: the function protects nothing that bypasses it.
statements.explanation: Anything that bypasses authorize is unprotected.

questions.source: What the toy boundary cannot guarantee
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the authentication and time limits.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A trustworthy workflow needs a real source for the approval decision and a scope that corresponds to the proposed action.
statements.explanation: This lesson supplies neither, so none can be assumed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A True fixture satisfies the Boolean check and proves nothing about consent.
statements.explanation: A fixture True is simulated, so it shows no consent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Rejecting one stable outside-pointing link proves resistance to every concurrent scenario.
statements.explanation: One stable link says nothing about concurrent changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You should not claim a race exploit was executed unless you performed and recorded a safe test of one.
statements.explanation: A race claim needs a recorded safe test behind it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This lesson implements a real approval source and scope.
statements.explanation: Neither an approval source nor a scope is implemented.

questions.source: What the toy boundary cannot guarantee
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the meaning and data-policy limits.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function judges whether an approved write's output serves the user's purpose.
statements.explanation: The function never judges whether the output serves the purpose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Permission answers whether the proposal satisfies a boundary, while review answers whether the proposed content is acceptable.
statements.explanation: These are separate questions, and the next chapter takes up the second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A contained file may hold restricted information that a later step discloses somewhere inappropriate.
statements.explanation: Location does not settle data obligations; the preflight has no destination-channel policy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approved write can contain a bad change.
statements.explanation: The function does not inspect a diff, so a bad change can pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A root is a description of every data obligation attached to the files inside it.
statements.explanation: A root is one useful boundary, not that description.

questions.source: What the toy boundary cannot guarantee
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how to write the "Not checked" line.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter lists eleven limits that a passing preflight leaves open.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists five limits.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Precision lets protections accumulate without one small protection impersonating the whole system.
statements.explanation: Each limit is stated narrowly, so protections can add up honestly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The limits are a reason for vague helplessness.
statements.explanation: None of this is a reason for vague helplessness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fluent list of limitations is as easy for Claude to produce as a fluent claim of security.
statements.explanation: Fluency is cheap; tying each limit to your own actions is not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For your artifact, each limit should be tied to what you actually did about it: inspected, tested, or left alone.
statements.explanation: A limit without a record of what you did is just a list.

questions.source: Ship It: a permission policy with evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the artifact you ship.

statements.label: A
statements.text: NEU grading logistics stay outside this chapter, and learner changes stay separate from the reference.
statements.explanation: Course logistics are kept separate from the chapter's content.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It states the approved root, allowed operations, approval owner or simulated approval source, denial cases, and actual test results.
statements.explanation: These are the items the artifact must contain.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A preflight-only experiment is incomplete unless a file is actually written.
statements.explanation: It is complete on its own terms when its stated task was to test preflight behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a later file operation was not performed, the artifact should omit that fact.
statements.explanation: The record must show what was and was not done.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The artifact is your gate, as run.
statements.explanation: The artifact reports the gate as actually run, not as intended.

questions.source: Ship It: a permission policy with evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the evidence record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You state one decision you revised after testing, with your original prediction and the result that changed it.
statements.explanation: Revision after testing shows the prediction was actually tested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The artifact does not need a denial connected to your capstone.
statements.explanation: It should include at least one denial that matters to your eventual capstone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For tests, the source of each approval value is recorded as a simulated fixture.
statements.explanation: Test approvals are never attributed to a person.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You record whether the function returned or raised and which branch decided.
statements.explanation: The branch shows which rule decided.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For each proposal, you preserve the requested target and the role its resolved destination played.
statements.explanation: A reviewer can then see why each decision was made.

questions.source: Ship It: a permission policy with evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fluent draft of the sign-off from Claude can be signed as written.
statements.explanation: Only your record shows what you did not test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If your evidence does not support signing, withholding is an honest result.
statements.explanation: A sign-off that claims more than the record supports is the failure the chapter warns about.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The line Claude will not write honestly is the one about what you did not test.
statements.explanation: Claude cannot know what you did not test; only your record can say.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The "Not checked" line lists the refusals your tests passed.
statements.explanation: The "Checked" line does; "Not checked" lists what remains open.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The "Not claiming" line says you are not claiming that anyone approved anything.
statements.explanation: The template lists what you are not claiming.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the chapter divides the work between Claude and you.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For choosing the root and the operation vocabulary, you decide the smallest root and vocabulary that suffices.
statements.explanation: Only you know what is in the folder.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For edge cases, you write the first list yourself, then choose which of Claude's proposals become tests.
statements.explanation: The first list is your understanding on the record.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can approve its own request when the evidence is strong.
statements.explanation: Authority and accountability are a person's.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For saying what a pass establishes, Claude chooses the verb and signs.
statements.explanation: You choose the verb and sign or withhold.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For the approver, you name the approver and the scope and make the grant.
statements.explanation: Authority and accountability belong to a person.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about recording the split between what you delegated and what you kept.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The root and the vocabulary stay with Claude because only Claude knows what is in the folder.
statements.explanation: Only you know what is in the folder, whose it is, and what disclosure would cost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each must point to a transcript line, a diff, or an edit you made.
statements.explanation: Pointers make the claim checkable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Implementation is delegated to Claude, but you run your tests on what it returns and compare it with your baseline.
statements.explanation: Claude writes the function fast; you run the tests and compare.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You record one task you delegated and one judgment you retained.
statements.explanation: The record shows the split, not just a claim of it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you cannot point to them, the split happened in your head and not in the record.
statements.explanation: Without a pointer, nothing in the record shows the split.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about verifying and auditing your work.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Safe should be read as secure against every attack once the tests pass.
statements.explanation: It should be replaced with the event and condition that occurred.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The research script demonstrates the stable symlink and traversal cases in disposable directories.
statements.explanation: Disposable directories keep the cases safe to run.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You run the demo and the six tests, then your additional fixture cases.
statements.explanation: The commands are given in the verification section.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The research script is evidence that every security property has been tested.
statements.explanation: It is evidence for those cases only.

statements.label: E
statements.text: authorize may mean a preflight decision or a complete approval system, so the noun and verb should be audited.
statements.explanation: Ambiguous words hide which event and condition occurred.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the distinctions the closing reflection asks you to consider.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reflection asks you to rate the function's security on a numeric scale.
statements.explanation: It asks which distinction you originally collapsed and which case separated them again.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reflection asks whether you collapsed the spelling of a path into its destination.
statements.explanation: A path's spelling and its destination can differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reflection asks whether you collapsed a location into an authority.
statements.explanation: Being inside the root is not permission to act.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reflection asks whether you collapsed a preflight into a performed operation.
statements.explanation: A preflight is not a performed operation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reflection asks whether you collapsed a Boolean into a human act.
statements.explanation: A True in a script is not a person's decision.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's Assessments.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Item 9 asks for a caller design that checks a path but later uses a different unchecked value.
statements.explanation: It shows why a call named authorize does not cover a later open.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Item 6 asks you to claim you demonstrated resistance to concurrent filesystem changes.
statements.explanation: Item 6 forbids claiming resistance to concurrent changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Item 10 asks you to present a speculative sequence as an observed exploit.
statements.explanation: The assessment says not to present speculation as observed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Assessments carry no points.
statements.explanation: They are ungraded practice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Item 7 says a function that rejected every proposal could pass a denial-only suite yet fail the intended workflow.
statements.explanation: Denial-only suites cannot detect an over-strict policy.

questions.source: What you can now defend
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the independence of operation, location, and write approval.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A returned Path is a completed file operation.
statements.explanation: A path is not an operation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Boolean approval fixture is a human act.
statements.explanation: A Boolean is not a person's decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An allowed operation can target an outside location.
statements.explanation: Operation and location are independent checks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A True approval cannot override an operation outside the allowlist.
statements.explanation: The allowlist is checked first and approval cannot widen it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A contained target can fail the write condition.
statements.explanation: Location passing does not satisfy the write condition.

questions.source: What you can now defend
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three jobs as they appeared in this chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Driving: you handed Claude the implementation and the list of edge cases.
statements.explanation: Implementation and edge-case listing are delegated; authority is not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Driving: you handed Claude the root, the vocabulary, the approver, and the verb.
statements.explanation: You kept the root, vocabulary, approver, and verb.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking: you ran the tests yourself and tried variants Claude did not write.
statements.explanation: Running them yourself makes the evidence yours, not Claude's report.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Conducting: you wrote the policy and the wrong versions your tests had to fail before Claude wrote a line.
statements.explanation: The policy and wrong versions come before any implementation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Conducting: the enforcement sat in the prompt, where careful wording could adjust it.
statements.explanation: It sat in code, where a request's wording could not change it.

questions.source: An authorized change can still be a bad change
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about authorized changes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chapter 6 turns to evidence-based review of a change.
statements.explanation: The chapter's closing hands the quality question to Chapter 6.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Permission without quality review can authorize a mistake.
statements.explanation: A permitted write may still be a wrong one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A permission boundary should inspect the diff of an approved write.
statements.explanation: It never inspects the diff and should not be asked to.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Quality without permission can produce an excellent change to the wrong thing.
statements.explanation: Quality without scope is aimed at the wrong target.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A proposed write can pass every check in the chapter, be performed under real, appropriately scoped approval, and still have contents that are not good.
statements.explanation: Permission never asks whether the contents are good.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the comparison with Claude Code permissions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The relevant connection is runtime enforcement.
statements.explanation: Executable rules mediate actions; prose does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The teaching function reproduces the product's safeguards.
statements.explanation: It is only a preflight illustration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The comparison should encourage bypassing a boundary to make the demonstration more dramatic.
statements.explanation: It should sharpen your permission policy instead.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Requesting caution in prose is not the same as constraining tool actions through permission rules.
statements.explanation: A request for caution in prose does not constrain actions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You inspect the available configuration without changing institutional settings, and mark unavailable information as uninspected.
statements.explanation: The comparison is read-only and honest about gaps.

questions.source: Opening (Chapter 6 - Claude Code and diff review)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the constructed comparison in the chapter's opening.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The same research run shows that the review function rejects a proposal when its approval flag is false.
statements.explanation: The research run records that outcome for approved = false.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The inadequate patch returns three for both input two and input five.
statements.explanation: The constant patch returns 3 and 3.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The inadequate patch fails on input two and passes on input five.
statements.explanation: It is the reverse: 3 equals the expected 3 at input two, and 3 does not equal the expected 6 at input five.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For inputs two and five, the old function `x - 1` returns one and four.
statements.explanation: The chapter reports 1 and 4 for inputs 2 and 5.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chapter presents the comparison as a real Claude Code failure recorded in a live session.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is a constructed comparison against the offline review exercise, not a real Claude Code failure.

questions.source: Opening (Chapter 6 - Claude Code and diff review)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the opening says the recipe got right and why the claim still fails.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The patch's small size is evidence that the change is safe.
statements.explanation: Nothing about the patch's size reveals the defect.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter's question is "what did the green test actually test, who decided that, and when?"
statements.explanation: That is the question the chapter poses.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One green test is enough to show the intended rule has been restored.
statements.explanation: Nothing about one green test proves the intended rule has been restored.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter says the main question is "what are the steps of a code review?"
statements.explanation: The chapter says the question is explicitly not that one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The defect was reproduced, a test was written, a patch was proposed, the test passed, and the diff was small, yet the claim still does not hold.
statements.explanation: The chapter says every step was performed and the claim still does not hold.

questions.source: Opening (Chapter 6 - Claude Code and diff review)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who writes the test and when.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test written after the patch, to fit the patch, is a retrospective blessing.
statements.explanation: The chapter uses exactly that phrase for a test written to fit the patch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Who wrote the test matters less than the fact that it passes.
statements.explanation: The chapter's whole question is who decided what the green test tests.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A test written by the patch's author is independent evidence simply because it lives in a separate file.
statements.explanation: Shared authorship is the problem, regardless of which file holds the test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The requirement is supposed to come from Claude's reading of the existing code.
statements.explanation: The requirement was supposed to come first, and to come from you.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test that Claude writes alongside its own patch shares an author with the code, and so shares whatever that author misunderstood.
statements.explanation: A shared author means a shared misunderstanding.

questions.source: Opening (Chapter 6 - Claude Code and diff review)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three jobs and how this chapter applies them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking Claude's work means writing down what you suspect before you run the check.
statements.explanation: The record of suspicion comes before the run.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Chapter 1's devices for the three jobs are the gate, the sign-off, and the driver's seat.
statements.explanation: Conduct, check, and drive each come with one of those devices.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Driving means Claude decides the scope and merges once its own tests pass.
statements.explanation: The scope decision and the merge are yours.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter advises matching Claude Code's speed by reading its results as fast as it produces them.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to compete with Claude's speed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Checking means letting the last sentence of Claude's report decide between accept, revise, and reject.
statements.explanation: The evidence, not the last sentence of Claude's report, decides.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter expects you to be able to do.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Explain a unified diff as changed behavior rather than decoration.
statements.explanation: Listed among the chapter's outcomes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Before running a check, record a verdict, a target, a suspected mechanism, and what would change your view, and keep that record intact.
statements.explanation: This is the audit record the chapter builds on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Trace every reason returned by the review function.
statements.explanation: Listed among the chapter's outcomes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ask Claude for a patch first and write the failing behavior afterward, so the patch guides the test.
statements.explanation: The failing behavior and prediction come before asking for a patch, so the patch cannot redefine the problem.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Bring Chapters 4 and 5, basic Python functions, and unit tests to the chapter.
statements.explanation: These are the stated prerequisites.

questions.source: Whose test is it? Reproduce before you repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reproducing a defect.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Behavior evidence and inspection evidence should be merged into a single entry in the packet.
statements.explanation: They should be kept apart, because reproducing a defect is not proving its cause.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reproduction is the smallest legitimate case that shows the gap between intended and current behavior.
statements.explanation: That is the definition given.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The result is wrong" is too weak a bug report because it names no input, expected result, observed result, or scope.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists exactly those missing pieces.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Observing `old(2) == 1` proves the cause of the defect is the `x - 1` expression.
statements.explanation: The observation contradicts the requirement; reading the source reveals the expression.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The evidence you will accept should be decided after reading the patch, so you can judge it in context.
statements.explanation: The decision has to be made while no patch exists, because a patch shapes how you see the problem.

questions.source: Whose test is it? Reproduce before you repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a regression test that contains only `assert candidate(2) == 3`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing at both inputs two and five proves the function is correct for all Python inputs.
statements.explanation: The pair rejects the demonstrated constant repair but does not prove correctness for all inputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Even the two-input test leaves open which input types are supported, what happens at boundary values, and whether the function belongs to a larger invariant.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists these open questions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding input five makes the constant patch fail.
statements.explanation: The constant returns 3, not the expected 6.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both the constant-three patch and the `x + 1` patch pass it.
statements.explanation: At input two, 3 equals 3 for both.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A packet that records only that command supports the claim that the candidate returns three for input two, and no more.
statements.explanation: The case did not separate the intended function from every wrong one.

questions.source: Whose test is it? Reproduce before you repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the regression test is written before the proposed fix.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test you write first from the rule is guaranteed to be complete.
statements.explanation: It is still your design and can still be incomplete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test written first, from the rule, represents the expected behavior, so when the patch arrives the patch is what is on trial.
statements.explanation: That is the point of the ordering.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A test written after seeing the patch is unaffected by the patch.
statements.explanation: It is shaped by the patch: you check the cases the patch handles and take expected values from what it returns.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When Claude writes the test alongside its own patch, a misunderstanding of the requirement sits on both sides of the comparison and cancels out.
statements.explanation: The shared author means the error cancels out.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test written first is mainly valuable because it runs faster than one written afterward.
statements.explanation: The reason given is provenance, not speed.

questions.source: Whose test is it? Reproduce before you repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the review habit of asking which different implementation could pass the current test.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Two passing inputs are enough to claim the bug is completely fixed.
statements.explanation: "Completely fixed" is the claim the two-input record cannot support.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The habit shows that one plausible counterexample is enough to show the evidence supports a narrower claim than "the bug is completely fixed."
statements.explanation: The chapter says exactly this about a counterexample.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The two-input test fully settles supported input types and boundary values.
statements.explanation: The two-input test leaves those questions open.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the exercise supplies no complete specification, the reviewer should invent one covering all input types.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to invent a specification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Figure 6.1 shows that a single test input is enough to distinguish the constant patch from `x + 1`.
statements.explanation: The figure shows the opposite: one test cannot distinguish both implementations.

questions.source: The gate: reproduction, test, and scope, before the patch
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gate should be written after Claude proposes its plan, so the plan can inform it.
statements.explanation: It is written before you ask Claude for a plan.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gate's design choices for the exercise (rule, inputs, allowed files) were produced by a model.
statements.explanation: The chapter says these are the author's choices and no model produced them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gate is the part Claude cannot do for you, because it is where your understanding of the requirement goes on the record.
statements.explanation: The gate records your understanding of the requirement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the constructed exercise, the allowed files are every file in the repository.
statements.explanation: The allowed files are `app.py` and its learner test file.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A phase gate is a specific, testable condition that must hold before the output moves downstream.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's definition of a phase gate.

questions.source: The gate: reproduction, test, and scope, before the patch
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the gate's contract and stop condition.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The stop condition requires the test to have been saved before the plan, which a file timestamp or a commit can show.
statements.explanation: That is the first element of the stop condition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The regression test should fail against `old` on both inputs.
statements.explanation: The contract says the test fails against old on both inputs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The stop condition is met once Claude reports that the tests pass.
statements.explanation: Claude's report is a claim about a run, not the recorded commands and exit status.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The stop condition is met as soon as the plan names only allowed files, even if no check has been run.
statements.explanation: The test and existing suite must also be run against the current diff, with commands and exit status recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The regression test should pass against `inadequate_patch` on input five.
statements.explanation: The contract says it fails against the constant patch on input five.

questions.source: The gate: reproduction, test, and scope, before the patch
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong versions your tests must catch and the "what a failure looks like" sentence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The failure sentence may be written after reading the test output, since it is then more accurate.
statements.explanation: Written after reading the output, it describes the output rather than testing your understanding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The constant three is a wrong version the gate's test must catch.
statements.explanation: The chapter names it as the wrong version to catch.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The failure sentence should be left undated so it can be reused.
statements.explanation: The sentence is dated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A patch with correct arithmetic that also edits an unrelated configuration file is not a concern for the gate.
statements.explanation: The chapter names that patch as a second wrong version the scope check must catch.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the test and scope check cannot tell the wrong versions from the right patch, the gate is still finished.
statements.explanation: In that case the gate is not finished.

questions.source: The gate: reproduction, test, and scope, before the patch
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the packet may claim and the gate's pass condition.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The packet may claim behavior on the declared integer examples.
statements.explanation: This is the first thing the packet may claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If your test against the three candidates does not give fail on both inputs for `old`, fail on five only for `inadequate_patch`, and pass on both for `intended_patch`, the gate is wrong and should be fixed first.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to fix the gate before anything else.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The packet may claim the function is correct for all inputs.
statements.explanation: The packet cannot claim correctness for all inputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The packet may claim that a person approved the patch.
statements.explanation: The packet cannot claim a person approved it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The packet may claim scope by filename.
statements.explanation: Scope by filename is the second.

questions.source: Read a diff as a behavioral proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reading a unified diff.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the recorded output, the header lines are `--- before.py` and `+++ after.py`.
statements.explanation: Those are the fromfile and tofile names in the recorded diff.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The leading minus and plus lines are arithmetic that the diff performs on the code.
statements.explanation: The markers are change notation, not arithmetic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The plus sign looks right" is an equally good explanation because it transfers across inputs.
statements.explanation: The chapter contrasts that explanation with "the plus sign looks right," which does not transfer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When Claude Code edits your files, the diff is the thing you review, and its narration is a second-hand account.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the diff is the change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A useful review explains that replacing subtraction with addition changes the rule from one below x to one above x.
statements.explanation: That explanation transfers across inputs.

questions.source: Read a diff as a behavioral proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a diff is evidence of.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It shows untracked changes even when the comparison omitted them.
statements.explanation: It does not show untracked changes omitted from the comparison.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It runs the code and reports the result.
statements.explanation: It does not run the code.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It shows what text differs between two supplied strings.
statements.explanation: That is exactly what it shows.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a real Claude Code workflow, you should record the command and scope used to inspect changes and connect the displayed diff to the working tree.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks you to record the command and scope.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It proves that either string was loaded from the intended repository file.
statements.explanation: It does not prove provenance of the strings.

questions.source: Read a diff as a behavioral proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about small diffs and review effort.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Review effort should follow behavioral consequence and uncertainty, not line count.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's rule for allocating effort.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A small diff means the reviewer needs no analysis of behavior.
statements.explanation: Small diffs reduce reading, but small is not safe.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Review effort should scale with the number of changed lines.
statements.explanation: Line count is exactly what effort should not follow.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A one-character operator change can alter every call.
statements.explanation: The `x - 1` to `x + 1` change is such an example.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A small diff is a safe diff.
statements.explanation: Small is not safe: a one-character change can alter every call.

questions.source: Read a diff as a behavioral proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the volume trap.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Irreducibly Human names the volume trap: generation scales with the machine, verification does not.
statements.explanation: This is the shape the chapter attributes to Irreducibly Human.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reading faster closes the gap.
statements.explanation: Reading faster does not close it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the volume trap, the gap between generation and verification fills with output nobody verified.
statements.explanation: Unverified output accumulates in the gap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Shrinking what must be read, and deciding in advance what the reading is for, helps close the gap.
statements.explanation: This is the remedy named.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The gate turns "read everything Claude changed" into "read these files, against this test."
statements.explanation: A test written first and a short allowed-file list do this.

questions.source: Scope is a testable property, not a mood
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the lesson's `review` function.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It adds `out of scope` when any changed filename is not in the allowed set.
statements.explanation: The set difference between changed and allowed names triggers it.

statements.label: B
