statements.text: It stops at the first failed obligation and returns only that reason.
statements.explanation: It accumulates every reason so more than one failure stays visible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It returns a dictionary with `merge_ready` and `reasons`.
statements.explanation: That is the return value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The four reasons it can give are no changes, out of scope, checks failed or absent, and human review required.
statements.explanation: Those are the four strings in the code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `merge_ready` is true when at least one of the four conditions is satisfied.
statements.explanation: `merge_ready` is true only when there are no reasons.

questions.source: Scope is a testable property, not a mood
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about an empty changed list.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function diagnoses why the changed list is empty.
statements.explanation: The function names only `no changes`; diagnosis remains outside.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An empty changed list means the fix is already in place and nothing needs to change.
statements.explanation: The chapter treats it as something needing explanation, not as success.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An empty changed list is rejected.
statements.explanation: The function adds `no changes`.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A claimed fix with no recorded file change deserves explanation, for example that the change was never applied or the wrong comparison was used.
statements.explanation: The chapter gives those possible explanations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For an empty list, the function reports `out of scope`.
statements.explanation: The reason is `no changes`.

questions.source: Scope is a testable property, not a mood
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about filename scope.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Filename scope is complete, so no further review of an allowed file is needed.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls filename scope useful and incomplete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A patch that rewrites unrelated functions in `app.py` is flagged `out of scope` when `app.py` is permitted.
statements.explanation: Such a patch can pass if the file is permitted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The set difference exposes any changed name that is not in the allowed set.
statements.explanation: That is what the set difference does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A renamed or generated file always maps cleanly onto a simple list of names.
statements.explanation: Such files may need a richer representation than a simple list.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The check inspects line-level scope inside an allowed file.
statements.explanation: It does not inspect line-level scope.

questions.source: Scope is a testable property, not a mood
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about widening the allowed list.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Making the allowed list the whole repository is a good response to the limits of filename scope.
statements.explanation: That erases the boundary the check was meant to enforce.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When the list is widened, record who widened it, when, and why, and rerun the checks on the resulting proposal.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks for that record and a rerun.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the patch reveals a legitimate dependency outside the initial scope, you should pause and revise the scope explicitly.
statements.explanation: The revision must be explicit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A finding in the patch can reopen an earlier design decision.
statements.explanation: Design first does not mean freeze the design.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The scope may be widened silently when the added file is obviously needed.
statements.explanation: It can be reopened, but not silently.

questions.source: Scope is a testable property, not a mood
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about scope, correctness, and who decides.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A behaviorally correct patch can include an unrelated change.
statements.explanation: Plus one with an extra config edit is the chapter's example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether the task should grow to include a new file stays with the person who owns the task.
statements.explanation: It is a decision about what the change is for.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude knows who else depends on a configuration file, so it should decide whether the task grows.
statements.explanation: Claude lacks that context, such as who depends on the file and what is in flight on another branch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The review function accumulates every reason so that more than one failed obligation stays visible.
statements.explanation: Reasons are collected, not short-circuited.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A perfectly scoped patch can be wrong.
statements.explanation: The constant three is in scope but wrong.

questions.source: Flags are claims about evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about `checks_passed=True`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Supplying True by hand in a fixture demonstrates the branch of the function.
statements.explanation: That is all a fixture value demonstrates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Supplying True by hand in a fixture shows that a real check passed.
statements.explanation: A hand-supplied True shows no real check passed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The function has no command, output, timestamp, environment, or association between a check and the current diff.
statements.explanation: The surrounding artifact must supply those things.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It means the caller said so.
statements.explanation: The flag is an assertion by the caller.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A packet can contain exact commands, outputs, and exit status, and then derive the Boolean for the policy summary.
statements.explanation: That is how the Boolean should be derived.

questions.source: Flags are claims about evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Claude Code's final message that says the tests pass.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tidy summary is the evidence needed to merge.
statements.explanation: A tidy summary is the finish, not the evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It carries a command, output, and a link to the diff you are about to merge.
statements.explanation: It carries none of these unless you go and get them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It stands exactly where `checks_passed=True` stands.
statements.explanation: Like the flag, it carries no evidence by itself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It is a claim about a run.
statements.explanation: The message reports on a run you did not see.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Chapter 4 made the point about loops that finishing is not succeeding.
statements.explanation: The chapter cites Chapter 4 for this.

questions.source: Flags are claims about evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the `approved` argument.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function requires the literal value True.
statements.explanation: It must be literally True, not just truthy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The function proves the reviewer saw this version of the diff.
statements.explanation: It does not prove the reviewer saw this version.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A required flag proves a person approved.
statements.explanation: A required flag only stops the caller from omitting approval; its meaning depends on the surrounding process.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The function authenticates the reviewer.
statements.explanation: It does not authenticate anyone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Chapter 13 will treat a digest of the proposal as proof of a person's identity.
statements.explanation: Chapter 13 binds a simulated decision to a proposal fingerprint while still refusing to treat a digest as identity.

questions.source: Flags are claims about evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the demo call `review(["app.py"], ["app.py"], True, False)`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It returns `merge_ready` false with the single reason `human review required`.
statements.explanation: Only the approval obligation fails in that call.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The lesson test that supplies True and sees merge-ready is a simulated input, not a human act.
statements.explanation: No human acted in that test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The function aggregates conditions without generating their evidence.
statements.explanation: That keeps the function small and testable and leaves integration to build trustworthy inputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A green indicator is trustworthy regardless of the records behind it.
statements.explanation: A dashboard is only as honest as the records behind its green indicators.

statements.label: E
statements.text: That result is evidence that a person declined the patch.
statements.explanation: It is an executed control-path result, not evidence that anyone declined.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the difference between an audit and a verification.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The audit consults no source and runs on your own model of how the thing should behave.
statements.explanation: The audit uses your held model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once the test has spoken, you can still tell whether your model fired or the test did the work.
statements.explanation: After the test speaks, the two cannot be told apart.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The audit consults the test run to confirm your suspicion.
statements.explanation: The audit consults no source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Verification consults a source such as a test run, a reference, or a recomputation.
statements.explanation: That is what makes it verification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "I audited it by running the tests" correctly describes an audit.
statements.explanation: Verification has leaked into the audit in that sentence.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Audit-First Protocol.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mechanism explains why the output drew your attention, or failed to.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of the mechanism.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The verdict answers whether the output needs verification.
statements.explanation: The verdict is "does this need verification?"

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Check the whole thing" is an acceptable target.
statements.explanation: A target must say what the verification should hunt for.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A complete audit produces a verdict, a target, and a mechanism, in that order.
statements.explanation: The order is verdict, target, mechanism.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Its inviolable rule is to render the verdict and name the mechanism before any lookup.
statements.explanation: That is the one inviolable rule.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about mechanisms and the fourth line of the audit record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter treats that split as an established taxonomy of expert intuition.
statements.explanation: The book labels the split a teaching scaffold, not an established taxonomy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fourth line is filled in after the results, once you know which evidence mattered.
statements.explanation: It commits you to what evidence would count before you see any.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The book names two mechanisms: pattern recognition and anomaly detection against a held model.
statements.explanation: Those are the two named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The audit record is written after reading the plan and diff and before running a command against them.
statements.explanation: That is the stated timing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fourth line asks you to state which verb the record supports.
statements.explanation: The fourth line asks what would change your mind; the verb ladder is a separate device.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's audit of a diff whose body is `return 3` in a function specified as input plus one.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The target is behavior at an input other than two.
statements.explanation: That is the target.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the rule written down turns out not to be the rule the task needed, you should go forward and run the check.
statements.explanation: That finding sends you back to the reproduction, not forward to the check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mechanism is pattern recognition, because the body looks unfamiliar.
statements.explanation: The mechanism is anomaly against a held model, because the body never mentions x.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The verdict is suspect.
statements.explanation: The chapter's verdict is suspect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The audit used one piece of knowledge: that the output depends on the input.
statements.explanation: Without that knowledge the audit goes silent.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the `cannot audit` verdict.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Fluency and groundedness come from the same process and correlate only by accident.
statements.explanation: The book's argument is that your instinct nevertheless reads them as one signal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a diff changes how a library call rounds a value and you have never used the library, your model is silent.
statements.explanation: Your held model has nothing to compare against.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The patch's polish can stand in for the model you lack.
statements.explanation: You may not let polish substitute for the model you lack.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The honest verdict then is `cannot audit`, naming the missing knowledge.
statements.explanation: Naming the missing knowledge is part of the verdict.

statements.label: E
statements.text: That verdict routes you to a source, a person who knows, or a narrower claim.
statements.explanation: Those are the three routes the chapter gives.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about keeping and using the audit record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After a disagreement, revise the record so it reflects what you meant.
statements.explanation: Do not rewrite the record afterward.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A strong intuition is permission to skip required checks.
statements.explanation: An intuition is a reason to investigate, not permission to skip checks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the check agrees with the prediction, your model is working in this corner.
statements.explanation: Agreement is a sign your model is working there.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After the run, put the result beside the prediction.
statements.explanation: That is the comparison the chapter asks for.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the check disagrees, the gap is the learning: either your model was wrong or the check was aimed at the wrong target.
statements.explanation: Those are the two possible explanations.

questions.source: Audit before you verify
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the gate and the audit.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gate is written before the patch exists and says what must hold.
statements.explanation: That is the gate's timing and purpose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Without the audit, the gate's checks run without a question.
statements.explanation: The audit supplies the question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gate and the audit do the same job, so one of them can be skipped.
statements.explanation: They do different jobs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Without the gate, the audit has no standard.
statements.explanation: The gate supplies the standard.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The audit is written after you have seen this particular patch and says what you suspect about it.
statements.explanation: That is the audit's timing and purpose.

questions.source: Accept, revise, or reject
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about an accept decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Accepting means the patch is verified correct for all inputs.
statements.explanation: The example accepts only the declared integer behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An accept decision should name the version reviewed, the scope inspected, the checks run, and the remaining limitations.
statements.explanation: That is the content of a good accept.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Looks good" is a sufficient accept decision because it is short.
statements.explanation: "Looks good" hides the basis of judgment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter's example accept sentence claims correct behavior for all Python inputs.
statements.explanation: It states that broader type behavior was not evaluated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The decision follows the gate, the audit, and the executed checks, not the last sentence Claude Code printed.
statements.explanation: Those three records are what the decision rests on.

questions.source: Accept, revise, or reject
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about revise and reject.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After a revise, the next action is to broaden approval.
statements.explanation: The next action is to change the implementation or narrow the claim honestly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Revise is appropriate when the goal remains valid but the evidence or implementation is insufficient.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's condition for revise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The constant patch is a clean revise case.
statements.explanation: It passes input two but fails a second case for the same rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Rejection claims that every line in the proposal is bad.
statements.explanation: Rejection is a decision about the proposal as a package under the current task boundary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unrelated file change can justify rejection even if the regression passes.
statements.explanation: Reject concerns scope, requirement, or risk, not only test results.

questions.source: Accept, revise, or reject
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who owns the accept, revise, or reject outcome.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude cannot summarize evidence or challenge a rationale.
statements.explanation: Claude can summarize evidence, challenge a rationale, and propose a recommendation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once Claude has proposed a recommendation, the reviewer's job is only to relay it.
statements.explanation: The responsible reviewer owns the decision where the workflow assigns that responsibility.

statements.label: C
statements.text: These labels are human review outcomes.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude's recommendation counts as the decision once it is stated.
statements.explanation: A recommendation is not a decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The AI should invent these labels on behalf of a person when that is convenient.
statements.explanation: They are not values the AI should invent for a person.

questions.source: Choose the verb the record supports
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the verb ladder.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Observe is the most defensible verb for a result from one run under stated conditions.
statements.explanation: One run under stated conditions supports observe.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Engineering evidence usually sits between conclude and prove.
statements.explanation: The chapter says engineering evidence usually sits between observe and find.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ladder is a universal scale of certainty.
statements.explanation: It is the author's editorial instrument, not a universal scale.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Conclude means the motivating question is settled, with alternatives considered and rejected.
statements.explanation: That is the minimum evidence for conclude.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Weakest to strongest, the ladder runs hypothesize, suggest, observe, find, show, demonstrate, conclude, prove.
statements.explanation: That is the frozen order.

questions.source: Choose the verb the record supports
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's table of patch-summary sentences.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "The data suggest the patch implements plus one on the declared integers" is a suggest sentence that the two-input record supplies.
statements.explanation: Two inputs point toward the rule and rule out the constant.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The two-input record supplies the evidence that "The patch completely fixes the bug" requires.
statements.explanation: Conclude needs alternatives rejected, the input domain covered, the suite run, and scope confirmed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The patch is safe to merge" belongs to a person, a named reviewer with the packet attached.
statements.explanation: It is a decision, not an evidence verb.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The patch is safe to merge" is an evidence verb.
statements.explanation: The table marks it as not a finding.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The patch returns three and six for inputs two and five" is an observe sentence that needs the command, inputs, and output, run on the current diff.
statements.explanation: The record supplies it, if it was run after the last edit.

questions.source: Choose the verb the record supports
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about downgrading a verb and about speed versus inspectability.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reader of "suggest" may ask for one more test.
statements.explanation: Weaker verbs invite more checking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reader of "conclude" may merge.
statements.explanation: Strong verbs invite action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter establishes criteria for removing human review once the evidence is strong.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it has not established such criteria.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Replacing "completely fixes" with "the data suggest" can change what a reader does next.
statements.explanation: A downgrade is not cosmetic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Manual review becomes ceremonial when the evidence is weak or the volume exceeds attention.
statements.explanation: The remedy is to improve the packet and the scope.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why you build the baseline yourself.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "You cannot audit what you do not know" is a line from Computational Skepticism.
statements.explanation: The chapter attributes the line to Irreducibly Human.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After building it, you should compare your version with the reference by line count and style.
statements.explanation: Name a difference in behavior, not in line count or style.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You build them anyway because the ability to read its patch and hear that something is off cannot be handed to you by Claude.
statements.explanation: That ability comes from having written them yourself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Your version is the baseline: the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
statements.explanation: It is also the instrument you measure Claude's version against.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude Code can write the candidates, the test, and the policy faster than you can.
statements.explanation: The chapter grants the speed.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the lesson's six tests and the two wrong versions of `review`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A green suite reports on what the suite asserts, and the part nobody asserted is the part nobody checked.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's lesson at lesson scale.

statements.label: B
statements.text: None of the six tests checks the reasons.
statements.explanation: None of the six checks the reasons.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A version of `review` that returns `merge_ready` false for every call is caught only by test 01.
statements.explanation: Only the positive case catches the always-false version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tests 02 through 05 each assert only that `merge_ready` is false.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A version that reports `no changes` as the reason whatever the failure is caught by the lesson tests.
statements.explanation: That version passes all five review tests.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how to hand the work to Claude Code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You may ask Claude to propose additional test cases before it writes the patch.
statements.explanation: Each proposed test is something you adopt or reject.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Put the issue, the reproduction, the failing regression test, and the allowed-file list where Claude Code can read them.
statements.explanation: That is the gate you hand over.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ask for a plan before any edit and check it against the allowed list.
statements.explanation: Plan first, then edit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A plan that names a file outside the list is an assumption Claude may make.
statements.explanation: Such a plan is a decision for you, not an assumption for Claude.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hand Claude your implementation so it can match your approach.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to hand it your implementation.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the order of work and the status of tests in the Use It section.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Run the targeted tests first and write the audit record afterward, so the record reflects the result.
statements.explanation: That order defeats the audit's purpose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the audit record, run the targeted regression and existing tests on the current diff, preserving commands, outputs, and exit status.
statements.explanation: Evidence must attach to the current diff.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After a bounded edit, read the diff and write the audit record before running anything.
statements.explanation: The audit comes before the run.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An adopted test becomes part of the gate.
statements.explanation: The packet records which tests came from Claude.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test Claude writes after seeing its own patch is an independent check.
statements.explanation: It is evidence of what Claude understood, not an independent check.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what to do after Claude's patch and your checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Compare Claude's patch with your baseline and name one difference in behavior.
statements.explanation: The comparison is by behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether your tests are enough can be judged by the system they are testing.
statements.explanation: That cannot be judged by the system under test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A difference can be one Claude silently ignored, which is a defect your test failed to catch.
statements.explanation: The test missed a defect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a deliberately wrong patch that Claude proposes still passes your tests, your tests were too weak.
statements.explanation: You found that out cheaply.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A difference can be a boundary Claude handled that you missed, which is a revision to your gate.
statements.explanation: The gate gets revised.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Anthropic's best practices and an unavailable Claude session.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It also recommends separating exploration, planning, and implementation where appropriate.
statements.explanation: This is the second recommendation cited.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter cites Claude Code best practices, checked during research on 2026-09-06, as recommending executable checks.
statements.explanation: The chapter gives the check date.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a session ran, preserve the actual transcript with the date and displayed model label.
statements.explanation: The date and model label belong in the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The toy review function is Anthropic's runtime.
statements.explanation: The mapping is an adaptation; the toy function is not Anthropic's runtime.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the Claude session is unavailable, report that and complete the offline exercise instead of manufacturing a plan or transcript.
statements.explanation: The chapter forbids invented dialogue.

questions.source: Ship It: the review packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the review packet's contents and how contributions are recorded.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The packet begins with the merge decision and then works backward to the gate.
statements.explanation: It begins with the dated gate, then the pre-patch reproduction, and ends with the decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Contributions recorded by named action say more than percentages, unless the assignment separately requires an estimate.
statements.explanation: Named actions are plan, code proposal, test suggestion, and summary for Claude.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The packet should be arranged as an argument, not a pile of screenshots.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to arrange it as an argument.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude's contributions are best recorded as percentages.
statements.explanation: The chapter prefers named actions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The artifact brief asks for issue, reproduction, plan, before-and-after diff, exact check commands and output, review notes, and merge decision.
statements.explanation: That is the brief's list.

questions.source: A packet is a chain, not a folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a packet as a chain.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If one link points to an earlier version, the packet is still sound as long as all the files are present.
statements.explanation: The packet can look complete while its argument has broken.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Putting the right filenames in one directory does not guarantee that the records refer to one another.
statements.explanation: Presence of files is not correspondence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plan should address the issue and respect the allowed scope.
statements.explanation: The plan ties to the issue and scope.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The issue should identify the behavior the failing test reproduces.
statements.explanation: The issue ties to the test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The test outputs should come after the current diff, and the decision should name that same proposal.
statements.explanation: The outputs and decision tie to the current diff.

questions.source: A packet is a chain, not a folder
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about identifiers, chronology, and negative space in a packet.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Otherwise use a saved diff digest or a dated working-tree description.
statements.explanation: These are the fallbacks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keep output as searchable text, because a pasted green badge without its command tells the reviewer less than it appears to.
statements.explanation: Searchable text beats a badge.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Use a commit hash when a real commit exists.
statements.explanation: That is the preferred identifier.

statements.label: D
statements.text: List the relevant checks you did not run and the files you did not inspect.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls this retaining negative space.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Chronology settles correspondence, so a test run after an edit must target the right module.
statements.explanation: A test run after an edit can still target the wrong module, so record the working directory and target.

questions.source: Keep the failure in the record
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about keeping the failure in the record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After repairing the harness, rerun and keep both records.
statements.explanation: Both the failed and repaired runs stay in the record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A syntax error in the harness shows that the candidate is wrong.
statements.explanation: A harness error does not show the candidate is wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The move from failure to correction is often the strongest demonstration that the final test matters.
statements.explanation: The failure shows what the test caught.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once a later revision passes, delete the earlier failure evidence to keep the packet clean.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to delete the evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unsuccessful patch deserves the same provenance discipline as a successful one.
statements.explanation: Record what version failed and which command exposed the defect.

questions.source: Keep the failure in the record
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how to regard the constant patch and AI involvement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Review should avoid both automatic deference to AI output and automatic suspicion of it.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's stance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Evidence-based rather than AI-proof" means the workflow proves AI involvement safe in general.
statements.explanation: The workflow only exposes the proposal, scope, checks, and accountable decision so this change can be judged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a human rather than Claude proposed it, `return 3` would behave differently.
statements.explanation: Attribution matters for the contribution record but does not change what `return 3` does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The constant patch is not malicious and need not be called foolish.
statements.explanation: The diagnosis is about code and evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It is a locally adequate response to one inadequate test.
statements.explanation: Many review failures arise that way.

questions.source: A worked decision from beginning to end
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the worked decision on the two candidate patches.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The example ends with a signature from the responsible human, recorded with the proposal version.
statements.explanation: The book cannot synthesize that event, so the example ends with a bounded recommendation, not a fabricated signature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The decision for the `return 3` candidate is reject.
statements.explanation: The decision is revise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For the `x + 1` candidate, the policy function still returns `human review required` when approved is false.
statements.explanation: That is correct for the simulated call, since no person is represented as deciding.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The `return 3` candidate is in scope and passes the input-two regression.
statements.explanation: Its diff is in scope and input two passes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It fails input five because three does not equal six.
statements.explanation: The expected value at five is six.

questions.source: A worked decision from beginning to end
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two changed assumptions in the worked decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the plus-one patch also edits an unrelated configuration file, the behavior tests can still pass.
statements.explanation: Behavior and scope are separate obligations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The right response includes inspecting why the file changed, reverting it or revising the scope explicitly, and rerunning the checks on the resulting proposal.
statements.explanation: Those are the steps given.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In that case the review function adds `out of scope`.
statements.explanation: The extra file is outside the allowed list.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the requirement was never confirmed, thorough tests can repair an invalid requirement.
statements.explanation: Testing cannot repair an invalid requirement; reopen the gate instead.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The right response is to ignore the file because the arithmetic is right.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to ignore it.

questions.source: The sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the evidence does not support signing, withholding is an honest result.
statements.explanation: A sign-off that claims more than the record supports is the failure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the decision is only your recommendation for someone else, present it as the final decision.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to label it as a recommendation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The template includes Proposal, Checked, How, Not checked, Not claiming, a strongest-verb line, Decision, and Signed or withheld.
statements.explanation: Those are the template's lines.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can draft the words of the sign-off in seconds, but you should write it from your record.
statements.explanation: The draft will be fluent, which is why it must come from the record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The "Not checked" line is the one an AI-written sign-off tends to leave out.
statements.explanation: The writing system has no record of what you did not do.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first three rows of the driver's seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For drafting the patch, you build your own baseline first and compare the two.
statements.explanation: You cannot audit what you have not built.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For the regression test, Claude writes it before the patch and you adopt it.
statements.explanation: You write the test before the patch; Claude proposes extra cases and a wrong patch that survives.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stating the rule and which inputs count as the defect stays with you, because the requirement lives in your task, not in the code.
statements.explanation: Claude can implement a wrong rule perfectly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test written after the patch tends to be independent of it.
statements.explanation: A test written after the patch tends to bless it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can propose minimal reproductions and edge inputs, and run them.
statements.explanation: That is Claude's role in the first row.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the last three rows of the driver's seat table and the evidence of the split.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude runs commands and captures output and exit status, while you choose which command bears on which claim.
statements.explanation: You also record what was not run.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you cannot point to the transcript line, timestamp, or edit that shows a test written before the patch, the split happened in your head and not in the record.
statements.explanation: The packet should record one test written first and one place you changed or rejected something.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A correct output can never be about the wrong target.
statements.explanation: The chapter says a correct output can be about the wrong target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For accept, revise, or reject, Claude can summarize evidence, challenge the rationale, and flag an overclaim.
statements.explanation: Your name is on the merge, so you decide, choose the verb, and sign or withhold.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude should report which files it needs and why, and you decide the allowed list and every revision to it.
statements.explanation: You know the callers, the branches, and whose release this is.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Verify and reflect section.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing test from before a later edit is stale evidence for the current proposal.
statements.explanation: Inspect the current diff after the checks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a check disagreed with your prediction, say which side was wrong and leave the record as written.
statements.explanation: Either your model or the aim of the check was wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Review evidence must remain attached to the exact proposal.
statements.explanation: That is the section's opening principle.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A narrower verb is timid even when it accurately communicates the tested boundary.
statements.explanation: A narrower verb is not timid when it matches the tested boundary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the review function received True only in a fixture, you may leave that out of the report.
statements.explanation: If True came only from a fixture, say so.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Assessments.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the Stale check, an earlier test result remains sufficient even after you alter the candidate.
statements.explanation: The earlier result no longer justifies the current patch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Assessments carry no points.
statements.explanation: They are ungraded practice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the Stale check, you restore the candidate by changing the reference.
statements.explanation: Restore through a new learner edit, not by changing the reference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the Revise the claim exercise, Claude can both list the strong verbs and judge the evidence behind them.
statements.explanation: Claude can list the strong verbs, but not judge the evidence behind them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Use the paired lesson's knowledge check, preserving your answers before viewing explanations.
statements.explanation: Answers are preserved before explanations are viewed.

questions.source: What you can now defend
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what you can now defend.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its Booleans create evidence rather than summarize it.
statements.explanation: The Booleans summarize evidence; they do not create it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The review policy's four obligations are that a change exists, changed filenames stay in scope, checks are asserted as passed, and approval is asserted as present.
statements.explanation: Those are the four obligations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You conducted: the reproduction, the test, the scope, and the stop condition were yours and came before the patch.
statements.explanation: That is the conducting job at this scale.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A final sentence from Claude Code summarizes a run in the same way the Booleans summarize evidence.
statements.explanation: Both are claims, not evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You drove: Claude proposed and implemented while you set the scope, ran your own tests, and held the merge.
statements.explanation: That is the driving job at this scale.

questions.source: Which source material reached the system?
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the section on which source material reached the system.

statements.label: A
statements.text: That can happen even when the resulting patch is syntactically tidy.
statements.explanation: Coherence is visible in a diff, but groundedness depends on what Claude was given.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The review packet tells you which information was selected before the change was proposed.
statements.explanation: The packet shows what changed and which tests ran, not what was selected.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Chapter 7 builds a tiny retrieval system using token-count vectors, cosine similarity, and ranking.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's preview.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A source-grounded task can fail upstream if the relevant passage never entered context.
statements.explanation: Upstream selection can fail.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Chapter 7 will show that ranking answers whether the selected passage supports the claim.
statements.explanation: Ranking cannot answer that; the question is left for after ranking.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Computational Skepticism note on verb choice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ladder keeps inferential caution and evidential strength on two separate lines.
statements.explanation: The ladder flattens them onto one line, which is why verb ladders wobble.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You cannot run the check on your own summary, because the feeling that your verb was right came from how the evidence sat in your head.
statements.explanation: A re-read no longer has that feeling's source.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mismatches you made are the ones you can easily see when you re-read your own summary.
statements.explanation: They are the ones you cannot see.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A peer's critique should name the sentence, the verb, the evidence that verb requires, and the verb the record supports.
statements.explanation: The note gives a worked example: "completely fixed" versus "suggest."

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Too strong" is a sufficient critique.
statements.explanation: "Too strong" is not a critique.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Conducting AI note on the audit.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing command is permission to merge.
statements.explanation: A passing command is evidence, not permission to merge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The follow-up question asks what specific knowledge made the finding possible, and whether a competent generalist without it would have caught the same thing.
statements.explanation: That is the book's follow-up question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A verdict you cannot explain is one you cannot teach, cannot defend to a skeptic, and cannot trust yourself.
statements.explanation: Without the mechanism you cannot tell whether you reasoned or merely reacted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For `return 3`, the answer is that a great deal of specialized knowledge was needed.
statements.explanation: For `return 3` the answer is almost nothing; anyone who knows the rule depends on x catches it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For a rounding change in an unfamiliar library, the answer is a great deal, which tells you who must review it and what belongs in "Not checked."
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's contrast.

questions.source: Chapter 7 (opening, before the first section)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two constructed cases that open the chapter (the office-hours query and the tuition-refund query).

statements.label: A
statements.text: A document saying "Office hours by appointment" can rank highly for the query "office hours" because the shared words are visible to the retriever.
statements.explanation: The first case ranks the document highly on visible shared words.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For the query "tuition refund", when the only relevant document says "fee reimbursement", the retriever returns nothing because its representation sees no shared token.
statements.explanation: In the second case the retriever returns nothing because no token is shared.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the tuition-refund case, the retriever returns the fee-reimbursement document at a low rank with a small positive score.
statements.explanation: The document is not returned at all, at any rank.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A human reader would also fail to see the relationship between "tuition refund" and "fee reimbursement".
statements.explanation: A human reader can see the relationship.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both cases are presented as measurements taken from a deployed Claude Cowork system.
statements.explanation: Both are constructed cases from the course's offline exercise.

questions.source: Chapter 7 (opening, before the first section)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the results recorded by the research run.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The run records a cosine similarity of 2 / sqrt(6), approximately 0.8164965809, between "office hours" and "office hours appointment".
statements.explanation: This is the recorded score for the published pair.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The run records no result for the synonym pair.
statements.explanation: The synonym pair produces no result under the count-vector implementation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The run records deterministic ordering for tied scores.
statements.explanation: Tied scores come back in a deterministic order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The recorded results are measurements of how Claude Cowork retrieves documents.
statements.explanation: They are results of the displayed implementation, not measurements of Cowork.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The recorded results show how neural embeddings treat synonyms.
statements.explanation: They are not measurements of neural embeddings either.

questions.source: Chapter 7 (opening, before the first section)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what happens when Claude sits downstream of a retrieval step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the synonym case, a step quietly dropped the only source that mattered, and nothing in the output says so.
statements.explanation: The chapter describes exactly this silent drop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the evidence reaching Claude is incomplete, Claude signals the gap through hedged wording in its answer.
statements.explanation: Claude writes a fluent answer from whatever reached it, without flagging gaps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: What Claude receives includes a note saying what was left out.
statements.explanation: Nothing it received says what was left out.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fluent answer built on incomplete evidence reads differently from one built on complete evidence.
statements.explanation: The sentence reads the same whether the evidence was complete or not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once the retriever ranks the "by appointment" passage highly, no human question remains about whether it says when to show up.
statements.explanation: A human still has to ask whether "by appointment" says when to show up.

questions.source: Chapter 7 (opening, before the first section)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three jobs the chapter applies to retrieval.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chapter 1 named the three jobs that stay with you: conduct, check, drive.
statements.explanation: The chapter attributes the three jobs to Chapter 1.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retrieval is where these jobs bite hardest, because it makes the most decisions and leaves the fewest traces.
statements.explanation: Many decisions and few traces make retrieval the hardest case.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Conduct means you decide what reaches Claude's context before the task runs.
statements.explanation: Conduct is the pre-task decision about Claude's context.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Check includes the points that relevance is not entailment and that ranking turns scores into omissions.
statements.explanation: Both phrases are the chapter's statement of Check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Drive means Claude decides what a source means in the world.
statements.explanation: Claude ranks and quotes; what a source means in the world is your reading.

questions.source: Chapter 7 (opening, before the first section)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how Chapter 7 relates to the earlier chapters and to the assistant it assumes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chapter 6 reviewed a proposed code change against its diff and tests, and Chapter 7 moves earlier to ask which source material reached the system.
statements.explanation: The chapter places retrieval earlier in the pipeline than the Chapter 6 review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A clean review packet can recover a passage that was ranked out of the selected context.
statements.explanation: A review packet cannot recover a passage that was never in the corpus or was ranked out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Python retriever runs offline with the standard library and spends no direct API credits.
statements.explanation: The retriever is offline and uses the standard library only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If you do not perform an actual interface task, you may write the output Claude Cowork would probably have produced so the packet looks complete.
statements.explanation: Without a live run, keep the packet labeled as proposed rather than inventing one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If you do perform an actual interface task, you should preserve its sources, prompt, output, and date.
statements.explanation: Those four items are what a real interface task must preserve.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter says you should be able to do after working through it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Turn short text into a token-count vector.
statements.explanation: The first listed ability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calculate cosine similarity by hand.
statements.explanation: Hand calculation is a listed ability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Predict ranking changes and explain deterministic tie-breaking.
statements.explanation: Both are listed together.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Distinguish no overlap from absence in the corpus.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists this distinction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Certify that a selected passage supports a claim from its cosine score.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists identifying a claim unsupported by selected passages, and a score is not support.

questions.source: What reaches Claude is the end of a chain of omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the seven narrowing stages between a stack of documents and a sentence in a report.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Eligibility, the first stage, decides which sources may be used at all.
statements.explanation: Eligibility is set by permission and scope.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ingestion decides whether an eligible file became text in the corpus.
statements.explanation: Ingestion is whether the eligible file became corpus text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Representation is decided by the scoring rule and k.
statements.explanation: The vectorizer decides representation; the scoring rule and k decide scoring and cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Use, the stage where the answer relies on shown passages, is decided by you rather than by Claude.
statements.explanation: Claude decides use, while generating.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The path has five stages.
statements.explanation: There are seven stages.

questions.source: What reaches Claude is the end of a chain of omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the seven stages leave visible in the final prose.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Five of the seven stages leave nothing in the final prose.
statements.explanation: Eligibility, ingestion, representation, scoring and cutoff, and selection leave nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Use leaves a citation in the prose, if you required one.
statements.explanation: A citation is the only trace of Use, and only if required.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A citation shows that the cited passage supports the claim.
statements.explanation: A citation asserts a relationship rather than showing it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Claim stage shows up in the prose through its verbs.
statements.explanation: The verbs are what the Claim stage leaves.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer who starts by judging the answer starts before any of the seven decisions have been made.
statements.explanation: All seven decisions have already happened when you read the answer, and none is visible.

questions.source: What reaches Claude is the end of a chain of omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's use of Computational Skepticism for AI on missing data.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The book's point is that you cannot compute the missingness of rows that never existed.
statements.explanation: The chapter quotes this as the point it keeps returning to.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The book's central question is why there are exactly N rows, and what N was supposed to be.
statements.explanation: The N question is the move the chapter borrows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The join that silently dropped differently formatted identifiers is presented as a single sourced incident.
statements.explanation: The illustration is labeled a composite of familiar failures, not a single sourced incident.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the chapter's analogy, the score table plays the role of the join.
statements.explanation: Ingestion is the join; the score table is the histogram.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In the chapter's analogy, a score table is precise about what arrived and silent about what did not.
statements.explanation: That is how the chapter describes the score table.

questions.source: What reaches Claude is the end of a chain of omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the boundary the chapter draws using the first tier of Irreducibly Human.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Finding a passage is a pattern task, where the machine is better at the task as specified.
statements.explanation: The book states the boundary this way for the first tier.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The human's remaining job ends once the machine has finished the pattern task.
statements.explanation: The human notices when the specification is wrong or the task only looked like a pattern task.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deciding whether a found passage answers the question is also a pattern task.
statements.explanation: Deciding whether a passage answers the question is not a pattern task.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Retrieval is specified by your query, representation, corpus, and k.
statements.explanation: Those four items are the specification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A ranking can be excellent only if the specification behind it is right.
statements.explanation: The ranking can be excellent while the specification is wrong.

questions.source: A representation decides what can match
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the count-vector representation keeps and discards.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Office office hours" becomes a mapping in which office has count two and hours has count one.
statements.explanation: The text is lowercased and the occurrences are counted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "hours office" and "office hours" receive the same vector.
statements.explanation: Frequency is kept and word order is discarded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Office" and "office" are separate coordinates because capitalization is preserved.
statements.explanation: The text is lowercased first, so capitalization is discarded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Most coordinates are zero, so the implementation stores only the tokens that appear.
statements.explanation: Only tokens that appear are stored.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Discarding word order is a failure that occurs after retrieval.
statements.explanation: It is a consequence of the information the representation retains, not a failure after retrieval.

questions.source: A representation decides what can match
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about tokenization with the regular expression `\b\w+\b`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An apostrophe splits "don't" into don and t.
statements.explanation: The chapter traces "don't stop" into don, t, stop.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hyphen splits "fee-reimbursement" into fee and reimbursement.
statements.explanation: The hyphen is not a word character.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An underscore does not split a token, because it counts as a word character.
statements.explanation: The underscore counts as a word character, so it splits nothing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The behavior of `\w` follows Python's regular-expression rules, not a universal linguistic analysis.
statements.explanation: The chapter says this explicitly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chapter's tokenization results can be assumed to hold for multilingual and code-heavy corpora.
statements.explanation: Do not infer performance for such corpora without testing their actual inputs.

questions.source: A representation decides what can match
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the limits of the count-vector representation and of the test `vector("Hi HI")["hi"] == 2`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test checks both lowercasing and counting for one case.
statements.explanation: It checks both behaviors, but only for one case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test proves that capitalization is irrelevant to meaning.
statements.explanation: It does not show that capitalization never matters.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Count vectors sacrifice word order and synonymy in exchange for visible overlap and transparent arithmetic.
statements.explanation: Those are the stated trade-offs of count vectors.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The right question about a representation is whether it is intelligent.
statements.explanation: The right question is whether the retained features suit the evidence-selection task and whether the misses are visible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Performance on adversarial corpora can be inferred from the chapter's short English fixtures.
statements.explanation: Such inference needs testing on the actual inputs.

questions.source: A representation decides what can match
questions.stem: A learner tokenizes "Don't stop, don't STOP" with the chapter's `vector` function (lowercase, then `\b\w+\b`, then Counter). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The resulting Counter has don with count 2.
statements.explanation: The text yields don twice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The resulting Counter has "don't" as a single key.
statements.explanation: The apostrophe splits the contraction into don and t.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The resulting Counter has stop with count 2.
statements.explanation: stop and STOP lowercase to the same token.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The resulting Counter has t with count 2.
statements.explanation: Each "don't" contributes one t.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The resulting Counter keeps the comma and the apostrophe as tokens.
statements.explanation: Punctuation is not captured by `\w+`.

questions.source: Cosine from first principles
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the dot product and vector length used for cosine similarity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The dot product multiplies matching coordinates and sums the products.
statements.explanation: That is the definition given for q . d.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tokens absent from one side contribute that token's count from the other side to the sum.
statements.explanation: Tokens absent from one side contribute zero.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The dot product shrinks as vectors grow, which is why it is normalized.
statements.explanation: The dot product also grows when vectors grow.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The implementation normalizes the dot product by the vectors' lengths.
statements.explanation: Cosine divides by both lengths.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Euclidean length of q is the sum of its counts.
statements.explanation: The length is the square root of the sum of squared counts.

questions.source: Cosine from first principles
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the published example: the query "office hours" against the document "office hours appointment".

statements.label: A
statements.text: The query's length is the square root of 2.
statements.explanation: Two tokens with count one each give sqrt(2).

statements.label: B
statements.text: The document's length is the square root of 3.
statements.explanation: Three tokens with count one each give sqrt(3).

statements.label: C
statements.text: The dot product is 2.
statements.explanation: office and hours each contribute one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cosine is 2 / sqrt(6), approximately 0.8165.
statements.explanation: 2 / (sqrt(2) * sqrt(3)) = 2 / sqrt(6).

statements.label: E
statements.text: The dot product is 3, because the document has three tokens.
statements.explanation: Only shared tokens contribute to the dot product, so it is 2.

questions.source: Cosine from first principles
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the hand calculation of 2 / sqrt(6) does and does not establish.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It establishes a lexical relationship under this representation.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it proves a lexical relationship under this representation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It proves that the document answers every question involving office hours.
statements.explanation: It does not show the document answers every question about office hours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Stanford information-retrieval text supports the normalized dot-product formulation used here.
statements.explanation: The source supports the formulation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The Stanford text turns this small implementation into a complete production retrieval system.
statements.explanation: Our use remains a small lexical example.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If an implementation disagrees with your hand-calculated score for this pair, you should trust the implementation over your arithmetic.
statements.explanation: A differing implementation, yours or Claude's, is the one to distrust.

questions.source: Cosine from first principles
questions.stem: A query is "office hours". Check each statement that is true about its cosine against the documents named.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Against "office hours by appointment" (four tokens, each count one), the dot product is 2.
statements.explanation: office and hours each contribute one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Against "office hours by appointment", the cosine is 2 / (sqrt(2) * 2), about 0.7071.
statements.explanation: The document length is sqrt(4) = 2, giving 2 / (1.414 * 2).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Against "office hours office hours" (office 2, hours 2), the cosine is 1.0, because identical direction scores one whatever the lengths.
statements.explanation: The dot product is 4 and the lengths are sqrt(2) and sqrt(8), so the cosine is 4 / 4.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Against "office" alone, the cosine is 0.5.
statements.explanation: The dot product is 1 and the lengths are sqrt(2) and 1, so the cosine is about 0.7071.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Against "hours office", the cosine is lower than against "office hours" because the word order differs.
statements.explanation: Order is discarded, so "hours office" scores 1.0, the same as "office hours".

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the `retrieve` function does.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It calculates every document's score before filtering.
statements.explanation: The function scores every declared document and filters afterwards.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It returns the dropped documents together with the reason each was dropped.
statements.explanation: The function does not return what it dropped or why.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It takes the top k rows first and removes nonpositive scores afterwards.
statements.explanation: Nonpositive scores are removed before the top-k slice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It always returns exactly k rows when the corpus holds at least k documents.
statements.explanation: It returns at most k rows, and only positive scores.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It scores only the documents that share at least one token with the query.
statements.explanation: Every document is scored; zero-overlap ones then score zero and are removed.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how `retrieve` validates k.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zero or negative k is rejected instead of silently returning nothing.
statements.explanation: The function raises a ValueError for a k below 1.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Boolean k is accepted because True equals 1.
statements.explanation: A Boolean is not accepted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The type check asks for exactly int.
statements.explanation: The check is `type(k) is not int`.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An isinstance check would let True slip through as a valid k.
statements.explanation: That is why the gate lists the isinstance check as a wrong version.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A k of 0 returns an empty list without raising an error.
statements.explanation: A zero k is rejected with an error.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how `retrieve` sorts its results.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The negative score in the sort key puts higher similarities first.
statements.explanation: The first sort key is the negated score.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The document key breaks ties in ascending order.
statements.explanation: The second sort key is the document key, ascending.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Relying on incidental mapping order for ties makes equal-score selection easier to explain.
statements.explanation: Incidental mapping order would make equal-score selection harder to explain.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ties are broken by descending document key.
statements.explanation: The tie-break is ascending, not descending.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sort uses a single key, the score.
statements.explanation: The sort uses two keys.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about top-k selection among positive matches.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Top-k introduces an exclusion even among documents with positive scores.
statements.explanation: The cutoff removes some positive matches.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With k equal to one, a second relevant document can be omitted because another score is larger.
statements.explanation: A larger competing score pushes it out.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With k equal to one, a second relevant document can be omitted because its tie-break key comes later.
statements.explanation: An equal score with a later key also loses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The returned list is selected candidates under a particular scoring and cutoff rule.
statements.explanation: That is how the chapter describes the returned list.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The returned list is all the available evidence.
statements.explanation: The returned list is not all available evidence.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the synonym miss between "tuition refund" and "fee reimbursement".

statements.label: A
statements.text: The two phrases have disjoint token sets under this vectorizer, so their dot product is zero.
statements.explanation: No token is shared, so the dot product is zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A human reader can see the relationship even though the retriever cannot.
statements.explanation: This is the opening contrast between human and retriever.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The zero-score document is excluded before top-k selection.
statements.explanation: Nonpositive scores are removed before the k cutoff.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A zero score is proof that the document is irrelevant.
statements.explanation: Zero means no counted token overlap, not irrelevance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a large enough k, the retriever would return the zero-score document.
statements.explanation: Zero-score documents are filtered out whatever k is.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a high similarity score does and does not show.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A document can repeat the query's terms while discussing a different policy, time period, or population.
statements.explanation: Repeated terms do not guarantee the same policy, period, or population.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A high score therefore does not prove that the passage is adequate.
statements.explanation: The chapter says a high score does not prove adequacy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lexical similarity is a verdict on whether a passage answers the claim.
statements.explanation: It is a candidate-selection signal, not a verdict.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A high score lets the next review skip reading the passage.
statements.explanation: The next review must inspect the passage against the actual claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A score precise to ten decimal places settles the question of support.
statements.explanation: Precision of the score does not turn relevance into support.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the audit view and what `retrieve` leaves out.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A list of winners gives you the same view the final prose does, one stage earlier.
statements.explanation: Winners alone hide the omissions, as the prose does.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The audit view lists every document with its score.
statements.explanation: The gate asks for every document with its score.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each document's fate in the audit view is one of selected, below the cutoff, or zero overlap.
statements.explanation: Those are the three fates the gate names.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fate of "rejected by Claude" is one of the audit view's three outcomes.
statements.explanation: The three fates do not include a Claude rejection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You can see an omission by reading the ranked list of winners alone.
statements.explanation: To see an omission you have to compute it.

questions.source: Ranking turns scores into omissions
questions.stem: A corpus is {a: "office hours appointment", b: "hours office", c: "office", d: "appointment only"}, the query is "office hours", and k is 2. Check each statement that is true of the audit view.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Document b is selected with a score of 1.0.
statements.explanation: "hours office" has the same vector as the query.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Document a is selected with a score of about 0.8165.
statements.explanation: dot 2, lengths sqrt(2) and sqrt(3), giving 2 / sqrt(6).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Document c has a positive score of about 0.7071 and its fate is "below the cutoff".
statements.explanation: dot 1 over sqrt(2) * 1 is about 0.7071, and it falls outside the top two.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Document d has the fate "zero overlap".
statements.explanation: "appointment only" shares no token with the query.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Document c's omission shows that it is irrelevant to the query.
statements.explanation: Omission is not proof of irrelevance; c simply scored below the cutoff.

questions.source: The synonym miss and a dangerous repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the synonym map as a repair for the synonym miss.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The tempting repair for a paraphrase miss is a synonym map applied before vectorization.
statements.explanation: The chapter names the synonym map as the tempting repair.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The decision hidden in a synonym map is who gets to say that two words mean the same thing.
