statements.explanation: That is the decision the repair hides.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Mapping tuition to fee is safe in every sentence.
statements.explanation: Fee is not interchangeable with tuition in every sentence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Proposing a map is Claude's work, while deciding whether to adopt it is yours.
statements.explanation: Whether two words are interchangeable is a fact about policy and population, so you decide.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Expanding both queries and documents leaves counts and vector lengths unchanged.
statements.explanation: Expanding both sides can change counts and vector lengths.

questions.source: The synonym miss and a dangerous repair
questions.stem: A learner maps tuition to fee and refund to reimbursement in the query only. The query is "tuition refund eligibility" and the document is "fee reimbursement for travel". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Before the mapping, the cosine is 0.0, because the two texts share no token.
statements.explanation: No token is shared before the mapping.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the mapping, the query is "fee reimbursement eligibility" and the cosine is about 0.5774.
statements.explanation: dot 2, lengths sqrt(3) and sqrt(4), so 2 / sqrt(12), about 0.5774.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The rise in the score shows that the travel document answers the tuition-refund eligibility question.
statements.explanation: Literal mapped overlap can rise while the policy question stays unanswered.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When you encode such a map, you should record the exact map and whether it applies to queries, documents, or both.
statements.explanation: The map is data that influences the result and needs provenance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This example is evidence about a real university's refund rule.
statements.explanation: It is a constructed counterexample, not evidence about a real rule.

questions.source: The synonym miss and a dangerous repair
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the tension between recall and review burden.

statements.label: A
statements.text: More recall can also return more distractors.
statements.explanation: More returned material includes more distractors.

statements.label: B
statements.text: More restrictive matching reduces the chance of omitting paraphrases.
statements.explanation: More restrictive matching can omit paraphrases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The cost of missing material versus reviewing extra candidates is the task owner's to price.
statements.explanation: That cost belongs to the task owner.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter establishes one universal threshold that balances this tension.
statements.explanation: The chapter does not establish a universal threshold.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recall can be raised without any added review burden.
statements.explanation: More returned material means more to review.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about relevance and entailment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Retrieval asks which documents are similar enough, under a rule, to inspect first.
statements.explanation: Retrieval selects what to inspect first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Evidence review asks whether a selected passage supports a specific claim.
statements.explanation: Evidence review checks support for a claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passage saying office hours are by appointment is irrelevant to office hours.
statements.explanation: The passage is relevant to office hours.

statements.label: D
statements.text: That passage supplies the "every Tuesday at two" time in a generated answer.
statements.explanation: The passage does not give the Tuesday time, so that is an unsupported addition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The review question can be collapsed into the retrieval question when the score is precise to ten decimal places.
statements.explanation: The second question cannot be collapsed into the first.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about claim-by-claim evidence review.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The review works claim by claim.
statements.explanation: The chapter prescribes claim-by-claim review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For each claim, you quote or identify the exact source passage within the permitted material.
statements.explanation: The passage must be identified exactly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For each claim, you record whether the passage supports, contradicts, or does not resolve it.
statements.explanation: Those are the three outcomes to record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A document-level citation counts as support for every sentence in a paragraph.
statements.explanation: A document-level citation is not support for every sentence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cited claim needs checking only at the paragraph level.
statements.explanation: Paragraph-level checking can hide an unsupported part.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who runs the support check.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the process that wrote the sentence also vouches for its citation, you have the first opinion run twice.
statements.explanation: Self-vouching is one opinion counted twice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude can quote the passage, propose a label, and hunt for the sentence that would change the label.
statements.explanation: That saves you the search.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The label that goes in the table is the one Claude proposed, because it saw the sentence first.
statements.explanation: The table label is the one you gave after reading the original.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When you disagree with Claude's label, noting that you read it differently is enough.
statements.explanation: You write down the sentence that decides it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When you disagree with Claude, you defer to it because it processed more text.
statements.explanation: The chapter assigns the final label to you.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about overriding Claude's label, following the discipline borrowed from Irreducibly Human.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A human correction adds signal whenever the human disagrees with the machine.
statements.explanation: A correction adds signal when it names what the machine misses in this kind of case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A human correction adds noise when it is a wordless hunch.
statements.explanation: A wordless hunch adds noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The book draws its line specifically for source labeling.
statements.explanation: The book draws it for validated imaging systems and statistical forecasts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "I read it differently" counts as a check.
statements.explanation: The chapter says "I read it differently" is not a check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "This sentence names the term but not the date" is a well-formed override.
statements.explanation: It names exactly what the passage lacks.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about source identifiers and insufficient evidence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The format contract from Chapter 2 can require source identifiers.
statements.explanation: A source-identifier requirement is useful for traceability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Has a source identifier" is a different obligation from "is supported by that source".
statements.explanation: The identifier is structure; support is substance.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A structural pass shows that the cited source supports the claim.
statements.explanation: A structural pass names only the obligation it passed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the selected context is insufficient, the correct result may be an abstention or a request for another source.
statements.explanation: An abstention or request for another source can be the correct output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When the selected context is insufficient, you should fill the gap with a plausible answer and cite the nearest passage.
statements.explanation: The chapter warns against filling the gap and citing the nearest passage.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about supplying an entire corpus versus a bounded selection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: More text can include the missing evidence.
statements.explanation: The whole corpus may hold what a selection missed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: More text can also contain contradictions and irrelevant material.
statements.explanation: It can also add contradictions and distractors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: More text can expose more content than a bounded task should.
statements.explanation: A bounded task may not warrant exposing everything.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Context selection is an engineering and data-governance decision.
statements.explanation: The chapter frames selection as engineering and governance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Supplying the entire corpus is automatically superior to a selection.
statements.explanation: The chapter says supplying everything is not automatically superior.

questions.source: Relevance and entailment are separate checks; Anthropics
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Anthropic's context-engineering article as the chapter uses it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter says the article was checked during the research pass on 2026-09-06.
statements.explanation: The research-pass check date is given in the chapter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The article discusses context as a designed collection of instructions, tools, data, and history.
statements.explanation: That is how the chapter summarizes the article.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter cites the article to claim that its count vectors implement Claude's context mechanisms.
statements.explanation: It is for comparing selection strategies, not for that claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter closes by asking you to compare deliberate context selection with supplying an entire corpus, and to record what your selection retains and omits.
statements.explanation: This is the closing Anthropics task.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chapter says lexical counts are the same thing as neural embeddings.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to imply that lexical counts are neural embeddings.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the retriever's contract in the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Cosine of count vectors is never negative.
statements.explanation: Counts are nonnegative, so the cosine cannot go below zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `retrieve` returns only positive scores, best first, equal scores in key order, at most k rows.
statements.explanation: That is the contract's statement of the return value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The audit view returns only the selected rows.
statements.explanation: The audit view returns every document with its score and one of three fates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The retriever may claim that a passage is relevant in the sense a reader means.
statements.explanation: It may claim only a ranking of overlap under one representation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The retriever may claim that its ranking is complete and that the top passage is supported.
statements.explanation: It may not claim completeness or support.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong versions your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Sorting worst-first is a wrong version that must fail at least one test.
statements.explanation: Worst-first sorting is on the list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Breaking ties by insertion order is a wrong version that must fail at least one test.
statements.explanation: Insertion-order ties are on the list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking k with `isinstance` so that True slips through is a wrong version that must fail at least one test.
statements.explanation: The Boolean slip-through is on the list.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Dropping the zero filter is a wrong version that must fail at least one test.
statements.explanation: So is dropping the zero filter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using Counter to count tokens is one of the listed wrong versions.
statements.explanation: Counter is part of the reference design, not a wrong version.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the lesson's six tests, as the gate reads them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The relevance test has a single positive-scoring document, so best-first and worst-first sorts return the same thing.
statements.explanation: A single positive document cannot distinguish the sort directions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Several of the six tests have two equal scores, so tie-breaking is already covered.
statements.explanation: No test has two equal scores.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The invalid-k test uses zero, which an `isinstance` check also rejects.
statements.explanation: Zero fails under both type checks, so it does not catch the isinstance version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: No test makes k smaller than the number of positive matches.
statements.explanation: No test truncates positive matches.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The way to confirm these gaps is to mutate a copy of the reference.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to confirm by mutating a copy.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the expected-source list in half two of the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For each source, the list gives a title or identifier, an owner, a version or date, and why it is authorized.
statements.explanation: Those four fields are named.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The list also gives the number of items you expect the corpus to hold.
statements.explanation: The expected item count carries the row-count question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The list is written before you ingest anything.
statements.explanation: Writing it before ingestion is the point.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The list is dated.
statements.explanation: The list is dated so the comparison later is honest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You should ask Claude what a corpus for this task should contain before you write your own list.
statements.explanation: You should not ask Claude before you have written yours.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why you should not ask Claude for the expected-source list first.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude's answer would be built from the task description you gave it, the same material you are trying to check.
statements.explanation: The frame would come from the same description you are checking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking Claude first is acceptable as long as you review its list afterwards.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to ask before you have written yours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent AI-generated frame carries extra information about missing sources because the AI has seen broader documentation.
statements.explanation: The book's warning is that such a frame contains no information, since the AI started from the same documentation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The list is mostly clerical, so Claude can write it and you can edit it.
statements.explanation: The list is where your understanding of the task goes on the record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can write the list without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: Claude cannot write it without defeating it.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the claims list and the evidence rules in half two of the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claims list has one sentence per question the report must answer.
statements.explanation: One sentence per question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each claim should be small enough for a single passage to support or not.
statements.explanation: Claims must be single-passage sized.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sentence containing "and" is acceptable if one passage supports both halves.
statements.explanation: The rule is that a sentence with an "and" is split.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The row labels (supported, contradicted, insufficient, not reviewed) are defined before you see a report.
statements.explanation: Defining labels first keeps them honest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The row labels are defined after you see the report so they fit what it says.
statements.explanation: Defining them afterward would tailor them to the report.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the evidence-row labels and who may use them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Supported means a quoted passage states the claim, within its scope, date, and population.
statements.explanation: Scope, date, and population are part of the definition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Insufficient means the nearest passage contradicts the claim.
statements.explanation: Insufficient means on topic but not resolving the claim, with the missing piece named.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A row may be marked supported by whoever wrote the report.
statements.explanation: The person who read the original authorized source may mark a row supported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the sources do not say, the report must say so and not fill the gap.
statements.explanation: The report must say the sources do not say.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Not reviewed is the label for a row whose passage contradicts the claim.
statements.explanation: A contradicting passage gets the contradicted label.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the abstention rule "refuse when no document scores above zero".

statements.label: A
statements.text: It avoids answering from an empty selection in the synonym fixture.
statements.explanation: With no positive score, the rule refuses in the synonym fixture.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Positive overlap can still be insufficient, so the rule establishes no support.
statements.explanation: A positive-scoring but insufficient passage passes the rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the threshold never excludes a useful short passage.
statements.explanation: Raising the threshold excludes some useful short passages.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The rule is a complete substitute for human review.
statements.explanation: Review remains; the chapter asks what review is left.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You need to write only the case the rule wrongly lets through.
statements.explanation: You also write the case a stricter threshold wrongly refuses, and what review remains.

questions.source: The gate: write the source list and the evidence rules first
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the packet may claim and about reopening the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The packet may say: under this corpus and these rules, these claims were supported by these passages.
statements.explanation: That is the bounded claim the chapter allows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The packet may call itself comprehensive without checking its inventory.
statements.explanation: "Comprehensive" needs an inventory that justifies the word.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can sharpen the gate by pointing out a claim that is not small enough.
statements.explanation: Claude can also flag rules with no failing case and insufficiencies with no row.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can write the expected-source list without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: Claude cannot write that list without defeating it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If ingestion turns up an unlisted source, you keep the original dated list and add the revision with its reason.
statements.explanation: Design first is not design frozen; the revision is added with its reason.

questions.source: Build It: preserve the scoring path
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It section.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You write your own version before opening the reference solution, as your baseline.
statements.explanation: The baseline records what you understood before Claude touched anything.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You calculate the office-hours example by hand before running it.
statements.explanation: The hand calculation comes first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You preserve the tokens, counts, dot product, norms, and final score, not a lone decimal.
statements.explanation: A lone decimal makes the mechanism harder to audit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You may describe the passing test total as complete retrieval coverage.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to describe the total as complete retrieval coverage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A synonym map belongs in the reference version so its provenance is clear.
statements.explanation: A synonym map stays in the learner version.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about conducting Claude Code against your gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You give Claude Code the contract, the test list, and the audit-view specification, not your implementation.
statements.explanation: Those three items come from the gate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You run your tests on what it returns, yourself.
statements.explanation: Running the tests yourself is part of the instruction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in your gate, which Claude cannot see because it has only what you wrote.
statements.explanation: Claude sees only what the gate says.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You give Claude your implementation so it can match your baseline.
statements.explanation: Your implementation is withheld; your baseline is what you compare against.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If Claude's report says the tests pass, you may skip running them.
statements.explanation: Accepting the report's last sentence is what the chapter warns against.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what to do with the result Claude Code returns.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Note which of your tests failed, if any.
statements.explanation: Failing tests point at gate gaps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Compare its implementation with your baseline and name one difference in behavior.
statements.explanation: A named difference is either a revision to the gate or a missed defect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ask Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version that still passes your tests, and check by hand whether it does.
statements.explanation: The wrong-version check tests your test list.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the wrong version does pass your tests, your list was too weak, and you found that out cheaply.
statements.explanation: That is the stated payoff.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When Claude critiques your representation, accept its suggestions if they are fluent.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to verify every suggestion against the displayed mechanism.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about building the corpus and the packet.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You build the corpus from material you are authorized to use, recording source identity, version or date, and inclusion criteria.
statements.explanation: Those fields are the stated record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You may upload restricted material if the interface can accept it, because the interface enforces the boundary.
statements.explanation: Do not upload restricted material merely because the interface can accept it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The data boundary from Chapter 5 is relaxed for Cowork tasks.
statements.explanation: The Chapter 5 boundary remains in force.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Who may read what is a decision people make, not one the interface makes.
statements.explanation: The chapter says exactly this.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Inclusion criteria are optional when the corpus is small.
statements.explanation: The inclusion criteria are part of the record regardless of size.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about running retrieval and responding to missing evidence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You inspect both selected and omitted candidates, using the audit view.
statements.explanation: Omitted candidates are visible only in the audit view.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You compare the inventory with the expected-source list you dated before ingestion.
statements.explanation: The comparison is the point of dating the list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For each required answer claim, you identify whether sufficient evidence appears in the selected context.
statements.explanation: Sufficiency is judged claim by claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If evidence is missing, you revise the query, representation, corpus, or task scope.
statements.explanation: The repairs are upstream of the prose.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Revising the final prose is enough to resolve an evidence problem.
statements.explanation: Revising the prose alone leaves the evidence problem in place.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code, then build a bounded Cowork task packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about running the task through Claude Cowork.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You preserve the actual interface details and output.
statements.explanation: Real details and output must be kept.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter cannot claim which internal retrieval steps the product used.
statements.explanation: The chapter makes no claim about Cowork internals.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing your packet with the interface task proves the interface uses the same retrieval as your retriever.
statements.explanation: The comparison is an observed workflow, not proof of internal equivalence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the interface is unavailable, you ship the offline corpus, retrieval results, and proposed packet, and mark the generation portion not run.
statements.explanation: This is the stated fallback.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the interface is unavailable, you must use direct API credits to complete the assessment.
statements.explanation: The mechanics remain assessable without direct API spending.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about debugging an unsupported final claim in the order information moves.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When a final claim is unsupported, you start upstream rather than rewriting the answer repeatedly.
statements.explanation: The stages from the opening table give the order of inspection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You start at the Claim stage and work backward to the corpus.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to start at the top, with eligibility.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You preserve the score of a document that fell below k rather than pretending it was never considered.
statements.explanation: A below-k score is part of the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Debugging ends when every stage has produced a green marker.
statements.explanation: Green markers are not the stopping condition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Debugging ends when the stated conclusion matches the actual evidence.
statements.explanation: That is the stated end of debugging.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first four rows of the debugging table (Eligibility, Ingestion, Representation, Scoring and cutoff).

statements.label: A
statements.text: An eligibility failure is a source excluded by a permission or scope decision, which retrieval cannot legally repair.
statements.explanation: The claim may need narrowing instead.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An ingestion failure looks like a skipped file format or the wrong folder being read.
statements.explanation: Those are the table's examples of ingestion failure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reference implementation demonstrates the ingestion step.
statements.explanation: The reference starts from a constructed dictionary and never demonstrates this step.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A better prompt after retrieval can repair a representation failure such as the synonym case.
statements.explanation: No prompt after retrieval repairs a representation that shares no coordinate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If a larger k brings in the missing evidence, there is no added review burden to record.
statements.explanation: A larger k adds review burden, which you record.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Debug the pipeline in the order information moves)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the last three rows of the debugging table (Selection into context, Use, Claim).

statements.label: A
statements.text: Use is the first stage where rewriting the answer helps.
statements.explanation: Before Use, rewriting the answer cannot help.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once the source is in context and Claude embellishes it, no separate support review is needed.
statements.explanation: Support is still a separate review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A selection-into-context failure is when another filter or a manual choice narrowed what the retriever returned.
statements.explanation: The table asks whether what Claude saw is what the retriever returned.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At the Claim stage, the repair belongs to the author of the retriever.
statements.explanation: The Claim stage belongs to whoever signs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A claim failure looks like a summary that calls the report comprehensive or verified.
statements.explanation: That is the table's example of a claim failure.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Chunk boundaries create another representation)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about chunking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reference treats each dictionary value as a complete document, so it does not implement chunking.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the reference does not implement chunking.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A claim and its qualification can fall in adjacent chunks, so retrieving only the claim-shaped fragment can make a passage look stronger than its source.
statements.explanation: Splitting can hide the qualification.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A large chunk can dilute lexical overlap with unrelated terms and lower its normalized score.
statements.explanation: Unrelated terms enlarge the vector length and lower the cosine.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Chunk overlap is free completeness.
statements.explanation: Overlap duplicates tokens and candidates and influences ranking and context volume.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A generated citation to chunk-7 is easy to audit even if the packet does not connect it to a document and passage.
statements.explanation: Chunk identifiers must preserve source identity and location.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the claim-to-source evidence table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It needs more columns than claim and citation.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it needs more than claim and citation columns.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It adds the exact supporting passage or stable location, a reviewer judgment, and a note about scope or missing qualification.
statements.explanation: Those are the added columns.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An insufficient row is actionable evidence: narrow the sentence, retrieve more material, or abstain.
statements.explanation: Insufficient rows point to a next action.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You should not force every row into supported merely because the report is supposed to be complete.
statements.explanation: Forcing every row to supported hides gaps.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the table cannot represent a gap, the reviewer is freed to report one.
statements.explanation: A table that cannot represent a gap pressures the reviewer to hide one.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.stem: For the office-hours hypothetical, a supplied sentence says office hours are available by appointment. Check each statement that is true about the claims in the evidence table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Appointments are mentioned" is supported by the supplied sentence.
statements.explanation: The sentence states that appointments are mentioned.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Appointments occur Tuesday at two" is insufficient because the time is absent.
statements.explanation: The passage does not give a day or time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A paragraph-level judgment is better because it shows the grounded and invented parts together.
statements.explanation: A paragraph-level judgment could conceal that one part is invented.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Atomic claims make visible that one part of a paragraph is grounded while another is invented.
statements.explanation: Atomic claims are what expose the mix.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Appointments occur Tuesday at two" is contradicted by the supplied sentence.
statements.explanation: The sentence is silent on the time; it does not contradict it.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the provenance of passages and about reviewing the table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A string entered by the learner is a constructed fixture.
statements.explanation: A learner-typed string is a fixture.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A passage copied from a real policy needs an authorized source, a version or retrieval date where relevant, and enough location information to revisit it.
statements.explanation: Real passages need a traceable source.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Constructed fixtures and real passages should not be merged in one table without labeling the roles.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to merge the roles unlabeled.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You ask Claude to label each row first, then check its labels yourself.
statements.explanation: You label each row yourself first, then ask Claude for the sentence that would change your label.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If another reviewer needs surrounding text you did not record, the record should improve.
statements.explanation: That is the stated test of whether the record is enough.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (Build an evidence table that can say no)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the selection record behind a report.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You preserve the query that actually produced the selection.
statements.explanation: The query behind the selection is part of the record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a revised query retrieves better evidence, its success is attributed to the original run.
statements.explanation: A revised query's success cannot be attributed to the original run; keep both and label the revision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You record any synonym a human supplied after seeing the failure.
statements.explanation: Human-supplied synonyms must be recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The source collection and the context finally shown to Claude can differ, for example twenty items in the corpus, two returned, and one received.
statements.explanation: Each narrowing between collection and context should be named.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without a selection record, blaming the generator for missing information is always justified.
statements.explanation: Without a record, a reviewer may blame the generator for information the workflow never supplied.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about accountable context and the omitted or insufficient case.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result is accountable context, not maximal context.
statements.explanation: Enough authorized material, a record of what was left out, and a route to say the evidence is insufficient.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The packet should include at least one omitted or insufficient case.
statements.explanation: That case shows the selection boundary.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The packet should explain whether a missing source was absent from the corpus, scored zero, or fell below k.
statements.explanation: Those are the three locations of a missing source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Maximal context is the goal of the packet.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the result is not maximal context.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A packet containing only the passages that made the answer look good can still reveal the selection boundary.
statements.explanation: Such a packet cannot reveal the selection boundary.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the packet's parts relate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The corpus inventory shows what was eligible.
statements.explanation: The inventory is the eligible collection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The retrieval record shows what the algorithm selected.
statements.explanation: The retrieval record is the algorithm's selection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The task packet shows what Claude was permitted and asked to use.
statements.explanation: The packet fixes Claude's permissions and request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The evidence table connects claims back to exact passages and records gaps.
statements.explanation: The table is the claim-to-passage link.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The dated expected-source list is placed at the end, after the conclusions.
statements.explanation: The expected-source list sits in front of all of them.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the verbs in the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Retrieved" describes what the selection rule returned.
statements.explanation: Retrieval is the selection rule's output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Quoted" describes what you copied.
statements.explanation: Quoting is copying.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Supported" describes a claim and a passage you actually compared.
statements.explanation: Support requires an inspected comparison.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Verified" and "comprehensive" need no more than this packet offers.
statements.explanation: Those words need more than this packet offers, unless you did the work behind them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A passage the retriever returned can be called "supported" when its score is high.
statements.explanation: A retrieved passage is not thereby a supporting one.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The packet, assembled)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off template.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The "Not checked" line does the work.
statements.explanation: The chapter says this line carries the sign-off.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An AI-written sign-off handles the "Not checked" line well because Claude keeps a record of every file it failed to load.
statements.explanation: An AI-written sign-off leaves it out, because the system has no record of sources you never opened or the file that failed to load.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If your evidence does not support signing, you sign and add a caveat.
statements.explanation: If your evidence does not support signing, you withhold.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sign-off may say the report is verified if Claude's tests passed.
statements.explanation: "Verified" needs more than this packet offers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The "How" line need not say which parts were done with Claude's help.
statements.explanation: The template says to name the parts done with Claude's help.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The driver's seat)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the driver's-seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For listing a folder, scoring and ranking every document, and quoting candidate passages, Claude should do it fast and show every score.
statements.explanation: Ranking is the part to hand over.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For that work, you should read the full audit view, not only the winners.
statements.explanation: Omissions are invisible in a list of winners, so reading what was left out is yours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For the expected-source list, Claude writes the first draft and you review it.
statements.explanation: You write the list first, from the task; Claude may propose missing-source questions afterward.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a synonym map, a chunk size, or a larger k, Claude proposes with cases that might break it, and you decide and record where each came from.
statements.explanation: Whether two terms are interchangeable is a fact about the policy and population.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For which sources may be used, Claude decides after flagging restricted material.
statements.explanation: Authorization is a decision people make.

questions.source: Ship It: the source-grounded task packet (The driver's seat)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about recording the split between delegated work and retained judgment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The packet records one task you delegated and one judgment you retained.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks for one of each.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you cannot point to a transcript line or an edit that shows each, the split happened in your head and not in the record.
statements.explanation: Evidence must be pointable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A statement of the split is enough without any evidence.
statements.explanation: The evidence is concrete: transcript, dated list, and differing labels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Only the delegated task needs evidence.
statements.explanation: Both the delegated task and the retained judgment need evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The evidence is the recomputed cosine score of the office-hours pair.
statements.explanation: The evidence is the transcript, the dated expected-source list, and the rows where labels differed.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Verify and reflect section.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You recalculate one cosine score independently.
statements.explanation: One independent recalculation is the check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You preserve the interpreter and the input corpus rather than reporting a score without its representation.
statements.explanation: A score without its representation is not auditable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You compare the expected-source list with the inventory and write the gap in one sentence.
statements.explanation: The gap is the learning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You rewrite the expected-source list to match what you found.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to rewrite the list to match.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You audit a claim only against the selected chunk, since that is the retrieved evidence.
statements.explanation: Audit against the original source, since chunk boundaries can omit qualifications.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Assessments.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The Assessments are ungraded practice and carry no points.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls them ungraded practice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In the zero-length warm-up, you predict the cosine with one empty vector and explain the returned value without calling an empty query meaningful.
statements.explanation: The returned 0.0 is a convention, not a finding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the tie-order exercise, you write the wrong version that orders ties by insertion and show which of your tests fails on it.
statements.explanation: The wrong version should fail a test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the top-k exercise, an omitted result is treated as proof of irrelevance.
statements.explanation: The exercise records the omitted result as an audit row and explains why omission is not proof of irrelevance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The paired lesson's knowledge check is graded.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the Assessments carry no points.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: The query is "office hours". Document d1 is "office hours appointment" and document d2 is "office hours". A learner adds the term "appointment" to the query, making it "office hours appointment". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Before the change, d2 scores 1.0 and d1 scores about 0.8165.
statements.explanation: d2 is identical to the query; d1 gives 2 / sqrt(6).

statements.label: B
statements.text: After the change, d1 scores 1.0.
statements.explanation: The new query equals d1's vector, so the cosine is 3 / (sqrt(3) * sqrt(3)).

statements.label: C
statements.text: After the change, d2 scores about 0.8165, because its dot product stays 2 while the query's length changes.
statements.explanation: The dot product stays 2, but the query length grows to sqrt(3), giving 2 / (sqrt(3) * sqrt(2)).

statements.label: D
statements.text: After the change, the ranking of d1 and d2 is the same as before.
statements.explanation: The order reverses: d1 now ranks above d2.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After the change, the dot product of d2 with the new query is 3.
statements.explanation: Only office and hours are shared, so the dot product is 2.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: The corpus is {doc-b: "office hours", doc-a: "office hours", doc-c: "office hours extra"}, inserted in that order, and the query is "office hours". Check each statement that is true of `retrieve`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: doc-a and doc-b both score 1.0.
statements.explanation: Both are identical in direction to the query.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With k equal to 1, `retrieve` returns doc-a.
statements.explanation: The tie is broken by ascending key, and "doc-a" sorts first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With k equal to 2, `retrieve` returns doc-b then doc-a, following insertion order.
statements.explanation: Ties are broken by key, so doc-a comes first.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With k equal to 3, doc-c is excluded because its score equals the others.
statements.explanation: doc-c scores about 0.8165 and is returned third.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With k equal to 1, doc-b is returned because it was inserted first.
statements.explanation: Insertion order does not decide ties.

questions.source: What you can now trace
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter says you can now trace.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A zero-overlap document may be semantically related.
statements.explanation: The synonym pair is the example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A high-overlap document may still be insufficient.
statements.explanation: A passage can repeat terms and still not support the claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The score and the support review have different jobs.
statements.explanation: One ranks candidates; the other judges support.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Facts A and B contradict each other.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is not a contradiction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the prose is wrong, the failure began in generation.
statements.explanation: The packet lets a reviewer diagnose whether the failure began in ingestion, representation, ranking, generation, or interpretation.

questions.source: A protocol connects capabilities
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the bridge from retrieval to Chapter 8.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chapter 8 builds a minimal Model Context Protocol server state machine.
statements.explanation: That is Chapter 8's stated build.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It traces initialization, tool discovery, request identifiers, and error results.
statements.explanation: Those are the traced steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It separates protocol compatibility from trust and authorization.
statements.explanation: Compatibility is not trust or authorization.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The question to carry forward is who decided what reaches Claude, and where is that written down.
statements.explanation: The closing question is about context decisions and their record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A compatible message is an authorized one, just as a high score is support.
statements.explanation: Just as a high score is not support, a compatible message is not an authorized one.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the access-boundary assumption from the companion Computational Skepticism chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A dataset's effective reach is its schema plus whatever its contents reference.
statements.explanation: That is the assumption.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The claim is sharpest for self-contained tables such as sensor readings.
statements.explanation: It is sharpest for reference-rich material such as email and weak for a self-contained sensor table.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You apply it by asking whether a passage quotes, links, or defers to a document that is not on your source list.
statements.explanation: That is the application to one passage in your corpus.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a passage defers to an unlisted document, the passage can still be read as complete.
statements.explanation: The passage cannot be read as complete without that document.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The dependency on an unlisted document is recorded in the packet as a resolved item.
statements.explanation: The dependency belongs in the packet as an unresolved item.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the row-trace step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You follow one answer passage back to its original source.
statements.explanation: The trace starts from an answer passage.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Where the original is unreachable, you document the opacity.
statements.explanation: Documenting opacity is the instruction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Documented opacity counts as a failure of the procedure.
statements.explanation: The chapter counts opacity as a finding, not a failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You record which of "not retrieved", "not in the corpus", and "not true" you could establish and which you could not.
statements.explanation: Those are the three claims to separate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two diagnostics are a measurement of this retriever and corpus.
statements.explanation: They are two questions for the packet, not a measurement of the retriever or corpus.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about two servers that both advertise a tool called `lookup`, both return valid JSON-RPC messages and copy request identifiers correctly, but only one of which writes files as a side effect.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The file-writing server could be recognized by how it copies request identifiers.
statements.explanation: Both servers copy identifiers correctly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Protocol syntax cannot tell the two servers apart.
statements.explanation: Syntax cannot show that they deserve different permissions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Interoperability answers whether components can exchange messages they understand.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's definition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A clean handshake settles whether this capability should run in this task.
statements.explanation: It settles the first question and is silent on the second.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Authorization answers whether components can exchange messages they understand.
statements.explanation: That is interoperability; authorization asks whether a capability should run in this task.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Claude being handed only the tool listing for two competing servers.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A tool description is a sentence the server wrote about itself.
statements.explanation: The description is the server's own testimony.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once Claude has compared the two descriptions, the decision to connect becomes Claude's.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the decision is yours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under the Drive job, Claude reads the transcript and lists every discrepancy while you keep the decision to connect.
statements.explanation: That is how the chapter divides the third job.

statements.label: D
statements.text: What Claude lacks is skill with JSON.
statements.explanation: It lacks a standpoint on whether this server belongs in the task.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude has no standpoint on whose data sits behind the server, what a stray file write would cost, or who maintains it.
statements.explanation: The listing supplies none of these facts.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's teaching server.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It implements initialization, an initialized notification, tool listing, and one read-only lookup.
statements.explanation: That is the whole feature list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It keeps two Boolean state variables.
statements.explanation: They are `initialized` and `ready`.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It rejects a tool request made too early.
statements.explanation: Tool operations are refused until the server is ready.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It also advertises a write-capable tool alongside `lookup`.
statements.explanation: Its only tool is the read-only lookup; the write-capable server is hypothetical.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It separates protocol errors from a tool result whose `isError` field is true.
statements.explanation: The two are distinct layers.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four recorded observations of the local Python server.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Looking up an unknown record produces a JSON-RPC error.
statements.explanation: It produces a tool result with `isError: true`.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Listing tools before initialization returns an error.
statements.explanation: That is the first recorded observation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An initialize request returns protocol version `2025-11-25`.
statements.explanation: That is the second recorded observation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: They are executed observations of this server, not claims about MCP generally.
statements.explanation: The chapter limits the claim to this server.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A valid initialized notification returns no response.
statements.explanation: That is the third recorded observation.

questions.source: Chapter 8 - MCP from scratch (opening)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's treatment of the version the server returns.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fixed fallback version is, by itself, a violation of the specification.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is not, by itself, a violation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When a server returns a different version, the server decides whether the client can continue.
statements.explanation: The client makes that decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under the versioned lifecycle specification, a server may return another supported version when the requested one is unsupported.
statements.explanation: The client then decides whether it can continue.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The teaching server is a full conformance implementation of the lifecycle.
statements.explanation: It remains a teaching subset.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The server returns its one supported version without inspecting the client's requested version.
statements.explanation: The branch never reads the requested version.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four questions the chapter wants you to keep apart for any connection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether the returned content supports the claim built on it is one of the four questions.
statements.explanation: It is the evidence question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether the code does what the listing says is one of the four questions.
statements.explanation: It is the capability question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether this task may use the connection is one of the four questions.
statements.explanation: It is the permission question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether Claude's summary of the exchange reads fluently is one of the four questions.
statements.explanation: The four are form, listing versus code, task permission, and content support.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once the exchange is well formed, the other three questions are answered as well.
statements.explanation: A well-formed exchange answers only the first.

questions.source: Four parties and one decision
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four parties in a connection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: MCP itself chose the tool and vouches for what comes back.
statements.explanation: MCP supplies a communication structure; it did not choose the tool and does not vouch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The server implements capabilities and describes them.
statements.explanation: That is the server's role.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude decides on its own which servers the task is authorized to use.
statements.explanation: Claude, or a workflow around it, only proposes using a tool.

statements.label: D
statements.text: People and policies define authority.
statements.explanation: Authority is the fourth party's role.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The host constructs requests, interprets responses, exposes selected tools to Claude, and decides what content enters context.
statements.explanation: That is the host's role.

questions.source: Four parties and one decision
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why three of the four parties cannot answer the fourth party's question.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The session supplies Claude with who owns the data, what the task is for, and what a wrong answer costs.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the session does not include those.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The server can answer whether it belongs in the task, because its description states what it does.
statements.explanation: Its description is its own testimony.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The question none of the three software parties can answer is whether this server, this data, and this action are appropriate for this task.
statements.explanation: That is the fourth party's question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can weigh a tool description against a request.
statements.explanation: But it only has what the session supplied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The host can both enforce and write the permission policy for the task.
statements.explanation: The host can enforce a policy but cannot write one.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two state variables in the reference server.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A valid initialize request also sets `ready` to true.
statements.explanation: Readiness waits for the initialized notification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tool operations are rejected until `ready` is true.
statements.explanation: Having `initialized` true is not enough.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A valid initialize request sets `initialized` to true.
statements.explanation: It also returns server information and capabilities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both `initialized` and `ready` start as false.
statements.explanation: Both are set false in `__init__`.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A `notifications/initialized` message sets `ready` to true only if `initialized` is already true.
statements.explanation: Otherwise nothing changes.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why initialization takes two steps.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stateless server would be shorter to write but impossible to hold to an order.
statements.explanation: Without state there is nothing to enforce the order.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The initialized notification lets the client say it has finished the initialization phase.
statements.explanation: The request and response only exchange protocol information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Readiness is inferred from the fact that the server process exists.
statements.explanation: The design deliberately avoids that inference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The design makes readiness a statement by the client and a precondition for the server.
statements.explanation: That is the stated design choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The price of the design is state, and every piece of state is a place where two parties can disagree about history.
statements.explanation: That is the cost the chapter names.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how `handle` treats incoming messages.

statements.label: A
statements.text: That check covers every JSON-RPC validity condition.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it a narrow rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The first check validates that the message is a dictionary with `jsonrpc` equal to `2.0`.
statements.explanation: That is the base validation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A message with no `id` is treated as a notification.
statements.explanation: That routes it to the notification branch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A notification that arrives before `initialize` gets an error response.
statements.explanation: Nothing changes and the handler returns `None`.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A message that fails that check gets an invalid-request error with a null identifier.
statements.explanation: The id is null because there is no usable id.

questions.source: Initialization is a state transition
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the silence that follows a `notifications/initialized` message.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because silence looks the same in both cases, the client must keep its own record of the lifecycle.
statements.explanation: It cannot read readiness off the wire.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Receiving nothing back tells the client that the server is now ready.
statements.explanation: Silence looks the same whether or not the notification took effect.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The missing response is a lost message that the server should patch with an invented acknowledgement.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to patch it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A valid initialized notification gets no response; the handler returns `None`.
statements.explanation: No response is the expected behavior on this route.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A notification that arrives before `initialize` still sets `ready` to true.
statements.explanation: It changes nothing because `initialized` is false.

questions.source: The initialize exchange
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the result of the initialize request.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The declared name and version are independent evidence that the server behaves as described.
statements.explanation: The process under review wrote them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The declared fields are inputs to a compatibility decision.
statements.explanation: They feed the decision; they do not prove behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The response omits the request's identifier because initialize is special.
statements.explanation: The response wraps the result with the JSON-RPC version and the request's id.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The `capabilities` field lists the `lookup` tool by name.
statements.explanation: It declares a tools capability with an empty object.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The result declares protocol version `2025-11-25`.
statements.explanation: The server returns that version.

questions.source: The initialize exchange
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the recorded run in which the client requests version `unsupported-fixture`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The server does not inspect a `params` object on initialize.
statements.explanation: It ignores what the client asked for.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Capability negotiation is narrow: the server declares a tools capability with an empty object and checks nothing about the client.
statements.explanation: That suffices for the tool list that follows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The server still answers `2025-11-25`.
statements.explanation: It answers the same regardless of the request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: On this branch the server can distinguish a supported request from a malformed one.
statements.explanation: It cannot.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The empty tools capability certifies the lifecycle clauses about capabilities.
statements.explanation: It does not certify any lifecycle clause.

questions.source: The initialize exchange
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how strongly to word a criticism of the teaching server.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'The teaching server does not evaluate the requested version or validate the required initialization fields' names mechanisms that are actually missing.
statements.explanation: Naming mechanisms makes the criticism testable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A broader criticism is stronger because it covers more possible defects.
statements.explanation: Breadth that cannot be tested is a weakness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'The fixed version violates MCP' overstates the case.
statements.explanation: A server may return another supported version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A claim that names the missing mechanism tells you which test to write next.
statements.explanation: That is what makes it useful.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A criticism too broad to test is one more fluent claim.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's warning.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the `tools/list` result.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The schema permits additional properties beyond `key`.
statements.explanation: `additionalProperties` is false.

statements.label: B
statements.text: After readiness, `tools/list` returns one tool named `lookup`.
statements.explanation: Row 7 of the table.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The input schema requires exactly one property, `key`, which must be a string.
statements.explanation: That is the declared schema.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Before the server is ready, `tools/list` returns an error instead of the tool description.
statements.explanation: Row 2 of the table.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The description says the tool reads a public course fixture.
statements.explanation: The text is 'Read a public course fixture'.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the word 'public' in the tool description.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A description can be technically accurate and still carry a word the server had no standing to assert.
statements.explanation: 'Public' is the example.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The server can tell you the fixture is public.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the code classifies anything.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Public' is a classification of data, and that word belongs in your permission ledger.
statements.explanation: It is filled in by whoever owns the data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The description is accurate in the author's sense, because the code consults one mapping.
statements.explanation: The chapter grants this.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The word 'public' is established by inspecting the lookup source.
statements.explanation: Source inspection shows what the code does, not how the data is classified.

questions.source: Discovery reveals a declared capability
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about evaluating a candidate server whose description sounds harmless.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A misleading description can steer which tool gets chosen before any runtime check runs.
statements.explanation: It competes for influence in context.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Faith in the description is adequate evidence for a candidate.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to use evidence instead.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a host places a tool description in Claude's context, it is more text competing for influence there.
statements.explanation: Chapter 1: a system prompt is a request, not a gate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A defective or malicious server could advertise a harmless purpose and do something else.
statements.explanation: A description is only a claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Evaluating a candidate takes source inspection, sandboxing, provenance, or other evidence appropriate to the deployment.
statements.explanation: Not faith in the description.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three layers at which a `tools/call` can go wrong.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The task layer covers a lookup that ran and found nothing.
statements.explanation: The failure belongs to the task result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reply cannot show which layer failed; you need the server's source to tell.
statements.explanation: The reply tells you which, if you read it that way.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The request layer covers a lookup that ran and found nothing.
statements.explanation: That is the task layer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The lifecycle layer covers a wrong tool name or wrong arguments.
statements.explanation: Those are request-layer failures.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The lifecycle layer covers a call that came too early.
statements.explanation: That is the first layer.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the server validates a `tools/call`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An additional argument alongside `key` also produces `-32602`.
statements.explanation: The arguments must contain exactly the key `key`.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A `key` that is not a string produces a tool result with `isError` true.
statements.explanation: It produces a `-32602` error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A missing `key` argument produces `-32602` with the message `Expected a string key`.
statements.explanation: Argument structure must be exact.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An unknown tool name produces JSON-RPC error `-32602` in this teaching implementation.
statements.explanation: Tool name is checked first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In all of these cases the tool never produced a content result.
statements.explanation: They are request-validation failures.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a lookup of a key that has no record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A host that ignores `isError` and presents `Record not found` as an ordinary fact is using the result correctly.
statements.explanation: That misuses a well-formed result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The request was well formed and the method existed.
statements.explanation: So the failure is not a protocol failure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Treating every negative result as a broken protocol is the right way for a host to handle `Record not found`.
statements.explanation: The distinct layers let the host choose among revising, reporting, or stopping.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The missing record is reported as JSON-RPC error `-32602`.
statements.explanation: It is a tool result whose `isError` is true.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The tool never ran its lookup, so the failure belongs to the request layer.
statements.explanation: The tool ran its lookup; the failure belongs to the task result.

questions.source: Requests, identifiers, and tool results
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a reply to a tool request does and does not show.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A successful response containing text makes the text correct.
statements.explanation: Correctness needs provenance appropriate to the source.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A matching id shows that the tool used the intended data.
statements.explanation: It says nothing about that.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A matching id shows that the result is safe to pass on.
statements.explanation: It says nothing about safety.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A matching id shows which response belongs with which request.
statements.explanation: Identifiers solve association.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The content of a successful response stays untrusted data.
statements.explanation: Success does not validate content.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the transition table shows for rows 2, 3, 6, and 7.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The only difference between those two rows is history.
statements.explanation: Row 2 starts at F, F and row 7 at T, T.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `tools/list` fails in row 2 and succeeds in row 7.
statements.explanation: Same message, different outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In row 3 nothing changes.
statements.explanation: The early notification leaves the state at F, F.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In row 6 readiness begins.
statements.explanation: The state goes from T, F to T, T.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rows 3 and 6 receive the same response and have the same effect on state.
statements.explanation: Same response (none), different state effects.

questions.source: History is part of the protocol
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about row 10, where a method named `bad` reaches a ready server.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The server returns `-32601` for an unknown method in every state.
statements.explanation: It does so only because the server was ready.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The same `bad` method sent in row 2's state would also have received `-32601`.
statements.explanation: It would have received `-32000`.

statements.label: C
