statements.text: Chapter 9 asked whether the proposed sequence is justified and bounded; this chapter asks what object will change.
statements.explanation: The two are the other way around: Chapter 9 asked what object will change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the interface is unavailable, write the plan yourself and present it as Claude-authored so the artifact looks finished.
statements.explanation: Do not invent a Claude-authored plan or human approval.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that the chapter lists among the abilities you should have after working through it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Identify all eight required plan fields.
statements.explanation: It is the first listed ability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Explain duplicate, unknown-prerequisite, and cycle rejections.
statements.explanation: It is a listed ability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Choose an objective from candidates that genuinely agree about what success means.
statements.explanation: The candidates must genuinely disagree about success.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Write a handoff condition that only its author can apply.
statements.explanation: The condition must be one another person can apply.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Say which parts of planning you handed to Claude and which you kept: the problem, the values inside it, the approval.
statements.explanation: This is the Drive ability.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a plan is in this chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A plan is worth the most after the work has run, when its content can be confirmed.
statements.explanation: It is worth the most before anything has run.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The plan is a record of Claude's private deliberation.
statements.explanation: It is not hidden reasoning and need not reproduce private deliberation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A plan should expose the destination, allowed inputs and scope, intended steps, tools, risks, evidence, and stopping rule while change is still cheap.
statements.explanation: That is the list the chapter gives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Planning exists to make proposed work inspectable before action.
statements.explanation: That is its purpose.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The plan is a public action contract another person can critique.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this directly.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the phase gate and design by contract as the chapter describes them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In design by contract, the agent writes the contract and you write the implementation.
statements.explanation: You write the contract; the agent writes the implementation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In this chapter's sense, a plan is that contract for a single function.
statements.explanation: It is the contract for a whole piece of work.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In design by contract, assertions or tests derived from your contract check the agent's implementation.
statements.explanation: That is how the contract is enforced.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A phase gate needs no testable condition as long as the specification of each side's work is clear.
statements.explanation: The gate includes a testable condition that must hold before output moves downstream.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A phase gate is the explicit point where Claude's work stops and a person's begins.
statements.explanation: That is the definition.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Boondoggle Score as the chapter treats it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It places a testable handoff condition between each Claude task and each human task.
statements.explanation: That is its third part.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It lays out the prompts for Claude in dependency order.
statements.explanation: That is one of its parts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It lists the human's actions in the same dependency order.
statements.explanation: That is its second part.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter treats it as an externally validated diagnostic.
statements.explanation: It says to treat it as a heuristic, not a diagnostic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The five sorting questions attached to it have no external validation behind them that the author knows of.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

questions.source: The plan is the design, and the review is the gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about revising a plan.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Design first" means that once reviewed, the plan must not change.
statements.explanation: Design first is not design frozen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In the discount-rule example, auditing the diff shows rounding was never specified, which reopens the requirement.
statements.explanation: The instruction is to log it and go back.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter's claim is that you should plan everything first.
statements.explanation: The claim is narrower: the first version should exist and be reviewed before Claude changes anything.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A plan is a controlled state with versions.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When a result contradicts an assumption, you keep the plan unchanged and note the surprise in the result.
statements.explanation: You revise the plan and record the reason.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about choosing the problem before planning.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter credits the phrase "error of the third kind" to Allyn Kimball, 1957.
statements.explanation: It cites that attribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A perfectly ordered plan can optimize the wrong objective.
statements.explanation: Order does not fix a wrong choice of problem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The error of the third kind is a wrong answer to the right problem.
statements.explanation: It is a right answer to the wrong problem.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cost of the wrong objective is highest when Claude executes it clumsily, because errors then show.
statements.explanation: The cost is highest when Claude executes it fluently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A polished, internally checked answer to the wrong question carries authority the question never earned.
statements.explanation: That is why fluency raises the cost.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about asking Claude to frame the problem first.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you have not named your anchor before Claude supplies its own, its anchor becomes yours by default.
statements.explanation: It arrives dressed as neutral analysis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter presents the claim that a text-continuing system tends toward the modal framing as a theorem on which the practice depends.
statements.explanation: It says the practice survives without it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The book argues that a system trained to continue text tends toward the common and likely, so its framing is the modal one.
statements.explanation: The chapter presents this as an argument about tendencies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Auditing Claude's framing afterward is safe because the audit stays independent of that framing.
statements.explanation: The audit comes too late because you check against the framing the output already assumes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Jane Darke's primary generator is a first, usually tacit idea of what the problem is really about.
statements.explanation: It decides which solutions you can see.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about candidate formulations and the distinctness test.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model's statement that two formulations are distinct replaces the test.
statements.explanation: You certify distinctness in your context by constructing results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Candidates should differ in what counts as success, not in wording.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two formulations are distinct if they would require different solutions even to test.
statements.explanation: That is the test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If one solution satisfies both formulations, they are one formulation in two outfits.
statements.explanation: They are the same problem.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Constructing results that one formulation accepts and another rejects is how you test whether the formulations differ.
statements.explanation: The chapter tests candidates by constructing results.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: In the plus-one regression a function should return its input plus one but returns the input minus one. Formulation A is that the single failing test, input two, goes green. B is that the declared plus-one behavior is restored without changing anything outside the learner module and its test. C is that the learner can explain the bug. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A patch that returns the constant 3, applied without diagnosing the cause, passes formulation B.
statements.explanation: For input five it returns 3, not 6.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A patch that returns the constant 3 passes formulation A.
statements.explanation: For input two the declared answer is 3.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A correct x + 1 patch accepted unread passes formulation A but fails formulation B.
statements.explanation: It passes B; it fails C.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For input five the declared plus-one behavior requires 6, while a patch that always returns 3 gives 3.
statements.explanation: Five plus one is six.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correct x + 1 patch that Claude wrote and you accepted unread passes formulation C.
statements.explanation: The learner cannot explain it, so C fails.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about choosing among formulations.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The most tractable framing is the one that best serves the people affected.
statements.explanation: It is the framing Claude would have picked unasked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If every criterion is about cost, time, and buildability, you have built a machine that selects the most tractable framing.
statements.explanation: Feasibility-only criteria favor tractability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is acceptable to write the constraint set after seeing how each candidate scores, as long as it is documented.
statements.explanation: It must be written before you score anything.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The constraint set should be written before you score anything.
statements.explanation: Writing it first stops criteria being fitted to a favorite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The book adds salience and whose interests the framing centers and decenters to the criteria.
statements.explanation: These go beyond feasibility.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the values decision in the plus-one example.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The values decision comes after the formulation, once the objective is fixed.
statements.explanation: It sits inside the formulation, not after it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One of the three formulations centers everyone, so choosing it leaves no one out.
statements.explanation: None centers everyone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Formulation B centers the maintainers and callers of the function.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Formulation C centers the maintainers and callers of the function.
statements.explanation: C centers the learner; B centers maintainers and callers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Formulation A centers whoever reads the test report.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this.

questions.source: Formulate before you plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about dividing the formulation work between you and Claude.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You should write your candidates first, then let Claude extend and criticize them.
statements.explanation: This keeps its anchor from becoming yours.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude should write the candidates first so that you can react to them.
statements.explanation: Its anchor would become yours by default.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Someone answers for centering the maintainer over the learner, and Claude has no name to put there.
statements.explanation: That is why the selection stays with you.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can make the values selection, because weighing interests is something it does quickly.
statements.explanation: The selection needs situated judgment and a name on the decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can find a result that passes one formulation and fails another.
statements.explanation: This is a real contribution.

questions.source: The eight fields are eight questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the FIELDS tuple.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its names are objective, inputs, scope, steps, tools, risks, verification, and stop.
statements.explanation: That is the list in the reference.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One of its names is approval.
statements.explanation: Approval is a gate condition, not one of the eight fields.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It declares eight names.
statements.explanation: They run from objective to stop.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The code can only see whether each name is bound to a value; a reviewer asks the question each name stands for.
statements.explanation: That is the split between code and reviewer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One of its names is owner.
statements.explanation: There is no such field.

questions.source: The eight fields are eight questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the question each field asks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inputs asks what outcome is stated so that someone can tell whether it happened.
statements.explanation: That is the objective question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Scope asks what may change and what must stay untouched.
statements.explanation: It is the scope question in the table.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verification asks what observation will support the completion claim.
statements.explanation: It is the verification question in the table.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Risks asks only whether any risk exists.
statements.explanation: It asks how the work could cause harm, error, or misleading evidence, and what each risk triggers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tools asks only which tool is used, so the entry "Claude Code" fills it well.
statements.explanation: That entry fills the field and does nothing; the field asks which capability, why, and which operation stays under human approval.

questions.source: The eight fields are eight questions
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the entries the chapter lists for the eight fields.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The entry "Be careful" fills the scope field and does nothing.
statements.explanation: It names no paths, operations, or exclusions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The entry "Stop after all scoped tests pass and the named reviewer accepts the current diff" fills the stop field and does nothing.
statements.explanation: That is the entry a reviewer can challenge.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The entry "An exact command, an expected invariant, or a source comparison" fills the verification field and does nothing.
statements.explanation: That is the entry a reviewer can challenge.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The entry "Stop when done" fills the stop field and does nothing.
statements.explanation: It names no observable exit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The entry "Improve the code" fills the objective field and does nothing.
statements.explanation: It cannot be challenged.

questions.source: What missing_fields actually checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how missing_fields decides that a field is missing.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A value of False counts as missing.
statements.explanation: False is false-valued.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The integer 0 counts as present because it is a real value.
statements.explanation: Zero is false-valued, so it counts as missing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An empty string counts as missing.
statements.explanation: An empty string is false-valued.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A field set to None counts as present because the key exists.
statements.explanation: None fails the truth-value check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It uses plan.get, so a field name that is absent from the plan counts as missing.
statements.explanation: plan.get returns None for an absent name.

questions.source: What missing_fields actually checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what missing_fields does and does not do.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It explains why an inadequate value is inadequate.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It requires each field to hold a particular type, such as a list for steps.
statements.explanation: It requires no particular type for any field.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It rejects plans that contain extra keys.
statements.explanation: It does not reject extra keys.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A nonempty list, string, dictionary, or even an unrelated truthy value can pass.
statements.explanation: Only truthiness matters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Its output is a dictionary that maps each missing field to a reason.
statements.explanation: Its output is an ordered list of names with no reasons.

questions.source: What missing_fields actually checks
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the value and limits of the presence check.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The check is deterministic and cheap.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A richer validator could catch more structural defects but still could not decide whether the command tests the right claim.
statements.explanation: It cannot decide whether the objective serves the right person either.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because it is blind to meaning, it should be dropped in favor of human review alone.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to use it to clear the easy failures.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The right use is to clear the easy failures so that human attention goes to the hard ones.
statements.explanation: That is the stated use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It fails differently from a reviewer: it never gets tired and never notices meaning.
statements.explanation: Its failure mode complements a reviewer's.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about steps as a graph of directed obligations.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ordering function decides which arrows exist.
statements.explanation: You decide which arrows exist.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If step verify has after: [build], then build must appear before verify.
statements.explanation: That is the directed obligation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verify may be called ready as soon as build has been scheduled.
statements.explanation: It is ready only when build has produced what verify needs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Steps are best treated as a flat list.
statements.explanation: The chapter says steps are not a list; they are a graph.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ordering function can only order the arrows you declared.
statements.explanation: It has no other knowledge.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the order function's validation errors.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A missing prerequisite and a mutual dependency between two present steps have the same remedy.
statements.explanation: The remedies differ.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A missing prerequisite is just a cycle reported with a different message.
statements.explanation: A missing prerequisite is not a cycle.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dependency naming an id that is absent from the graph raises Unknown prerequisite.
statements.explanation: The code checks this before ordering.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If verify depends on test but test is absent, the plan references nonexistent work.
statements.explanation: The chapter gives this example.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Duplicate ids are rejected because one key could not unambiguously represent two steps.
statements.explanation: The graph is keyed by step id.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the ordering loop in order.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The function runs the steps and establishes that their descriptions are useful.
statements.explanation: It does neither.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ready ids stay in the graph so that later steps can still see them.
statements.explanation: They are removed and deleted from the remaining prerequisite sets.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the graph is nonempty but has no ready step, the function raises Dependency cycle.
statements.explanation: The remaining dependencies contain a cycle.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each pass finds all steps whose prerequisite sets are empty; these are the ready steps.
statements.explanation: That is how readiness is defined.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ready ids are returned in the order they were inserted into the graph.
statements.explanation: They are sorted for deterministic output.

questions.source: Dependencies are directed obligations
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the research example and ties within a batch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A self-dependency is the smallest example of a cycle and appears in the tests.
statements.explanation: The step can never become ready.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Alphabetical order is evidence that alphabetical execution is best.
statements.explanation: It is not evidence of that.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When several steps are ready at once, alphabetical id order decides which appears first within that batch.
statements.explanation: It is a convention for determinism.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The alphabetical tie-break says only that, under the supplied relations, those steps do not depend on one another.
statements.explanation: It carries no further claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In the research example inspect has no prerequisites, build comes after inspect, and verify comes after build, giving the order inspect, build, verify.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what an acyclic graph does and does not show.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Three steps a, b, and c with no dependencies make the function raise an error because nothing orders them.
statements.explanation: It returns them in sorted order.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The graph also confirms that the declared prerequisites are the real ones.
statements.explanation: It is silent on that.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An omitted dependency can make the graph acyclic while the work remains impossible in that order.
statements.explanation: The graph cannot see what a step needs in the world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An arrow defines the handoff object passed from one step to the next.
statements.explanation: It says one step comes after another; it does not define the handoff object.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The graph answers whether there is an order in which every declared prerequisite comes first.
statements.explanation: That is its one question.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a plan that is acyclic but unsafe.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A cycle check cannot reject the delete step as unsafe.
statements.explanation: A cycle check only looks at declared prerequisites.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Inspect, delete, verify is a valid ordering if represented without a cycle.
statements.explanation: Graph validity is structural.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Planning before acting means automatically executing any valid graph.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Semantic review must compare each action with scope, authority, and consequence.
statements.explanation: That is the review the graph cannot do.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The graph has no operation allowlist and no approval model.
statements.explanation: It cannot compare actions with authority.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about cycles and how to resolve them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Removing the inconvenient edge is the recommended way to resolve a cycle.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to resolve every cycle by removing an edge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cycle can reveal that two steps were poorly defined.
statements.explanation: Removing an edge may hide that.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Plan review approves a proposed method, and result review evaluates actual output.
statements.explanation: They are different obligations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If implementation needs review and review needs a completed implementation, one overloaded word is doing two jobs.
statements.explanation: The word review covers two obligations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Renaming the obligations gives the sequence result review, implementation, plan review.
statements.explanation: It gives plan review, then implementation, then result review.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about testable handoff conditions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Reviewed" and "reasonable" are testable because reviewers know what they mean.
statements.explanation: Five reviewers will do five different things and all call it reviewing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Five reviewers given the condition "reviewed" will converge on the same checks because the word is familiar.
statements.explanation: They will do five different things.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Computational Skepticism's chapter on delegation claims that delegation is a contract, not a partition of labor.
statements.explanation: The handoff condition is its load-bearing clause.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Looks good" is a handoff condition.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Testable means someone who did not build the pipeline can read the condition, observe the system, and decide whether it holds.
statements.explanation: That is the standard.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the symlink plan and its edges.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the run to review edge, the handoff can require the exact commands, exit statuses, output, and a current diff hash or version description.
statements.explanation: The reviewer can then check the checks against the proposal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Its steps run inspect, test, fixture, run, review.
statements.explanation: The order is inspect, fixture, test, run, review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For the fixture to test edge, the handoff can require resolved paths proving both locations are disposable and the destination lies outside the approved subdirectory while remaining inside the temporary parent.
statements.explanation: This lets another student predict what the test exercises.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The symlink plan adds one denial test to the Chapter 5 learner permission function.
statements.explanation: That is the running hypothetical.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The plan permits editing the course reference.
statements.explanation: The course reference is something it may not touch.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who produces the evidence on an edge.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An AI describing its own check is the first opinion run twice.
statements.explanation: It adds no independence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude's sentence describing its own check counts as the evidence for the edge.
statements.explanation: It is not that evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On the run to review edge, the exit status and output come from the test runner.
statements.explanation: The runner, not Claude, produces them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test runner's output is weaker evidence than Claude's summary of it because the runner cannot explain itself.
statements.explanation: The runner fails differently from the model, which is what the edge needs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An edge needs evidence that fails the same way as the thing it certifies.
statements.explanation: It needs evidence that fails differently.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the five Boondoggle sorting questions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: How fluent the sequence diagram looks is one of the five sorting questions.
statements.explanation: A fluent diagram cannot make an unsafe transition acceptable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How cheap the output is to verify is one of the five sorting questions.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists verification cost among the five.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whether the step will leave a trail you can review is one of the five sorting questions.
statements.explanation: The trail is one of the two that do most of the work here.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether the action can be undone is one of the five sorting questions.
statements.explanation: Reversibility is one of the two that do most of the work here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether the input is ordinary or a tail case is one of the five sorting questions.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists it among the five.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about which edges need the most evidence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the learner workspace is under version control, a new test can be reverted from the diff, so its edge needs evidence but not a human gate.
statements.explanation: The change is reversible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A command that writes outside the fixture can be reverted from the diff like a new test.
statements.explanation: It cannot be reverted from a diff.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A command that writes outside the fixture, or deletes, gets a hard human approval or falls outside the scope.
statements.explanation: It cannot be undone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evidence should be attached to read-only edges first.
statements.explanation: State-changing edges come first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cheapness of verification and the fluency of the diagram do most of the work in deciding which edges need the most evidence.
statements.explanation: Reversibility and the trail do most of the work here.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the two-team scenario from the delegation chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A clear map shows that the decisions inside it are good.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The team whose documentation specified each handoff could be reviewed on substance.
statements.explanation: The map was reviewable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The team with documented handoffs was approved automatically.
statements.explanation: The chapter says only that it could be reviewed on substance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The team that wrote "the loan officer reviews" was tabled because nobody could say what its pipeline did.
statements.explanation: The handoff was not specified.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A clear map can be reviewed.
statements.explanation: That is what the scenario shows.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three exits of a stop field.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Halt names the conditions under which the work is finished.
statements.explanation: Halt names conditions under which action stops before completion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "When it looks good" is an acceptable completion exit.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is not an exit.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A turn budget and a finish action answer the same question as the stop field.
statements.explanation: They answer different questions; the stop field answers a third.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Completion names the observable task outcome.
statements.explanation: For code, that includes a targeted regression, existing tests, and a reviewed diff.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The stop field asks who decides, on what evidence, that the work is over or must not continue.
statements.explanation: That is the third question.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the defer exit.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Partial artifacts should be discarded when a time or turn limit is reached so that the record stays clean.
statements.explanation: They are preserved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reaching a time or turn limit yields an incomplete status, never a fabricated final result.
statements.explanation: The status must be honest.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The defer exit should name the partial artifacts to preserve and who decides whether to resume.
statements.explanation: Both are required.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reaching a turn limit is evidence that the task is complete.
statements.explanation: It is not evidence of success.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A time or turn limit bounds effort without proving success.
statements.explanation: Reaching a limit says nothing about whether the task succeeded.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about who owns each exit.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An automated test can decide whether a newly discovered risk changes scope.
statements.explanation: A person must decide that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A summary is a decision with a name on it.
statements.explanation: A summary is not a decision with a name on it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each exit needs an owner.
statements.explanation: Every exit must name who decides.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A person must decide whether a newly discovered risk changes scope.
statements.explanation: That decision cannot be automated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A human decision can be handed to Claude because it can summarize the evidence well.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to hand it over.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about refusal paths.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the symlink plan, a required edit to the course reference instead of the learner copy is a scope stop.
statements.explanation: The reference is out of scope.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A plan written only for success pressures every observation into forward motion.
statements.explanation: That is why refusal paths are added.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the symlink plan, a resolved target outside the disposable parent is a reason to continue cautiously.
statements.explanation: It is a hard stop.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the symlink plan, a failed existing test routes back to diagnosis.
statements.explanation: It does not route to approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Refusal means the workflow preserves its state and reports what blocks the next transition.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's meaning of refusal.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about refusal outputs and uncertainty.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude can grant permission that the user or the institution has not given.
statements.explanation: It can help search approved sources or propose a smaller task, but it cannot grant permission.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A refusal needs outputs: why the step stopped, what evidence was available, and what decision would allow safe resumption.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists these three.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the same check fails again with no new evidence, the next step is an identical retry.
statements.explanation: The next step is diagnosis, revising the plan, or deferring.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An unexplained halt is easy to tell from a crashed workflow.
statements.explanation: It is hard to tell apart, which is why outputs are needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Every uncertainty is a block.
statements.explanation: Missing information obtainable within scope differs from a decision that needs new authority.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a plan as a prediction and a result as a record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The steps predict what will be done, the verification field predicts what you will observe if it worked, and the stop field predicts which events end the work.
statements.explanation: Each is a prediction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the plan is edited after the run to match the run, it has become a description of the result.
statements.explanation: The review that justified acting is gone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plan and the result are best kept as one document that you keep up to date.
statements.explanation: The habit worth building is keeping them apart.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A result is a record of what happened.
statements.explanation: It is a different document from the plan.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You should write what a wrong outcome would look like after you read the result.
statements.explanation: You write it before and do not revise it afterward.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reviewing the plan against itself.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If no step writes, a write-capable tool is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Steps are reviewed against tools.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Objective against verification asks whether the check measures the outcome the objective names.
statements.explanation: That is the first cross-field review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An available tool is automatically permitted for the task because the environment makes it available.
statements.explanation: Capability does not create authority.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a step needs a capability the tools field lacks, the plan is feasible but incomplete.
statements.explanation: The plan is infeasible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test that confirms a file exists establishes that its contents implement the behavior.
statements.explanation: It does not.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the remaining cross-field reviews.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The risks review states which risks are accepted, which trigger a mitigation, and which trigger deferral.
statements.explanation: Each risk needs a stated consequence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A bare id relation between two steps gives order without correspondence.
statements.explanation: The handoff object must be defined.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ownership of a risk should not be assigned to a fictitious human.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can serve as the signer of a human decision.
statements.explanation: Claude should not be used as the signer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A late change to the objective can invalidate earlier risk and verification analysis.
statements.explanation: Versions are preserved and the review rerun.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the counterexamples the chapter describes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An objective can be specific but wrong for the stakeholder.
statements.explanation: That is a realistic counterexample.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Scope can be precise but authorize too much.
statements.explanation: That is a realistic counterexample.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A stop condition can be observable but trigger only after harm has occurred.
statements.explanation: That is a realistic counterexample.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A realistic counterexample is incoherent or empty, like the all-x plan.
statements.explanation: Realistic counterexamples resemble plans people accept.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Verification can be executable but test a proxy.
statements.explanation: That is a realistic counterexample.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about writing counterexamples before approval.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A pre-mortem with executable consequences proves the plan cannot fail.
statements.explanation: It shows only that identified failure modes shaped the design.

statements.label: B
statements.text: When prerequisites are technically complete but the receiving step lacks a needed artifact, add another arrow.
statements.explanation: Add the handoff condition, not another arrow.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For safe writing, construct an out-of-scope path, since an in-scope path is already safe.
statements.explanation: The counterexample is an in-scope path with an unapproved operation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude decides which counterexamples are plausible here, since it has no stake in the outcome.
statements.explanation: Which are plausible is your call.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For source grounding, construct a valid citation that does not support the claim.
statements.explanation: The chapter gives this example.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the symlink-plan gate in the chapter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The scope allows changing the course reference.
statements.explanation: The course reference is something it may not touch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The inputs are the learner code, existing tests, pathlib documentation, and a temporary-directory fixture.
statements.explanation: That is the inputs entry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The objective is to demonstrate rejection of an outside-pointing symlink in a disposable fixture without accessing unrelated data.
statements.explanation: That is the objective entry.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scope allows changing the learner implementation freely.
statements.explanation: It allows it only if evidence requires it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The tools field includes a direct API call.
statements.explanation: It states no direct API call.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the stop and predicts entries in the symlink-plan gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan defers, keeping partial artifacts, if a needed source is unavailable.
statements.explanation: That is its defer exit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The plan halts if any command targets material outside the disposable arrangement or scope must expand without review.
statements.explanation: That is its halt exit.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plan finishes when the fixture demonstrates the rejection, existing tests pass, the diff stays within scope, and the report limits its claim to the stable preflight case.
statements.explanation: That is its completion exit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A failing existing test means the plan was wrong and reopens it.
statements.explanation: That is the predicts line.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The predicts line is written after the run so that it can match what happened.
statements.explanation: It is dated before the run.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about running missing_fields and order on the encoded gate plan.

statements.label: A
statements.text: order returns inspect, fixture, test, run, review.
statements.explanation: Each step is after the one before.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing both checks shows the gate plan is right.
statements.explanation: The plan can still be wrong, for example if the learner code differs from the reference.

statements.label: C
statements.text: missing_fields returns the same empty list the all-x plan produced.
statements.explanation: Every field is present.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The improvement over the all-x plan is that another person can predict the actions and challenge the evidence.
statements.explanation: That is the stated improvement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The same output from different plans is separated only by the review the chapter describes.
statements.explanation: The checks cannot tell them apart.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first three conditions for clearing a plan to go downstream.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan names one interest the choice leaves out.
statements.explanation: That is part of condition one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An empty missing_fields result alone is enough to clear the plan.
statements.explanation: Neither the check nor the cross-field review alone is enough.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The objective was chosen from at least three candidates that pass the distinctness test pairwise.
statements.explanation: That is part of condition one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Every state-changing edge needs a human gate regardless of whether the action is reversible.
statements.explanation: A reversible new test needs evidence but not a human gate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Choosing the objective from two candidates is enough if they pass the distinctness test.
statements.explanation: The condition is at least three candidates.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the last three conditions and what happens after the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once the gate is passed, the plan is frozen even if a result later contradicts it.
statements.explanation: A contradicting result reopens it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If nobody has approved the plan, its status is pending and nothing consequential runs.
statements.explanation: That is the stated rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The stop field has completion, halt, and defer exits, each with an owner.
statements.explanation: That is condition four.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The gate fixes the version Claude implements against.
statements.explanation: It does not freeze the plan, but it fixes the version being implemented.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You wrote one counterexample before approval and the plan rejects it, or you revised the plan until it did.
statements.explanation: That is condition five.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit the plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It stage.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Your version is the baseline: the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
statements.explanation: It is also the instrument you measure Claude's version against.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The six tests cover empty order, dependency order, self-cycle, unknown prerequisite, duplicate id, and empty plan.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You read the six tests first and predict the results.
statements.explanation: The prediction comes before the run.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You read Claude's version first and then rewrite it in your own words.
statements.explanation: The build comes before the reference.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You implement missing_fields and order in your learner workspace before you open the reference.
statements.explanation: You cannot audit an ordering you have never computed.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against the plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Use It sequence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You let Claude Code start implementing and review the diff afterward.
statements.explanation: It acts only after the gate passes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You ask Claude to critique your plan and then accept each criticism it makes.
statements.explanation: You check each criticism against the plan and the code yourself.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At the planning stage, what returns from Claude Code is an approved plan.
statements.explanation: It is a proposal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: First you do the formulation work yourself: three candidates, the pairwise results, the selection, and the interest it leaves out.
statements.explanation: That comes before asking Claude for a plan.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You then give Claude Code the bounded objective and the exclusions and ask for a plan in the eight fields, saying explicitly that it should change no file yet.
statements.explanation: What returns is a proposal.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against the plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about judging Claude Code's account and keeping the record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude's account of why it chose a step is a story about the system, not a trace of it.
statements.explanation: Chapter 1 argued this.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You judge the plan by how well it is argued.
statements.explanation: You judge it by what it commits to.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You preserve the transcript: your prompt, the plan, each revision, the diff, the commands and outputs, the date, and the displayed model label.
statements.explanation: That is the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If Claude Code is unavailable, you invent a plausible session transcript and label it as illustrative.
statements.explanation: You label the plan as your constructed artifact, record that the session did not run, and do not invent its output or an approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You judge the plan by what it commits to.
statements.explanation: A commitment can be checked; an argument can merely persuade.

questions.source: Ship It: the reviewed plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Ship It artifact.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The artifact brief asks for the proposed plan, validation failures, human revisions, stop conditions, and the final approved scope.
statements.explanation: These are its listed contents.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The field-validation result and the dependency order are included as semantic approval.
statements.explanation: They are included, but not as semantic approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The final version replaces the initial proposal so that there is one clean plan.
statements.explanation: Versions are preserved rather than replacing the initial proposal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If approval is pending, the plan remains pending.
statements.explanation: Claude cannot supply the approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The artifact is the reviewed plan.
statements.explanation: It is the chapter's deliverable.

questions.source: Ship It: the reviewed plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter's template is a signature.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is the template, not a signature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sign-off says the work succeeded.
statements.explanation: It says only that the plan survived the review described.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The "Not checked" line does the work.
statements.explanation: It records what the review did not cover.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Withholding is an honest result when the evidence does not support signing.
statements.explanation: The sign-off allows approved, returned for revision, or withheld.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sign-off should be drafted by Claude because it can write fluent words quickly.
statements.explanation: Write it from your record; fluency is not evidence.

questions.source: Ship It: the reviewed plan
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the driver's-seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approval, wider scope, and stopping on a new risk: Claude decides and records it.
statements.explanation: You decide and record it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Evidence conditions on edges: Claude proposes candidates, and you apply the stranger test and mark who can apply each.
statements.explanation: A condition only its author can apply is not yet a handoff.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Drafting steps, tools, and order: Claude drafts and runs the ordering, and you build missing_fields and order yourself first, then revise the draft.
statements.explanation: You cannot audit an ordering you have never computed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Framing the problem: Claude adds candidates you missed, and you write your candidates first, certify they differ, and select one.
statements.explanation: Selection centers some interests and decenters others.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Counterexamples: you generate many quickly, and Claude judges which are plausible here.
statements.explanation: Claude generates; you judge plausibility.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the verify and reflect step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You name which claim each check addresses and trace each error to duplicate, unknown dependency, or cycle rather than saying ordering failed generically.
statements.explanation: The tracing is part of the check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You check whether your graph omits real dependencies or invents unnecessary ones.
statements.explanation: The function cannot do this for you.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two steps that are both ready under the function can safely run concurrently.
statements.explanation: Parallel readiness means no declared dependency, not proof that concurrent execution is safe.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You preserve at least one unsafe or useless plan that still passes the structural checks.
statements.explanation: It shows what the structure cannot catch.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Planning is valuable when it merely predicts the steps you already took.
statements.explanation: It is valuable when revision happens before the cost of action.

questions.source: A plan predicts action; a result records it
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the closing sections on Chapter 11 and the Anthropics comparison.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The final answer may skip the chain from plan to tool result to independent check.
statements.explanation: It must not skip that chain.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Anthropics section asks you to explain whether the task needs a fixed sequence or model-directed choices.
statements.explanation: That is its comparison question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Chapter 11 follows one planned tool request through validation, dispatch, result association, and independent checking.
statements.explanation: The plan is carried forward as the prediction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tool result supplies evidence about what did happen, while a plan says what should happen.
statements.explanation: They are different kinds of record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The eight fields come from Anthropic's Building effective agents guidance.
statements.explanation: The eight fields remain this course's own review instrument.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Computational Skepticism refinement of testability.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A condition only its author can apply has not yet become a handoff condition.
statements.explanation: It fails the stranger test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An acyclic graph makes the handoff trustworthy.
statements.explanation: It orders work; it does not make the handoff trustworthy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You should leave edge conditions untiered so that every condition counts equally.
statements.explanation: Mark each with its tier.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether a cited clause really governs the change is a condition any non-author can apply.
statements.explanation: Only a qualified reviewer can apply it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Testability is graded: some conditions any non-author can apply, while others only a qualified reviewer can.
statements.explanation: That is the refinement.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Conducting AI practices the chapter adds.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Applying the change-the-actor move to your plan means asking whether the binding constraint is the test, the function, or the caller's expectation.
statements.explanation: The chapter poses that question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The three moves are cited research, so their outputs need no further test.
statements.explanation: They are the book's own scaffolds, so every output gets the distinctness test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One move for producing candidates that really differ is to zoom out until the original metric becomes a symptom.
statements.explanation: It is one of the three moves.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The appendix's companion check is to mark every constraint in your scope field as real or assumed and test one you suspect is assumed.
statements.explanation: If none ever turns out to be assumed, you are not looking.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One move for producing candidates that really differ is to change the actor by asking whose constraint actually binds.
statements.explanation: It is one of the three moves.

questions.source: Chapter opening (the 42 versus 99 fixture)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's opening fixture, in which the tool returned 42 and the assistant then said 99.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 99 came from a live Claude session that happened to make an arithmetic error.
statements.explanation: The 99 came from a scripted fixture, not a live transcript.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fixture was deliberately constructed and run offline for the chapter's research.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it a deliberately constructed offline fixture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The controller reported its own status as finished.
statements.explanation: The reported status was finished.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tool returned 42 and the assistant's final sentence said 99.
statements.explanation: That is the 42-versus-99 trace.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The controller compared the assistant's final sentence with the tool result before reporting its status.
statements.explanation: The controller never compared the final sentence with the tool result.

questions.source: Chapter opening (the 42 versus 99 fixture)
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the opening trace got right.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The request to add 17 and 25 was well formed.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the request was well formed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The result carried the matching identifier.
statements.explanation: The result carried the matching identifier.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A well formed request, a validating dispatcher, a matching identifier, and a recognized loop exit together guarantee that the final sentence is true.
statements.explanation: "A correct recipe is not a check"; the trace can still end in a false sentence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The dispatcher validated the request.
statements.explanation: The dispatcher validated it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The loop ended in a recognized state.
statements.explanation: The loop ended in a recognized state.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four prediction questions the chapter asks before the trace.

statements.label: A
statements.text: One question asks whether Python will accept True as the number 1.
statements.explanation: The first prediction concerns True and the number 1.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter says the value of the predictions lies in guessing correctly.
statements.explanation: The value is not guessing correctly but exposing the model of the machinery you brought.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter asks you to write the predictions down and date them.
statements.explanation: The predictions are to be written down and dated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One question asks whether an unknown tool will crash the program or be silently ignored.
statements.explanation: The question is whether an unknown tool becomes a Python exception or a returned tool error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One question asks whether the loop will call the outcome verified when the assistant stops after saying 99.
statements.explanation: The question is whether the loop will call that outcome finished.

questions.source: What you will be able to do
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the outcomes the chapter says you should reach.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Audit a final claim using evidence that is chosen to agree with it.
statements.explanation: The outcome is evidence that can disagree with the claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Design failure behavior on the assumption that every response requests a tool.
statements.explanation: The outcome is bounded failure behavior "rather than assuming every response requests a tool".

statements.label: C
statements.text: Explain why a tool schema is an invitation rather than an execution engine.
statements.explanation: A listed outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Match every result to its request identifier and state what that match does not show.
statements.explanation: A listed outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Validate a proposed call before dispatching it and state what the dispatcher must refuse as a contract you wrote.
statements.explanation: A listed outcome.

questions.source: Three jobs at the scale of one tool call
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three jobs at the scale of one tool call.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A finished status establishes that the controller saw a stop signal.
statements.explanation: That is all finished establishes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Under Conduct, you leave it to the loop to decide what counts as done.
statements.explanation: You decide what the loop may call done.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent sentence at the end of the trace counts as evidence for the claim it states.
statements.explanation: A fluent sentence establishes nothing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A matching identifier establishes that the final answer is correct.
statements.explanation: A matching identifier establishes only who asked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Under Conduct, you decide which operations must be exact and therefore live in your program.
statements.explanation: Exact operations belong in your program, not the model's continuation.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the choice between Claude writing 17 + 25 = 42 and a dispatcher returning 42.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter says Claude's arithmetic is rarely right.
statements.explanation: It is "very often right".

statements.label: B
statements.text: A dispatcher's 42 comes from an operation you can read, re-run, and break with a test.
statements.explanation: The dispatcher's number is inspectable and testable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The design question is how often Claude's sentence is right.
statements.explanation: The question is whether anything in the path would tell you the one time it is not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nothing outside the continuation recomputes the sum when Claude writes it directly.
statements.explanation: Nothing recomputes it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When Claude writes 17 + 25 = 42, that sentence is a continuation, ranked and sampled like any other.
statements.explanation: Chapter 1's loop makes the sentence a sampled continuation.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about verifiability-first engineering as the chapter presents it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reason given is that the most constrained tool is the one you can check.
statements.explanation: The most constrained tool is the one you can check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rule is to choose the most capable model that can do the step.
statements.explanation: The rule is the lowest capability that does the step.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Arithmetic, exact lookups, deterministic transforms, and schema validation belong inside the probabilistic layers.
statements.explanation: They belong outside the probabilistic layers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The "easier to verify" value ranks how reliable each layer is.
statements.explanation: It is not a ranking of reliability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The five-layer capability stack is an industry standard.
statements.explanation: The stack is a teaching device, not an industry standard.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the book's example of totaling every line item over $10,000 across 200 invoices.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Only the sum, not the filter, is handed to deterministic code in the better design.
statements.explanation: Both the filter and the sum go to deterministic code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The example concerns 200 invoices and line items over $10,000.
statements.explanation: Those are the example's figures.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Extracting fields per invoice and handing the filter and the sum to deterministic code leaves seams where you can compare records with invoices.
statements.explanation: The seams are where you compare records and recompute the sum.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Handing the sum to deterministic code makes the total certain to be correct.
statements.explanation: Deterministic code is inspectable, not infallible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking a chat window for the total gives a number you can audit step by step.
statements.explanation: The chat window gives a fluent number with nothing behind it to audit.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the costs of routing a step out to deterministic code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the chapter's division, Claude proposes the call and interprets the trace while Python owns exact argument validation and arithmetic.
statements.explanation: That is the deliberate division.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deterministic code that encodes the wrong formula will produce the error inconsistently, so it is easy to spot.
statements.explanation: It will encode the wrong formula consistently.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Every operation granted to the dispatcher is authority granted.
statements.explanation: The second honest cost.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A one-tool allowlist is hard to audit because it can do almost nothing.
statements.explanation: It is easy to audit precisely because it can do almost nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Routing a step out makes it inspectable, not infallible.
statements.explanation: The first honest cost.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the `add` tool schema.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The schema authorizes the model to run arbitrary Python.
statements.explanation: It grants no such authority.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The schema tells Claude which request shape the application is prepared to consider.
statements.explanation: It describes the request shape.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The schema imports an `add` function into the model.
statements.explanation: No function is imported into the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The schema is part of a protocol conversation, while the runtime remains application code.
statements.explanation: The runtime stays in the application.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The schema proves that the application enforces the schema.
statements.explanation: Enforcement is a separate matter.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: A model proposes the calls below. Check each statement that is true about how the course `dispatch` function treats them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Name `add` with input {"a": True, "b": 2} raises ValueError.
statements.explanation: The exact-type rule rejects a Boolean.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Name `subtract` with input {"a": 5, "b": 3} raises ValueError.
statements.explanation: The name must be exactly add.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Name `add` with input {"a": 1} is accepted and b is treated as 0.
statements.explanation: A missing key fails the exact-keys rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Name `add` with input {"a": 17, "b": 25} returns 42.
statements.explanation: Exact keys, exact int types, finite sum 42.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Name `add` with input {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3} is accepted and the extra key is ignored.
statements.explanation: The keys must be exactly a and b, so the extra key is refused.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Boolean check in `dispatch`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A specification that never mentions `True` still gives an implementer a reason to refuse it.
statements.explanation: A silent specification gives no reason to refuse it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The implementation relies on `isinstance(v, (int, float))` to reject that impostor.
statements.explanation: It uses `type(v) not in (int, float)`, not isinstance, to reject it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Python, `bool` is a subclass of `int`.
statements.explanation: The subclass relationship is why the guard matters.

statements.label: D
statements.text: `isinstance(True, int)` is true.
statements.explanation: Hence isinstance admits True.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A casual numerical guard would admit `True + 2` and produce 3.
statements.explanation: True + 2 gives 3.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about finite numbers and validation in the `add` tool.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The refusals in the contract are decisions about what the operation means.
statements.explanation: The refusals are decisions, and they are the author's.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Validation is decoration before the real work.
statements.explanation: Validation defines what the operation means.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Infinity and not-a-number are ints in Python.
statements.explanation: They are floats.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A JSON-facing description that says "number" tells Python exactly which values to accept.
statements.explanation: Python still needs rules for the values it actually receives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two finite inputs always produce a finite sum.
statements.explanation: Finite inputs can overflow when added, so the result is checked separately.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the application, not the model, dispatches the proposed name.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Exact argument rules replace the need for an allowlist.
statements.explanation: Argument rules narrow each operation within the allowlist; they do not replace it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool schema is a substitute for the dispatcher's enforcement checks.

statements.label: C

statements.label: D
statements.text: Chapter 5 said the model should decide who may do what.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Letting the model decide how to execute the name collapses description, authority, and implementation into one unreviewable gesture.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the result builder that catches ValueError.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The application pretends the tool ran and returns a default value.
