statements.label: B
statements.text: A caught ValueError becomes a tool_result that carries the request's identifier.
statements.explanation: The row repeats the identity.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rejected proposal is designed to crash the whole conversation.
statements.explanation: The conversation does not crash.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The model can see that a particular request failed and why.
statements.explanation: The error becomes evidence for the next turn.

statements.label: E
statements.text: That result is marked `is_error: True`.
statements.explanation: The error flag is set.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the result builder deliberately does not catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Catch everything" is a form of verification.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it is not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An unexpected programming defect should not be laundered into a routine model-visible message.
statements.explanation: Laundering a defect hides it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It catches only ValueError, a bounded and anticipated validation failure.
statements.explanation: ValueError is the anticipated failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Catching every exception and relabeling it as a tool error would be stronger verification.
statements.explanation: Catch-all is not verification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Relabeling a defect as a routine tool error would let the host stop in a known state.
statements.explanation: The host would continue in an unknown state.

questions.source: Identifiers create correspondence, not truth
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a request identifier does and does not establish.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The identifier answers which result belongs to which request.
statements.explanation: Its job is correspondence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Like a luggage tag, the identifier inspects what is inside the suitcase.
statements.explanation: A tag helps establish ownership, not contents.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A result matched to the right request must be correct.
statements.explanation: Correspondence is not correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A matched result can still be wrong because the dispatcher contains a bug.
statements.explanation: A dispatcher bug survives a matching ID.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the identifier matches, stale data from an external service cannot be the cause of a wrong result.
statements.explanation: A matched result can still be wrong because of stale data.

questions.source: Identifiers create correspondence, not truth
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the duplicate-identifier guard in `results`.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The `seen` set is local to one invocation of `results`.
statements.explanation: A fresh set is made on each call.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Duplicate identifiers within one processed assistant content batch are rejected" matches the implementation.
statements.explanation: That wording states the scope of the check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The guard establishes global uniqueness across every turn of a conversation.
statements.explanation: Uniqueness is only within one batch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Duplicate identifiers are rejected" is the precisely scoped statement of the guard.
statements.explanation: That wording is too broad.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `results` raises ValueError when two tool requests in one content batch share an identifier.
statements.explanation: The executed fixture observed this rejection.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the `loop` controller is set up.

statements.label: A

statements.explanation: Each response is appended to the trace.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Injecting `call` is what makes the controller testable offline.

statements.label: C

statements.label: D
statements.text: Optional live transport requires writing a different controller.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `loop` accepts a callable named `call`, a request body, and a bounded number of turns.
statements.explanation: Those are the parameters.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the exits of the `loop` controller.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

statements.label: E
statements.text: A `tool_use` stop ends the loop immediately with status `stopped`.
statements.explanation: A tool_use stop builds results, appends them, and continues unless the budget is exhausted.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the turn budget.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

statements.explanation: It does not certify safety.

statements.label: C

statements.explanation: It does not guarantee progress.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A budget of four turns makes any single turn safe.
statements.explanation: An unauthorized operation could be damaging on the first turn.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A turn budget prevents unbounded continuation.
statements.explanation: That is its purpose.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the word `finished` and the word `verified`.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

statements.label: D

statements.label: E

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the worked example uses scripted responses.

statements.label: D

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two-turn trace in the chapter is a single recorded run of a live Claude session.
statements.explanation: The two-turn trace composes the pieces, and `sum-1` is an illustrative identifier.

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim

statements.label: B

statements.label: C

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the recorded 42 result supports.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It records 42 together with matching identifiers.
statements.explanation: The research script recorded 42 with matching identifiers.

statements.label: B

statements.label: C

statements.label: D

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about changing one boundary at a time in the `sum-1` example.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Two tool-use blocks with ID `sum-1` in one batch produce two error results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `results` turns that rejection into a result tied to `sum-1` with `is_error: True`.

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim

statements.label: B

statements.label: D

statements.explanation: Hand arithmetic avoids the dispatcher entirely.

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: Design independence around failure modes.

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim

questions.source: Worked example: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the final row of the evidence matrix, the teardown.

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the verbs that tool reports use.

statements.label: B

statements.label: E

questions.source: Verification surfaces for real tools

statements.label: E

questions.source: Verification surfaces for real tools

statements.label: E

questions.source: Verification surfaces for real tools

statements.label: A

statements.label: B

questions.source: Building a reusable tool evidence matrix

statements.explanation: Each absent field is a decision nobody made, and nothing in the store prompts anyone to ask.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The source field is caller-supplied text describing provenance.
statements.explanation: It records claimed provenance but does not prove it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The author identity can be inferred from the source string.
statements.explanation: None of the absent fields can be inferred from the fields that exist.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The version field is a local revision counter.
statements.explanation: It counts revisions of the record locally, nothing more.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The record includes an expiry time that the store can enforce.
statements.explanation: No expiry time is stored.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the read method.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A restart loses the dictionary.
statements.explanation: The records live in process memory.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The lock and deep copy together make the class a distributed database.
statements.explanation: Neither mechanism does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Code that touches the records dictionary directly is still protected by the lock.
statements.explanation: It bypasses the lock.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a caller appends to a returned list, a later read still sees the unchanged stored list.
statements.explanation: The repository test executes that boundary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The read method holds a process-local lock and returns a deep copy.
statements.explanation: The lock guards the read and the deep copy isolates the caller.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about optimistic concurrency control as the chapter describes it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stale work may need to be discarded, reconsidered, or merged.
statements.explanation: That is the stated trade-off.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A worker reads a version and works on the assumption that the record will not change.
statements.explanation: That is the optimistic assumption.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At commit time the worker supplies the version it read, and the store compares it with current state.
statements.explanation: The write method takes an expected version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Optimistic" means the store locks the record for the whole of the worker's work.
statements.explanation: Workers proceed without locking for the whole of their work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: On a mismatch the store can tell you whether to discard, reconsider, or merge the stale work.
statements.explanation: The store cannot tell you which.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the version comparison happens inside the lock.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The lock makes the check-and-replace atomic across processes, restarts, and machines.
statements.explanation: Only among threads sharing the same object.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing inside the lock lets the store decide whether the new value is true.
statements.explanation: The check is about versions, not truth.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With an unguarded check, the stale writer would still be rejected, so the lock is a formality.
statements.explanation: The unguarded version lets a silent overwrite through.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With comparison and write as separate unguarded steps, two threads could both compare against version zero before either writes.
statements.explanation: The race the lock removes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In that race both threads could write version one, and the second would silently overwrite the first.
statements.explanation: Both passed the same stale comparison, so the later write replaced the earlier one without error.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the revision boundary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The store works out the revision boundary automatically from the values written.
statements.explanation: It is a choice you make before any worker runs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A version number guards one key.
statements.explanation: It says nothing about other keys.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If one decision reads three keys, all three version numbers can be current while the decision is stale.
statements.explanation: A per-key version cannot see cross-key staleness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If two locations share one key, a single conflict covers both.
statements.explanation: A shared key means a shared version, so one conflict covers both locations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A current version on a key shows that a plan built from that key and a separate document is still current.
statements.explanation: A version says nothing about the document a plan was built from.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the input checks in the write method.

statements.label: A
statements.text: True is accepted as expected version 1 because Booleans behave as integers.
statements.explanation: The exact-type check rejects it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The source must be a string containing something besides whitespace.
statements.explanation: A blank source raises an error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The expected version must have exact type int, which rejects Python Booleans.
statements.explanation: Booleans otherwise behave as integers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The checks validate that the source identifies a real, current document.
statements.explanation: They are input-shape boundaries only.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A source of three spaces passes the check because it is a string.
statements.explanation: Whitespace-only sources are rejected.

questions.source: Worked example: two workers, one key
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the constructed two-worker trace in the worked example.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A's successful write is a verified observation.
statements.explanation: It is a successful write only.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Changing A's source label from "unverified-observation" to "authoritative-sensor" would authenticate a sensor.
statements.explanation: The class trusts caller-written provenance as data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The trace is constructed: the chapter chose the key, values, and sources, and no recorded run produced it.
statements.explanation: Stated before the trace.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Worker A's write of "red" with expected=0 on a fresh store succeeds and returns 1.
statements.explanation: Current version 0 equals the expected int 0.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Worker B's later write with expected=0 raises ValueError("Stale memory version").
statements.explanation: The current version is one at commit time.

questions.source: Worked example: two workers, one key
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the incident timeline table for the two workers.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Step 3 establishes that B's premise conflicts with the current revision.
statements.explanation: The stale error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Step 1 establishes only local absence at read time.
statements.explanation: The default read of a missing key.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Step 5, where a human checks the evidence, is performed inside the store.
statements.explanation: It happens outside the store.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Step 2 establishes that the claim "red" is correct.
statements.explanation: It establishes that A's update committed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Step 4, where a reviewer reads version 1, establishes whether the claim is true.
statements.explanation: It shows current process-local state.

questions.source: Worked example: two workers, one key
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the executed sequential fixture on the key claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fixture was built so that red is the wrong value, and nothing in the store was told that.
statements.explanation: The version check never receives any information about which value is right.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The accepted step-2 write carried the source label "unverified source label".
statements.explanation: A label that names no source.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The fixture shows how the store behaves under real concurrent load.
statements.explanation: It is sequential and shows version behavior, not contention.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The rejected step-3 write carried value blue with source s1 at expected version 1.
statements.explanation: It was rejected as a stale version.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If blue were the stale value and red the correction, the store would behave differently.
statements.explanation: It would behave identically.

questions.source: Worked example: two workers, one key
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what should happen after the stale rejection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The rejection shows that the stale worker's value is the wrong one.
statements.explanation: The version check decides order, not merit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Blindly rereading and retrying is the recommended response because it satisfies concurrency control.
statements.explanation: It satisfies concurrency control while ignoring what the conflict means.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The conflict might mean A corrected B, A is wrong, they observed at different times, or the key collapses two locations into one name.
statements.explanation: These are the interpretations the chapter offers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The conflict is a signal to go back to a decision.
statements.explanation: Not a prompt to retry.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The storage mechanism cannot answer what should happen next.
statements.explanation: Whether to withdraw, merge, or reopen a decision is outside the store.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about writing the failure down before running the stale-writer fixture.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sentence is dated and not revised afterward.
statements.explanation: The gap between sentence and result is the lesson.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sentence says what a wrong coordinator would do, such as retry at the fresh version, keep whichever write arrived last, or swallow the exception and log success.
statements.explanation: These are the chapter's examples.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing a test is not the same as supporting a claim.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls this the trap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sentence may be edited after the run to match what happened.
statements.explanation: Do not revise it afterward.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The gap between the sentence and the result is what you are learning from.
statements.explanation: Writing the failure first makes the surprise measurable.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the guards in the chapter's table of what each establishes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The lock establishes that check-and-replace is atomic among threads sharing this object.
statements.explanation: That is its entry in the table.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The expected-version check establishes that the new value is true.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The expected-version check establishes that the writer's premise matched current state at commit.
statements.explanation: That is its entry in the table.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Deep copy on read establishes that the stored value is valid.
statements.explanation: It prevents aliasing, nothing more.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The lock establishes atomicity across processes, restarts, and machines.
statements.explanation: It does not.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the remaining rows of the chapter's table of guards.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The version counter establishes commit order for one key.
statements.explanation: That is what it establishes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A nonblank source string establishes that someone supplied attribution.
statements.explanation: That is what it establishes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A nonblank source string establishes that the source exists, says this, or is current.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two sessions agreeing establishes two independent routes to the claim.
statements.explanation: It shows only that two runs produced similar text.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The version counter establishes when anything was observed.
statements.explanation: It does not.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / Freshness is not truth
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about freshness and the version counter.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A newer claim can be a newer mistake.
statements.explanation: Recency says nothing about whether the observation was correct.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A version counter establishes the time of observation.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A timestamp proves that a claim is accurate.
statements.explanation: Even a timestamp does not prove accuracy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Freshness is defined relative to a use.
statements.explanation: The same age can be fine for a draft and stale for a train board.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A version counter orders a record's local history.
statements.explanation: That is its job.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / Freshness is not truth
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about expiry and freshness policy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Expiry tells you whether the refreshed observation is correct.
statements.explanation: It says only when evidence must be refreshed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Yesterday's building address is too old to use even in a draft.
statements.explanation: It may be current enough for a draft.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Storing observed_at, valid_until, and source_id separately lets the application flag a record outside its interval.
statements.explanation: Separate fields let code test the interval; they still do not validate the observation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One expiry interval suits every record, because the policy does not depend on consequence.
statements.explanation: Expiry policy is tied to consequence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A train departure board may be stale after seconds.
statements.explanation: The chapter's example of a short freshness window.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / Freshness is not truth
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the clocks a record might need.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A broken source cannot supply a fresh claim, because freshness is checked at write time.
statements.explanation: A broken source can provide fresh falsehoods all day.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Revision time, observation time, event time, ingestion time, and expiration time answer different questions.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to name the clocks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The version counter doubles as the observation time of the record.
statements.explanation: It orders commits, not observations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single field called timestamp invites later code to pick the most convenient meaning.
statements.explanation: The reason for separating the clocks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once an expiry time is stored, naming the other clocks separately is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: The different clocks answer different questions.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / A source label is a place to put provenance
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the source field.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The class requires a source because unattributed memory is hard to audit.
statements.explanation: The stated reason.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A required source guarantees every record can be traced to a document that exists.
statements.explanation: It does not verify that the source exists.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Practical provenance might include a stable source identifier, a retrieval date, the exact supporting passage, and a transformation record.
statements.explanation: Each element supports an audit of where the value came from.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The code verifies that a syllabus produced the office location named in a source string.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The source is only a nonblank string.
statements.explanation: Nothing more is checked.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / A source label is a place to put provenance
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about derived values and authentication.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A signed message makes the claim in it true.
statements.explanation: It may show who produced the bytes but does not make the claim true.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If an agent summarizes a source, the record should preserve that the value is a derived summary.
statements.explanation: So a model's paraphrase is not mistaken for source text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Authentication is a separate layer from recording provenance.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it another layer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Concurrency control, provenance rules, and domain verification should be merged into one check.
statements.explanation: Keep the jobs separate so you can test each.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model's paraphrase can be stored as if it were source text, since the source string covers it.
statements.explanation: Preserve that it is a derived summary.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes / A source label is a place to put provenance
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about three jobs the chapter says to keep separate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A nonblank-source rule decides whether the claim is true.
statements.explanation: It only rejects missing attribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Domain verification evaluates support.
statements.explanation: It asks whether the evidence supports the claim, which the store never does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Provenance rules reject missing attribution.
statements.explanation: It enforces that some attribution exists.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The version check evaluates whether a claim is supported by its source.
statements.explanation: That is domain verification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Concurrency control rejects stale versions.
statements.explanation: It orders commits and rejects premises that are out of date.

questions.source: The handoff is where claims gain authority
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the cascade pattern.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter reports cascade frequencies as rates to plan around.
statements.explanation: Look for the patterns; do not read them as rates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checking each worker in isolation is enough to detect a cascade.
statements.explanation: That tells you little about it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cascade requires the first worker to be wrong with high probability.
statements.explanation: The chapter says wrong with some small probability.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In a cascade a second worker conditions on a first worker's output, a third on the second's, and so on.
statements.explanation: The chain structure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: By the end, the system's error is governed by how errors compound across the chain.
statements.explanation: Per-worker accuracy does not capture compounding along the chain.

questions.source: The handoff is where claims gain authority
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about authority laundering.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The pattern comes from a large controlled trial that measured its rate.
statements.explanation: It comes from an exploratory study of one framework, two frontier models, two weeks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tracking provenance across workers addresses the pattern.
statements.explanation: Seeing the origin across hand-offs is what lets a receiver check the claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The data takes on the standing of the channel it arrived through.
statements.explanation: The definition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Limiting what a single worker may access prevents the pattern.
statements.explanation: It does not prevent it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A worker passes data to another as a legitimate output, and the receiver cannot verify where it came from.
statements.explanation: The definition.

questions.source: The handoff is where claims gain authority
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the constructed lineage in which note-7 (source s1) leads to summary-A, summary-B, and a report that cites summary-B.

statements.label: A
statements.text: summary-B counts as a confirmation of note-7 because it is a separate document.
statements.explanation: It derives from summary-A, which derives from note-7.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The lineage records 0 independent confirmations of note-7 and 1 lineage.
statements.explanation: The chain note-7, summary-A, summary-B, report is a single path.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Version history proves the claim in the note.
statements.explanation: It proves the order of commits, not the claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The report citing summary-B adds an independent confirmation.
statements.explanation: It remains the same lineage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ten summaries of one wrong note are one lineage, not ten confirmations.
statements.explanation: Repeating a derived claim adds copies, not independent routes to it.

questions.source: The handoff is where claims gain authority / Shared notes are an input boundary
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about shared notes as an input boundary.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Inserting stored text into a later prompt turns the record store into a possible instruction channel.
statements.explanation: Stored text re-enters the prompt, where it can be read as an instruction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Version checks preserve instruction-like text and deep copies protect it from accidental mutation, but neither decides whether it is evidence, data, or an instruction.
statements.explanation: Preserving and copying text is different from classifying it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prompt warning is an authorization system.
statements.explanation: It is not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Deep copying a note neutralizes instruction-like text in it.
statements.explanation: It only prevents accidental mutation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The stored prose of a note decides what the note may cause.
statements.explanation: The application decides.

questions.source: The handoff is where claims gain authority / Shared notes are an input boundary
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about controls for shared notes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Delimit shared notes from application instructions.
statements.explanation: Separating the channels keeps stored prose from being read as the application's instructions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Preserve the provenance of shared notes.
statements.explanation: Knowing where a note came from is needed to weigh it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A quarantine state deletes suspicious records so they cannot be read.
statements.explanation: It keeps them out of prompt construction without deleting what an incident review needs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Validate proposed actions at execution time.
statements.explanation: The tool boundary, not the note, decides what may actually happen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once the prompt warns the model about notes, the tool boundary no longer has to reject out-of-scope operations.
statements.explanation: The tool boundary must still reject operations outside scope.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what Claude does in the chapter's split between coordinating and deliberating.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude keeps the original outputs and summarizes disagreement without flattening it.
statements.explanation: Preserving originals keeps disagreement visible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude owns the final decision because it holds all the original outputs.
statements.explanation: The decision has a human owner whose name goes on it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude holds the initial interpretation formed before the synthesis.
statements.explanation: Humans hold it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude weighs what a conflict means for the stakes.
statements.explanation: Humans do.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude routes tasks and compares artifacts.
statements.explanation: Routing and comparing are mechanical coordination tasks.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what humans do in the split.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Humans weigh what a conflict means for the stakes, hear dissent, and decide.
statements.explanation: These are judgments about stakes that belong to a named owner.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Humans bring local knowledge the shared notes never contained.
statements.explanation: A synthesis cannot contain what nobody wrote into the notes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Humans preserve dissent by averaging it into smooth prose.
statements.explanation: The practice is to preserve dissent rather than average it away.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Humans hold the initial interpretation formed before the synthesis.
statements.explanation: It must exist before the synthesis can anchor it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The decision is owned by the coordinator session, whose name goes on it.
statements.explanation: The decision has a human owner.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about independence among Claude sessions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reviewer who sees the researcher's conclusion first may anchor on it.
statements.explanation: Seeing the conclusion first can anchor the reviewer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Independence is a design question about failure correlation: would the two routes fail for the same reason?
statements.explanation: Independence concerns whether failures are correlated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two sessions may share a model, training influences, tool configuration, source corpus, and prompt author.
statements.explanation: These shared factors are what undermine independence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two copies of a model count as independent judgments as long as each has a different prompt.
statements.explanation: Copies are not independence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Role labels such as "researcher" and "reviewer" make two sessions independent.
statements.explanation: Role labels do not manufacture independence.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how agreement between automated checks can fail to be independent.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A reviewer who sees the researcher's conclusion first is more independent for having more context.
statements.explanation: Anchoring is the risk.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two agents retrieving from one incomplete corpus can agree for the same cause.
statements.explanation: A shared incomplete corpus gives both agents the same blind spot.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Agreement between two sessions on the same passages counts as two confirmations if their roles differ.
statements.explanation: Role differences do not create independence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A deterministic checker is independent of specification errors because it is code.
statements.explanation: It inherits the mistaken specification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Python checker written from the same mistaken specification ratifies the mistake deterministically.
statements.explanation: A deterministic checker repeats whatever the specification gets wrong.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Condorcet's jury theorem and the sequencing practice as the chapter uses them.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Without independence the theorem says nothing.
statements.explanation: The theorem's guarantee depends on independence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sequencing practice is to collect initial judgments before showing a synthesis, then deliberate with sources visible and preserve dissent.
statements.explanation: Variety must be captured before a synthesis can collapse it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter relies on "invisible groupthink" as an established finding.
statements.explanation: It flags the label as a hypothesis and does not rely on it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The book argues that showing the synthesis first preserves variety.
statements.explanation: Reversing the order collapses variety before it can do any work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: As the book retells it, the theorem rests on two assumptions: the voters are independent and each is better than chance.
statements.explanation: Both assumptions must hold for many judgments to beat one.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about role contracts.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In the reviewer example any "cannot tell" verdict goes to the coordinator, who routes it to the named human reviewer.
statements.explanation: Escalation reaches a named human rather than being settled by the model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A role contract is bounded by inputs, outputs, tools, budget, and escalation.
statements.explanation: Vague roles like 'review the work' bound none of these.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the reviewer example the verdicts are limited to pass or fail.
statements.explanation: They are supported, unsupported, or cannot tell.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the reviewer example the tools are read only, with no writes to memory.
statements.explanation: The reviewer can read but cannot change memory or files.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Review the work" is not a role contract.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so directly.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about preserving disagreement and about a solo learner.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A solo learner writes a dated initial interpretation before reading any Claude synthesis.
statements.explanation: The solo form of the same rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A solo learner can skip the initial interpretation because Claude's synthesis covers it.
statements.explanation: The interpretation must come first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You must not fabricate teammates.
statements.explanation: Only real people count as teammates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The coordinator keeps the original outputs so synthesis cannot erase disagreement.
statements.explanation: The originals are the evidence of disagreement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two model personas count as two people for independent review.
statements.explanation: They are not two people.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about integration and the re-engagement trigger.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The re-engagement trigger comes from the Computational Skepticism companion.
statements.explanation: It comes from Conducting AI.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Integration holds the parts at once so a finding in one can reach backward and reopen another.
statements.explanation: That backward reach is what makes it integration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A re-engagement trigger is an event: a locatable moment when you noticed something that made an earlier decision unsafe and went back.
statements.explanation: A locatable event can be written down and checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Stay flexible" is an acceptable form of re-engagement trigger.
statements.explanation: The trigger is an event, not an attitude.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sequencing runs the parts one after another and then writes a summary.
statements.explanation: It is sequential work followed by a summary.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about triggers that reopen earlier decisions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stale-version exception is the only kind of trigger that matters.
statements.explanation: It is only one kind.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Before any worker runs you need to decide only what the record holds.
statements.explanation: You also decide what events reopen what, and who notices.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A newer source, a reviewer's correction, and a failed spot check are triggers the store cannot raise.
statements.explanation: They come from outside the store.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Triggers from outside the store are less consequential than the stale-version exception.
statements.explanation: The more consequential ones come from outside.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stale-version exception is a trigger the store raises on its own.
statements.explanation: The version check inside the store is something it can raise itself.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why a gate that includes reopening conditions is not waterfall.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan from Chapter 10 is revised automatically when its evidence is gone.
statements.explanation: Without reopening conditions it stays in force.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Design-first does not mean freeze the design.
statements.explanation: The design stays open to new evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A plan without reopening conditions is already a gate.
statements.explanation: The reopening conditions make it a gate rather than a plan.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter recommends a waterfall process in which the design is frozen before workers start.
statements.explanation: The chapter says this is not waterfall.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The gate written before the prompt includes the conditions under which you will reopen it.
statements.explanation: Reopening conditions are what make it a gate rather than a plan.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the course-schedule simulation in which record version three says an assignment closes Friday, a researcher finds an official schedule saying Monday but has not written it, and an explainer worker is generating Friday-facing instructions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stale-version exception is raised as soon as the researcher finds the new schedule.
statements.explanation: Nothing has been written yet.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It is not a version conflict, because only one new proposal exists.
statements.explanation: Only one proposal exists, so no two writes conflict.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The explainer worker's Friday-facing instructions will be rejected by the store.
statements.explanation: The store sees no conflicting write.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It is a dependency conflict between ongoing work and new evidence.
statements.explanation: The explainer's work depends on a value the new evidence challenges.

statements.label: E
statements.text: No version check can see it.
statements.explanation: Version checks compare writes, and no competing write has been made.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the incident states in the course-schedule simulation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The researcher's evidence moves the assumption directly to superseded.
statements.explanation: It moves it to challenged; superseded comes after human review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The previous record becomes superseded as soon as the researcher finds the evidence.
statements.explanation: Only after a named human reviews the source and the Monday date applies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A coordinator needs only the two states success and failure.
statements.explanation: It needs richer states such as active, challenged, paused, reviewed, superseded, and resumed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Downstream tasks whose correctness depends on the closing date move to paused.
statements.explanation: Their premise, the Friday date, is now challenged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Work moves to resumed as soon as the new version is committed, before affected work is regenerated.
statements.explanation: Resumed comes only after regeneration.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the dependency map in the incident example.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Memory correctness at the key is not workflow correction everywhere the value traveled.
statements.explanation: Fixing the record does not fix outputs already produced.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Version numbers order the records, but the dependency map says what must pause.
statements.explanation: Ordering and dependency are different information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Committing the corrected value to the key regenerates downstream outputs automatically.
statements.explanation: The store does not do that.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The store's version history identifies every output that depended on a given version.
statements.explanation: The dependency map does that job.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without a dependency map the store can accept the correction while Friday instructions already produced keep circulating.
statements.explanation: The store has no knowledge of where the value was used.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about reconstructing an incident from logs.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Missing events are marked as gaps.
statements.explanation: Mark gaps as gaps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent reconstruction of the missing events makes the replay complete.
statements.explanation: Do not fill missing events with fluent reconstruction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If logs show a worker read sometime before version four but not the returned version, the version is recorded as unknown.
statements.explanation: Do not guess a number the logs do not preserve.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can be relied on to flag fragments that do not fit when it reconstructs an incident.
statements.explanation: It will write a coherent account including fragments that do not fit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A replay that marks what is unknown has failed.
statements.explanation: A replay that marks what is unknown is the desired detection evidence.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a second worker whose Monday update arrives with expected=3 after the reviewer has committed version four.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The write fails because it is based on a stale version.
statements.explanation: The current version is four.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Version conflict is a merge algorithm that combines the two proposals.
statements.explanation: It is not a merge algorithm.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The write succeeds because its proposal is correct.
statements.explanation: The version check does not judge correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The stale worker must reread, compare the semantic changes, and either withdraw or create a new reviewable proposal.
statements.explanation: The approved value may differ in meaning from the stale proposal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retrying automatically at version four would be unsafe.
statements.explanation: The human-approved value may carry a qualification the proposal lacks.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Re-engagement Log.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Entries may describe plausible events the fixture did not produce, to keep the log complete.
statements.explanation: Write entries only for events that happened.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Orderly sections are enough evidence that the work reached backward.
statements.explanation: The log exists because sections can look orderly without reaching back.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each entry records only the version read and the final decision.
statements.explanation: It also records the evidence, the owner, what paused, and what allowed resuming.

statements.label: D
statements.text: This course adopts the companion book's grading of the log.
statements.explanation: It takes the idea, not the grading.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It consists of discrete entries proving that the work reached backward.
statements.explanation: The log exists to show events, not tidy structure.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about duplicate actions and the memory store.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Consequential tools need idempotency keys or coordination at the action boundary.
statements.explanation: Protection must sit where the action occurs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If two workers both send the same email, rejecting a stale memory update afterward does not undo the effect.
statements.explanation: The effect already happened outside the store.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Duplicate action is distinct from duplicate writes.
statements.explanation: A rejected write does not reverse an external action.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stale-version rejection in the store prevents the duplicate email from being sent.
statements.explanation: It cannot undo or prevent the external effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Memory is the action system.
statements.explanation: Memory is not the action system.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing / Tear down a complete incident state machine
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about retention and replay.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Redaction preserves interpretability automatically.
statements.explanation: Redaction must be designed to preserve interpretability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Redacting every value costs nothing for replay.
statements.explanation: If every value becomes [REDACTED] the trace may no longer show why a decision occurred.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You define what is stored, for how long, who can read it, and how deletion works.
statements.explanation: Each is a policy decision about retained traces.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Retention and replay do not compete.
statements.explanation: Retention competes with replay.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Complete prompts and tool results aid incident review but may hold private information.
statements.explanation: That is why retention is a tradeoff.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Next to each item you write who decided it: you, or a suggestion of Claude's that you accepted.
statements.explanation: It records which decisions were yours.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude can write the gate for you without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: The gate is where your understanding of the stakes goes on the record.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gate is written before Claude implements anything, and Claude's work is tested against it.
statements.explanation: That order makes the gate a test target for Claude's work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter starts one layer earlier than choosing what memory text to place in the prompt, by asking what record must exist so that reliance can be audited.
statements.explanation: Auditable reliance comes before prompt contents.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can sharpen the gate if you ask it for the trigger you missed.
statements.explanation: Claude's challenge is useful; its authorship of the gate is not.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the fuller teaching record with fields such as source_id, verification, and valid_until.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Every added field creates a validation problem.
statements.explanation: Each new field needs rules for who sets it and what it means.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A richer schema helps by itself, even when code and policy do not enforce the meanings.
statements.explanation: It helps only when they do.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is a design sketch, not output from the current implementation.
statements.explanation: Its fields are not produced by the current class.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A verification value of "human-reviewed" shows that a human reviewed the record.
statements.explanation: Who may set it is itself a policy question.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A valid_until of None has one unambiguous meaning.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks what None means for expiry.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three separations in the design of the record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Facts are not instructions: render {"due_day": "Monday"} as a quoted claim with provenance.
statements.explanation: Never into the system instruction channel.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stored fact may be rendered into the system instruction channel once it comes from a reviewed version.
statements.explanation: Never into the system instruction channel.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Proposed is not accepted: a research worker should often write to a proposal queue.
statements.explanation: A reviewer checks meaning before a coordinator commits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Shared" means every worker sees every record.
statements.explanation: Reads follow purpose.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer checks meaning after the coordinator commits against the expected version.
statements.explanation: The reviewer checks before the coordinator commits.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first row of the trigger table, in which a newer official schedule contradicts version 3 of due_day.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The owner is the explainer worker.
statements.explanation: The owner is the named course-staff reviewer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resuming requires a reviewed version to be committed and each paused task to reread it.
statements.explanation: Rereading ensures paused work uses the reviewed value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The work that pauses is any task rendering due_day into instructions.
statements.explanation: Only work that renders the value is affected.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Work resumes once the researcher's proposal is accepted by the store.
statements.explanation: A reviewed version must be committed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The earlier decision it reopens is which source counts as authoritative for deadlines.
statements.explanation: Which source is authoritative is the decision a newer schedule reopens.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the second row of the trigger table, in which a stale-version exception hits a key an active task read.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The resume condition is that the coordinator retries at the fresh version.
statements.explanation: Both proposals and evidence are preserved and a reviewer decides.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every task in the system pauses.
statements.explanation: Only that task's writes and any action depending on it pause.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The only permitted resolution is for the reviewer to commit.
statements.explanation: The reviewer may also reject with a recorded reason.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The earlier decision it reopens is the assumption that the key was stable during the task.
statements.explanation: A stale exception shows the key changed during the task.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The owner is the coordinator, then the decision owner.
statements.explanation: The coordinator notices first and the decision owner decides.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong implementations your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A store whose read returns the stored list passes every version test, and the copy-isolation test catches it.
statements.explanation: Version tests never mutate a returned list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A coordinator that retries stale writes at the fresh version passes "the write was rejected."
statements.explanation: But it fails the preservation test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The retrying coordinator also passes "the proposal was preserved and a reviewer decided."
statements.explanation: It fails that one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing threaded test proves the absence of the unlocked-comparison fault.
statements.explanation: It can provoke the fault but cannot prove its absence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A store that compares the version outside the lock passes every sequential test.
statements.explanation: Sequential tests cannot expose a race between check and write.

questions.source: The gate: design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the record may claim and about moving output downstream.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The record may claim that a named reviewer committed this version.
statements.explanation: A named reviewer's commit is the human step the record can attest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Workers may act on a record once Claude reports that its tests passed.
statements.explanation: The stale-write test must pass, every trigger row needs an owner and resume condition, and the replay must mark gaps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The record may claim that the value is true.
statements.explanation: It may not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An item you cannot write a test for can simply be dropped from the gate.
statements.explanation: It belongs in the sign-off's "not checked" line.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The record may claim commit order for one key within one process.
statements.explanation: That is all the version counter orders.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It stage.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Your version is the baseline: the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.
statements.explanation: You measure Claude's version against it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The six tests are best read together as "the code works".
statements.explanation: They are six distinct questions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The six tests are read as six distinct questions, including the default for a missing key and the isolation of a returned copy.
statements.explanation: Each test isolates one behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The demo and tests need an API key because they call Claude.
statements.explanation: They run offline.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You write your own Memory in learning-artifacts/week-12/ before opening the reference.
statements.explanation: Building first gives you a baseline to audit against.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the tests and extensions in Build It.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You should change several inputs at once to cover more cases per run.
statements.explanation: Change one input at a time so a difference has an identifiable cause.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You should read the reference implementation before writing your own so you know the target.
statements.explanation: Build before consulting reference.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You can audit a version check you have never broken by reading it carefully.
statements.explanation: You cannot audit one you have never broken.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An expiry field with a rejected-when-expired test forces the question of what "expired" means.
statements.explanation: Why it is a good extension.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You add a meaningful success outside the demo and a failure that would matter in your capstone.
statements.explanation: The two tests the lesson asks for.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about handing the work to Claude Code.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You give Claude your gate (the contract, the trigger table, the test list) and not your implementation.
statements.explanation: Claude works from the gate rather than your solution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude's report that your tests passed is sufficient.
statements.explanation: You run your tests on what it returns, yourself.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A failing test is a flaw in Claude to be fixed without revisiting your gate.
statements.explanation: A failure is often a gap in your gate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The harness pauses a task when a stale exception hits a key it depends on, preserves both proposals, and does not resume until a reviewed version is committed and the task rereads it.
statements.explanation: The harness encodes the gate's pause-and-resume rule.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The harness may resume the paused task automatically once the stale exception clears.
statements.explanation: Nothing resumes until a reviewed version is committed and reread.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three things to do with Claude's result.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A boundary Claude handled that you missed is a reason to revise your gate.
statements.explanation: That is a gap in the gate, not in the code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If Claude's version passes all your tests, no comparison with your baseline is needed.
statements.explanation: The comparison is still part of the exercise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in your gate, which Claude could not see because it had only what you wrote.
statements.explanation: Claude sees only what you wrote.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You compare Claude's implementation with your baseline and name one difference in behavior.
statements.explanation: Naming a difference forces you to compare behavior.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If a deliberately wrong version from Claude still passes your tests, your test list was too weak.
statements.explanation: A weak test list lets wrong versions pass.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the multi-agent half of Use It.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Proposed updates go through a coordinator, and conflicts are recorded rather than resolved by last-writer-wins.
statements.explanation: A coordinator surfaces conflicts instead of overwriting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You write your initial interpretation after reading the synthesis so you can see the disagreements.
statements.explanation: Write and date it before reading any synthesis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the two sessions agree, you ask what they shared before counting the agreement as anything.
statements.explanation: A shared model, prompts, or sources can explain agreement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a session failed or did not run, you substitute a fixture and record it as that session's output.
statements.explanation: Record that it failed rather than substituting a fixture.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sessions work as researcher and reviewer on sanitized fixtures, each with a bounded role contract and preserved source IDs.
statements.explanation: Bounded roles and source IDs keep the handoff auditable.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the premortem.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Each row needs only a control and a residual risk.
statements.explanation: Each row needs a trigger, owner, evidence, response, and recovery condition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Monitor for stale memory" is an operational control.
statements.explanation: It is not operational.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It covers stale reads, prompt injection in shared notes, duplicate actions, privacy retention, and an incident replay.
statements.explanation: The five failures named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A control that detects a failure removes the need to test recovery.
statements.explanation: Test recovery, not only detection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Each control has its own failure, so the residual risk is recorded beside the mitigation.
statements.explanation: No control is perfect, so its failure mode is recorded.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the rows of the premortem table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For privacy retention, the detection evidence is an effect log showing two executions.
statements.explanation: That belongs to duplicate actions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For stale reads, the detection evidence is a stale exception on a key an active task read.
statements.explanation: That is the premortem's evidence for stale reads.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For prompt injection in shared notes, a residual risk is a quarantine nobody reviews.
statements.explanation: A quarantine that no one reviews fails silently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For duplicate actions, the control is an idempotency boundary at the external action and a residual risk is a key scoped wrongly.
statements.explanation: Duplicate actions are controlled at the external action.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For incident replay, the control is a quarantine state for suspicious records.
statements.explanation: That belongs to prompt injection.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about testing recovery in the premortem.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A workflow that always accepts the newest proposal has automated last-writer-wins behind a review-shaped ceremony.
statements.explanation: Without a rejection path, review is only ceremony.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Testing detection of the stale conflict is sufficient, because recovery follows from detection.
statements.explanation: Test recovery, not only detection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Deleted from this dictionary" may be reported as "deleted everywhere" once a deletion test passes.
statements.explanation: Deleted from this dictionary must not become deleted everywhere.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You also test the opposite decision, where the reviewer rejects the change with a recorded reason.
statements.explanation: Rejection must be a real option.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You create the stale conflict, pause a dependent fixture, commit the reviewed replacement, and prove the task rereads before resuming.
statements.explanation: Recovery is tested, not just detection.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The "Not checked" line does the work.
statements.explanation: Its contents come from your record of what you did not do.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent Claude draft of the sign-off can be signed as written.
statements.explanation: Write it from your record.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If your evidence does not support signing, withholding is an honest result.
statements.explanation: Claiming more than the record supports repeats the chapter's failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The contents of "Not checked" must come from your own record, not the template.
statements.explanation: The template's items are examples only.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An AI-written sign-off leaves out the "Not checked" line because the system that wrote it has no record of what you did not do.
statements.explanation: Only you know what you did not check.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off template.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its "Checked" line should list only the behaviors Claude reported as passing.
statements.explanation: It names behaviors checked by your own tests.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Its "Not claiming" example includes that the stale write was rejected.
statements.explanation: The rejection is something you observed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Its "Not checked" example says deletion in backups was verified.
statements.explanation: Deletion in backups is listed as not checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Its "Not checked" example includes contention under real concurrent load because the fixtures are sequential.
statements.explanation: As in the template.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Its "Not claiming" example includes that two sessions agreeing is independent confirmation.
statements.explanation: As in the template.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first two rows of the driver's-seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude should challenge them by proposing the trigger or failure you missed.
statements.explanation: Claude's role is to challenge, not author.

statements.label: B
statements.text: You build your baseline after Claude's implementation arrives.
statements.explanation: You build your own baseline first.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Which earlier decision a finding reopens depends on stakes that Claude can state for you.
statements.explanation: It depends on stakes only you can state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude should implement the store fast, run your tests, and propose a wrong version that passes.
statements.explanation: Speed is Claude's strength; auditing is yours.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You write the record, the revision boundary, and the triggers first and name an owner for each.
statements.explanation: Only you can state the stakes behind them.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the remaining rows of the driver's-seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In parallel research and review you form an initial interpretation before the synthesis and bring context the notes lack.
statements.explanation: Your judgment is not a product of the shared model.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In resolving a conflict between proposals you decide: commit, reject with a reason, or leave it unresolved.
statements.explanation: The decision has an owner whose name goes on it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude should decide the conflict because it laid out both proposals and their evidence.
statements.explanation: The decision has a human owner.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because two sessions are available, you can skip your own initial interpretation.
statements.explanation: Two sessions share a model, prompts, and sources.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude should choose the verbs for what the replay supports and sign it.
statements.explanation: You choose the verbs and sign or withhold.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about recording the split between delegation and judgment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The replay should list only the tasks you delegated.
statements.explanation: It also records a retained judgment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A timestamp on the AI summary alone shows when your interpretation was formed.
statements.explanation: You need evidence of your own interpretation's timing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You need a transcript line or timestamp showing your initial interpretation came before the AI summary.
statements.explanation: Otherwise the split happened in your head, not in the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Remembering that you formed your interpretation first is sufficient evidence.
statements.explanation: The split must be in the record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The incident replay records one task you delegated and one judgment you retained.
statements.explanation: The split must be visible in the record.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how the chapter says to verify the work.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing suite establishes universal reliability.
statements.explanation: It does not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A passing suite establishes only the tested behavior.
statements.explanation: Not universal reliability or permission to act.
