statements.text: The recorded fingerprint must equal a newly computed fingerprint of the proposal now under consideration.
statements.explanation: That is the content-binding condition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The `approved` value must be the exact Boolean `True`, so the string `"yes"` does not pass.
statements.explanation: The check uses `is True`.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The decision must be a dictionary.
statements.explanation: That is the first condition.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a `True` result from `approved` means.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It means the decision record has the required shape and content binding.
statements.explanation: That is the narrow reading the chapter gives.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It means a real authorized human gave informed consent.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to read it that way.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The implementation contains evidence that a person saw the proposal.
statements.explanation: It has no such evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The implementation includes an expiry time and a revocation list.
statements.explanation: It has no login, signature, role registry, delegation rule, expiry time, revocation list, or decision ID.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The string `"human"` in the test is the authenticated identity of the reviewer.
statements.explanation: It is fixture data.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the chapter's code binds an approval to.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The code records which authority the approver holds.
statements.explanation: The person binding is not done by any code in the chapter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The code establishes that the approver read the proposal.
statements.explanation: No code can do that alone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The code limits how often a decision may be used.
statements.explanation: No consumption or use limit exists in the six-test lesson.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The fingerprint comparison ties a decision to the exact serialized proposal.
statements.explanation: That is content binding, which the code does.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The code limits how long a decision lives.
statements.explanation: Scope and time are code "you have not written yet."

questions.source: Worked example: approval that cannot follow a changed target
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the demo proposal and decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: `approved(proposal, decision)` is true because the proposal's contents were judged adequate.
statements.explanation: The predicate validates record shape and content binding, not adequacy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The exact digest carries semantic meaning about the proposal.
statements.explanation: The chapter says we need not pretend it does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: All six values of the demo proposal are nonempty, so `fingerprint` returns a 64-character SHA-256 hexadecimal string.
statements.explanation: The proposal meets the precondition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: `approved(proposal, decision)` returning true is a fixture result, not a human sign-off.
statements.explanation: The decision was generated to test content binding.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The demo decision was produced by a human reviewer reading the proposal.
statements.explanation: It was generated to test the mechanism.

questions.source: Worked example: approval that cannot follow a changed target
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about changing the target to `"elsewhere"` after the simulated decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The changed dictionary serializes to different bytes and receives a different fingerprint.
statements.explanation: One changed field changes the serialization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A changed target creates a new decision object, and the reviewer must see it and decide again.
statements.explanation: That is the intended behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: `approved(changed, decision)` returns false because the old digest no longer equals the current proposal's digest.
statements.explanation: The comparison fails.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The system does not ask whether "elsewhere" is similar, safer, or probably what the reviewer meant.
statements.explanation: It only compares digests.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rejection is a defect that a production gate should remove so old approvals carry over.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the rejection is what we want.

questions.source: Worked example: approval that cannot follow a changed target
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about representation changes versus proposal changes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing only dictionary insertion order while preserving all key-value pairs leaves the fingerprint the same.
statements.explanation: Keys are sorted before serialization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two path spellings that resolve to the same file hash differently as strings.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint is over the text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A target string can stay identical while the filesystem object it names changes.
statements.explanation: The string does not guarantee the object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Content binding is fully semantic: the fingerprint reflects what the target actually is on disk.
statements.explanation: It is only as semantic as the proposal representation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A gate should avoid demanding new approval for irrelevant formatting while reliably detecting consequential change.
statements.explanation: That is the stated goal.

questions.source: Worked example: approval that cannot follow a changed target
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what each observation in the chapter's evidence table supports.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A digest mismatch after a target change supports the conclusion that the changed action is necessarily harmful.
statements.explanation: That is listed as unsupported.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Six truthy fields support the conclusion that the minimum shape passes.
statements.explanation: That is the supported conclusion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A decision that matches the original digest supports the conclusion that the record binds to the original content.
statements.explanation: That is the supported conclusion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Six truthy fields support the conclusion that the descriptions are adequate.
statements.explanation: That is listed as unsupported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A target change with a digest mismatch supports the conclusion that the serialized proposal changed.
statements.explanation: That is the supported conclusion.

questions.source: Worked example: approval that cannot follow a changed target
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the evidence table does and does not support.

statements.label: A
statements.text: That all six lesson tests pass tells you the reference meets six statements.
statements.explanation: It tells you no more than that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A recorded fingerprint is evidence that a record was written against these bytes.
statements.explanation: That is what it shows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A recorded fingerprint is evidence that someone read the proposal.
statements.explanation: It is not evidence that anyone read it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nothing in the evidence table supports the claim that a person reviewed the proposal.
statements.explanation: The chapter says this absence is the sign-off standard.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Six passing tests show that six statements are enough for a safe gate.
statements.explanation: Passing six tests does not show that six statements are enough.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what a fingerprint does and does not answer.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fingerprint answers "is this still the proposal?"
statements.explanation: It detects content change.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fingerprint does not answer "may this be done now, here, once?"
statements.explanation: Those are separate decisions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A gate that leaves scope, time, and use to defaults has made no decision about them.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it has made those decisions anyway.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Scope is fully determined by the proposal content, so it needs no separate design.
statements.explanation: Approval needs scope beyond content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the proposal says "write report.md", the fingerprint alone limits how many times the operation can repeat.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint alone does not limit replay.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Check each statement that matches the chapter's guidance on preventing replay of a single-use decision.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking that a decision is unused in one step and marking it used in a later step is equivalent to atomic consumption.
statements.explanation: Two workers can both pass between the steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Add a unique decision ID and consumption state for single-use actions.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's remedy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The authorization service must own the single-use rule where the action occurs.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The decision ID should be checked and consumed atomically at the effect boundary.
statements.explanation: Atomicity closes the race.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without atomic check-and-consume, two workers can present the same valid decision simultaneously.
statements.explanation: That is the stated failure.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about expiry and revocation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Expiry needs an explicit time basis and comparison policy.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Revocation withdraws a still-unexpired decision.
statements.explanation: That is its definition.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A revocation record needs only to say that the decision was withdrawn.
statements.explanation: It should record who revoked, under what authority, which proposal, and how started work is handled.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Expiry is not just a timer, because new evidence can invalidate approval early.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A deadline in local time without a zone is ambiguous.
statements.explanation: The chapter gives this example.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about binding environment identity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Candidate identities to bind include resolved target, account, repository revision, data classification, and tool version.
statements.explanation: These are the chapter's candidates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Approval for a test database must not authorize production merely because the query text matches.
statements.explanation: The environment identity matters.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Matching query text is sufficient to show that the same environment is meant.
statements.explanation: Environment identity must be bound separately.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Which identities should force reconsideration is a judgment about consequence, not a property of the hash.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You should bind as many identities as possible, since extra bindings cost nothing.
statements.explanation: Add the identities whose change should force reconsideration and no others.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about rollback claims.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once a change has been approved through a gate, it can be assumed to be a good change.
statements.explanation: An approved change can still be a bad one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sending a message, disclosing data, or triggering a payment may be irreversible.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Restore previous file" also assumes no dependent effects have occurred and that restoration is semantically sufficient.
statements.explanation: These are named assumptions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Restore previous file" assumes a previous copy exists and the writer can access it.
statements.explanation: These are named assumptions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A gate should say "no complete rollback" rather than inventing reassurance.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

questions.source: The gate: write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Design part of the gate you write.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The decision owner can be named as "the team."
statements.explanation: The owner should be a role that can be asked, not "the team."

statements.label: B
statements.text: The review budget should be stated as a measured fact even when it is only an estimate.
statements.explanation: It is labeled an assumption unless you measured it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude should propose which identities force a new decision, since it can see the whole plan.
statements.explanation: These are your choices; no model produced them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Friendly targets in the six fields are replaced by resolved identities.
statements.explanation: The Design item says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You write the gate after Claude's first implementation so you can see how the behavior turns out.
statements.explanation: You write the gate before asking Claude for any code.

questions.source: The gate: write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the contract for the approval predicate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A timeout with no reviewer response counts as approval once the deadline passes.
statements.explanation: A timeout authorizes nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Refusal and deferral are errors that should be logged as failures.
statements.explanation: They are recorded outcomes, not errors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The fresh fingerprint is computed at the effect boundary, not at review time.
statements.explanation: That is the stated requirement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The check should read the current time inside itself so tests exercise the real clock.
statements.explanation: The chapter would pass the current time in so tests can say "one second after the deadline" without waiting.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Absence, silence, a timeout, a model's confidence, and a favorable automated score authorize nothing.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists them.

questions.source: The gate: write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the wrong predicates your tests must catch.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The six lesson tests catch the check-then-mark version, because the lesson includes replay tests.
statements.explanation: The lesson has no consumption, so it has no test for it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A predicate that fingerprints only the six named fields passes all six lesson tests.
statements.explanation: The lesson tests do not catch it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A predicate that tests `approved` for truthiness rejects the string `"no"`.
statements.explanation: A nonempty string is truthy and approves.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A predicate that tests `approved` for truthiness lets the string `"no"` approve.
statements.explanation: A nonempty string is truthy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With the six-field-only predicate, adding `"environment": "production"` to an approved proposal forces a new approval.
statements.explanation: The extra field is outside the fingerprint, so nothing changes.

questions.source: The gate: write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the failure sentence and what the gate may claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gate may claim content binding, expiry, and single use under a fixture clock and a simulated approver.
statements.explanation: That is the stated claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The failure sentence should be written before you read any output.
statements.explanation: That is the instruction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The gate may claim that a person reviewed it, because the fixture records an approver string.
statements.explanation: It may not claim that a person reviewed, understood, or was authorized.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can write the whole gate for you without defeating its purpose, because the owner, budget, and identities are mechanical.
statements.explanation: They are judgments about consequence that go on record in your words.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Written afterward, the failure sentence describes the output instead of testing you.
statements.explanation: That is the stated reason.

questions.source: Build an evaluation set that can embarrass the proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the expected gate behavior in the chapter's compact evaluation set.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The "changed target" case expects the old decision to be rejected.
statements.explanation: It blocks approval drift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The "vague evidence" case expects the proposal shape to be rejected.
statements.explanation: It expects a structural pass and a human defer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The "reordered keys" case expects a new fingerprint.
statements.explanation: It expects the same fingerprint.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The "missing rollback" case expects a structural pass and a human defer.
statements.explanation: It expects the proposal shape to be rejected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The "exact original" case exists to test refusal.
statements.explanation: It establishes the happy path.

questions.source: Build an evaluation set that can embarrass the proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a proposal whose evidence says only "looks good."

statements.label: A
statements.text: It is a workflow failure whenever the function fingerprints a vague statement.
statements.explanation: It becomes one only if documentation claims the function evaluated evidence quality.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is a failing test of the function whatever its documented contract says.
statements.explanation: It is not a failing test if the contract is structural content binding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A well-named field such as `evidence` can perform the plausibility audit automatically.
statements.explanation: No field name does it; it is the reviewer's work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The current Python function will fingerprint it because the string is nonempty.
statements.explanation: The function checks truthiness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Plausibility auditing means judging whether a claim is credible and consistent with what you know, independent of how confidently it was stated.
statements.explanation: That is the chapter's definition.

questions.source: Build an evaluation set that can embarrass the proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that matches the chapter's guidance on running the evaluation and reporting results.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single aggregate score gives the reviewer the trace they most need.
statements.explanation: A single aggregate score discards that trace.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Expected outcomes should be locked before running.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With a tiny fixture, one held-out result can be reported as a reliability percentage.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to inflate it that way.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When an observation differs from expectation, the expectation should be edited quietly so the suite passes.
statements.explanation: The change should be investigated and preserved.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When an observation differs from expectation, you investigate whether the implementation, the test expectation, or the original requirement is wrong, and preserve the change.
statements.explanation: That is the instruction.

questions.source: Build an evaluation set that can embarrass the proposal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about using model graders in a gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model may reward fluent rollback prose that omits an irreversible effect.
statements.explanation: That is a named failure mode.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model grader that agrees with the deterministic checker removes the need for human review.
statements.explanation: Human review remains, proportional to stakes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Model graders can assist with qualitative fields, but their judgments need calibration and failure analysis.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Qualitative grading should be paired with deterministic checks and human review proportional to the stakes.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two graders that share a prompt assumption and agree provide a second opinion.
statements.explanation: They can agree and still be wrong together.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about how presentation can undermine a strong backend predicate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Even a strong backend predicate can be undermined by presentation.
statements.explanation: That is the section's thesis.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the reviewer sees a friendly summary while the fingerprint covers hidden fields, the decision binds to bytes the reviewer did not meaningfully inspect.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Truncating a target or collapsing effects behind a disclosure panel can leave a record mechanically exact and socially uninformed.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the fingerprint is computed correctly, the interface cannot weaken the control.
statements.explanation: Presentation can undermine it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reviewer's view is irrelevant as long as the same fingerprint is stored.
statements.explanation: The decision should bind to what the reviewer saw.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: Check each statement that matches the chapter's guidance on how an approval screen should present a proposal.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A green continue button beside a muted refusal link is acceptable because refusal is still available.
statements.explanation: It is listed as a dark pattern.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Urgency language generated by the requesting agent helps reviewers prioritize.
statements.explanation: It is listed as a dark pattern.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A default-selected approval is an acceptable convenience if the reviewer can change it.
statements.explanation: It is listed as a dark pattern.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Link evidence claims to their artifacts rather than copying a green label.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Present the action and target first.
statements.explanation: That is the instruction.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: Check each statement that matches the chapter's guidance on what a decision binds to and what happens at execution.

statements.label: A
statements.text: On a fingerprint mismatch at execution, it is appropriate to ask the model to explain why the old approval probably still applies.
statements.explanation: The chapter says never to invite that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The decision should bind to the representation the person actually saw, together with any referenced immutable artifacts.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Someone can understand a proposal and still lack authority over the target, the data, or the recipient.
statements.explanation: Understanding is not authority.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If evidence can change at the same URL after approval, binding only the proposal text leaves another substitution path.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At execution, recompute the fingerprint; on a mismatch, show the changed fields and return to review.
statements.explanation: That is the stated procedure.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the volume trap and why a perfectly bound proposal can still be reviewed superficially.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because a proposal is perfectly bound by its fingerprint, the quality of the review is guaranteed.
statements.explanation: A perfectly bound proposal can still receive superficial review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Speeding up the approval button restores the reviewer's judgment.
statements.explanation: It turns the gate into a queue or a click ritual.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter presents this as the book's argument, not a measurement of any team.
statements.explanation: It says so directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The case for generating ten times as much in the same time is real, but the ability to verify ten times as much does not come with it.
statements.explanation: That is the volume trap as the chapter states it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude sits on the generating side of the gap.
statements.explanation: It can produce proposals faster than a careful reviewer can read them.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Five proposals arrive while one reviewer can carefully inspect two in the stated period. Check each statement that is true about the chapter's treatment of this scenario.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The shortfall is three proposals beyond careful-review capacity.
statements.explanation: Five minus two is three.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A naive system shows all five as urgent and lets dependent agents wait indefinitely.
statements.explanation: That is the naive pattern described.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because checks can run automatically on all five, the system can also supply the three missing units of human attention.
statements.explanation: It cannot manufacture human attention.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A governed system classifies consequence, preserves arrival and dependency information, and applies a declared queue policy.
statements.explanation: That is the governed pattern described.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The capacity of two is a labeled assumption, not a measured result.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Proposal A is a reversible local formatting change, B sends material to an external recipient, C changes a production target, D duplicates B's effect, and E depends on C. Check each statement that is true about the chapter's handling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A proposing model's urgency label can be used directly to order the queue.
statements.explanation: Urgency labels written by the proposer should never set priority unvalidated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ordering the chapter gives is the universally correct queue policy.
statements.explanation: The chapter says the point is that someone must choose and document a policy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: B and C may receive priority because their effects are external or high-impact.
statements.explanation: That is the stated reasoning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: D should be detected as a potential duplicate and held.
statements.explanation: It duplicates B's effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: E remains blocked on C.
statements.explanation: It depends on C.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what to do when the queue exceeds reviewer capacity.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pending decisions should stay valid until their deadline even when the evidence they relied on has gone stale.
statements.explanation: Pending decisions should be invalidated when evidence or environment goes stale.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Past the available attention, more prompts produce habituation rather than more oversight.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cutting the information shown so reviewers can click faster is not capacity planning.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The main remedy for a long queue is to shorten what reviewers are shown so each decision is faster.
statements.explanation: The remedies are to pause intake, narrow scope, add qualified reviewers, or defer work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Timeout or queue delay can be treated as approval after a long enough wait.
statements.explanation: Timeout, absence, and queue delay are not approval.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about standing policies and the feedback loop on review quality.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If reviewers keep receiving nearly identical low-consequence proposals, a team can ask whether a narrow standing policy should authorize that class, with monitoring and revocation.
statements.explanation: That is the stated option.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reviewers should be scored on throughput to keep the gate fast.
statements.explanation: Scoring on throughput trains the gate to become ceremonial.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Refusal and deferral should be tracked, not just approvals.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Authorizing such a class is a governance decision, not an agent shortcut.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If every decision is yes, that is evidence the gate is working well.
statements.explanation: The chapter says to ask whether reviewers have real options, adequate evidence, and support for saying no.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off experiment from the companion book.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The experiment asks an agent for the sign-off statement for the thing you just validated.
statements.explanation: That is the setup.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The predicted paragraph is empty, because unless you supplied the record the system has nothing to say about what was done or skipped.
statements.explanation: That is why it is empty.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The shape of a sign-off is hard to produce while its substance is easy.
statements.explanation: The shape is easy to produce; the substance is not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The system can be relied on to know which checks were skipped even if given no record.
statements.explanation: It has nothing to say without the record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The predicted result is a fluent, structurally complete paragraph that names a person and asserts a review happened.
statements.explanation: That is the prediction.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the four-part attestation standard.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "What was not tested" names the conditions not probed and the failure modes known and not reached.
statements.explanation: That is part two.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calibrated verbs mean "passed" should mean passed a stated test, and a weaker verb such as "believe safe" should say that it is weaker.
statements.explanation: That is part four.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Who cleared which gate" names a person or role per decision who can be asked and who answers if the gate was cleared wrongly.
statements.explanation: That is part three.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The team" is an acceptable answer for who cleared a gate.
statements.explanation: The chapter says a named person or role, not "the team."

statements.label: E
statements.text: "What was tested" names the specific checks, against the specific criteria, with the results.
statements.explanation: That is part one.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the "what was not tested" part of an attestation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An empty "Not checked" entry shows that nothing was left untested.
statements.explanation: If you cannot fill it with real entries, you have not looked hard enough.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An affected person cannot act on a clean-bill list when the untested region is where harm lives.

statements.explanation: Unknown labels are caught later.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An empty data_classes list is caught by the missing-field check, not by the shape check.
statements.explanation: The missing check already rejects it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The shape check rejects the label "personal" because it is not in the allowlist.
statements.explanation: The allowlist comparison comes next and flags it for review.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the classroom allowlist of data classes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The allowlist contains public, synthetic, and internal.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Anything outside those three labels produces a review issue.
statements.explanation: The code appends a sensitive-or-unknown issue.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The allowlist is case-sensitive, so a capitalized "Public" also goes to review.
statements.explanation: Stated trade-off.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the machine cannot tell, the conservative routing action sends the decision to a person.
statements.explanation: Stated principle.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A class labeled internal is therefore safe for the proposed workflow.
statements.explanation: The code does not decide that.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about external_write and the returned status.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A truthy external_write adds "external action approval" to the issues.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The check identifies the external target and authenticates the approval.
statements.explanation: It does neither.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The check marks a condition that needs another control.
statements.explanation: It does not execute Chapter 13's fingerprint gate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The status is review-required when issues exist.
statements.explanation: Otherwise it is ready-for-human-review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A truthy external_write on an otherwise complete record yields the status incomplete.
statements.explanation: It adds an issue, so the status is review-required.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why the demo record returns ready-for-human-review.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Thirty has exact type int and is nonnegative.
statements.explanation: It passes the retention check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: data_classes is a list whose only item is a string, and "public" is in the allowlist.
statements.explanation: It passes the shape and allowlist checks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A truthy external-write flag was present but ignored.
statements.explanation: There is no truthy external-write flag.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The result shows that a particular instructor accepted the approval responsibility.
statements.explanation: "Instructor" may describe a role without such proof.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The result is strong evidence that someone confirmed each line.
statements.explanation: It is accurate about the function but weak as governance evidence.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the weaknesses the chapter finds in the demo record.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Project team" may name no accountable individual.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Citation audit" leaves the sampling, checker, criteria, and failure response unstated.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Project owner" may be unreachable to affected people.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Thirty days says nothing about caches, backups, exported artifacts, or deletion verification.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The validator's ready-for-human-review output is inaccurate about the function.
statements.explanation: The result is accurate about the function.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about running assess on different records.

statements.label: A
statements.text: assess({}) returns incomplete with all seven field names in issues.
statements.explanation: A useful negative case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting data_classes to ["personal"] with other required values present raises ValueError.
statements.explanation: It yields review-required with the sensitive-or-unknown issue.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Setting external_write=True on a public-data record leaves the status ready-for-human-review.
statements.explanation: It adds the external-action issue.

statements.label: D
statements.text: These cases demonstrate agreement by named people and stakeholder consent.
statements.explanation: They demonstrate routing only.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A review-required status shows the sensitive class has been mitigated.
statements.explanation: It only routes the decision to a person.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the structurally complete but weak record with owner "everyone", purpose "help", retention 99999, approver "manager", evaluation "looks fine", and incident contact "team".

statements.label: A
statements.text: The current function can return ready-for-human-review for it.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so.

statements.label: B
statements.text: That is not a defect relative to the function's narrow contract.
statements.explanation: The contract is structural.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is a counterexample to broad claims about what the status means.
statements.explanation: The status is not approval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The retention of 99999 is rejected because it is too large.
statements.explanation: It is a nonnegative integer and passes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Human review can be skipped for it since the validator passed it.
statements.explanation: The human review must interrogate meaning.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's evidence table, which pairs a register observation with what it supports and what remains open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Seven fields present" supports a minimum record shape, while adequacy and acceptance remain open.
statements.explanation: First row.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Retention is a nonnegative integer" supports that the declared day count has valid shape, while the actual deletion lifecycle remains open.
statements.explanation: Second row.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Classes are known labels" supports that classification is accurate.
statements.explanation: It supports only that no unknown label appears under the course allowlist.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "External-write issue" supports that the external target is authorized.
statements.explanation: It supports a routing trigger; target, authority, and outcome remain open.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Ready for human review" supports that consent, ethics, and compliance were established.
statements.explanation: Those remain open.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the verb ladder the chapter offers for describing a register line.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Use the weakest verb your evidence supports.
statements.explanation: Stated rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Listed" fits when a name appears.
statements.explanation: Lowest rung.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Exercised" fits when you ran the route and watched it work.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Verified" fits when you inspected the store yourself.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ladder is an industry standard for audit evidence.
statements.explanation: It is a teaching device for this chapter, not an industry standard.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about generic risk language and concrete harms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "There may be bias or privacy concerns" can be pasted into almost any register and tells no one what to do.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Applied ethics asks who can be affected, through which mechanism, with what consequence, and whether they can contest it.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a public-course-note summarizer, affected groups may include students whose work is quoted and maintainers who must correct errors.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Omitting a required accommodation route is one concrete harm for such a summarizer.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The person who pays for a harm is usually the same person who could have prevented it.
statements.explanation: Usually a different person.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the distribution questions the chapter asks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chapter asks who receives the benefit.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The chapter asks who bears false positives and false negatives.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter asks who is absent from the development examples.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter asks who can reach a human when the output is wrong.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The distribution questions concern only average accuracy across all users.
statements.explanation: They ask who pays and who is exposed.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Agent A (reads public notes, creates a local draft, retains inputs for one day, requires human publication) and Agent B (reads internal records, publishes externally, retains complete traces for a year), which have the same measured accuracy on the same bounded evaluation set.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Agent B has a broader action surface than Agent A.
statements.explanation: B publishes externally.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Agent B has a longer privacy exposure than Agent A.
statements.explanation: A year of traces versus one day.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal accuracy gives the two agents equal risk.
statements.explanation: Equal accuracy does not produce equal risk.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Accuracy describes the surrounding power and consequences, while governance describes selected outputs under selected trials.
statements.explanation: It is the other way around.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ethics can be appended after model selection because accuracy fixes the harm surface.
statements.explanation: Architecture choices shape the harm surface before the first score.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the constructed case of two summarizers that make the same number of deadline errors on the same bounded set.

statements.label: A
statements.text: One errs by stating a deadline its sources do not support.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The other errs by leaving the deadline out when sources conflict.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Students who plan around a wrong date bear the first error.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Students who must ask, and the maintainers who field their questions, bear the first error.
statements.explanation: They bear the second.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The accuracy figure tells the team which error to prefer.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the number says; that is a choice about whose cost counts.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the companion book's point on fairness definitions for systems that rank or evaluate people.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal rates of favorable prediction across groups is one of three reasonable definitions.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The three definitions cannot all hold when the groups' base rates differ, short of perfect prediction.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The book treats each definition as a values claim about which error or which equality matters.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The book treats choosing among the definitions as an optimization problem.
statements.explanation: It is a decision with an owner, not an optimization.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In the sentencing risk-score case, the disagreement arose because one party reported inaccurate numbers.
statements.explanation: Both reported accurate numbers and disagreed about which should count.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about owners, thresholds, and mitigations.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A mitigation without an owner is a wish.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An owner without authority or resources is a label.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A threshold without an observable signal is prose.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 99 percent pass rate shows that no severe harm occurred.
statements.explanation: It can conceal one severe disclosure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Every threshold should trigger an immediate stop on a single occurrence.
statements.explanation: Some events do; others justify trend monitoring.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the rewritten record that begins "The content owner reviews every unsupported-source flag before publication."

statements.label: A
statements.text: It names a signal, threshold, owner, response, scope, and recovery condition.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists these.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Another person can now test whether the process ran.
statements.explanation: That is the benefit of the rewrite.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is complete, and nothing about it can be improved.
statements.explanation: It can still be improved, for example in what counts as approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Work resumes as soon as the incident contact has examined the affected drafts.
statements.explanation: It resumes only after correction and a repeated citation audit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The standard for a threshold is that a stranger can tell, from the record, whether it fired.
statements.explanation: Stated standard.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about retention as a lifecycle.

statements.label: A
statements.text: retention_days: 30 is a policy input, not a deletion mechanism.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Only the application log needs tracing; caches, backups, and repository history are outside the lifecycle.
statements.explanation: The trace covers every copy in scope, including those.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stores you inspected are verified; the provider's and the backups' are, at best, listed.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Removed from this dictionary" means the data is erased everywhere.
statements.explanation: It is not "erased everywhere."

statements.label: E
statements.text: Unknown provider or backup behavior should be assumed to match the stated retention period.
statements.explanation: Mark unknowns; do not turn a desired policy into a claim.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what to state for each data class.

statements.label: A
statements.text: State why it is collected and the minimum needed.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: State who can access it.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: State when the clock begins.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: State how deletion is performed and how deletion is checked.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Derived summaries cannot reveal source information.
statements.explanation: Derived summaries may still reveal source information.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about zero-day retention and incident replay.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Zero-day retention may mean delete immediately after the task, do not persist application data, or retain only de-identified evidence.
statements.explanation: Three readings.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Temporary memory and provider-side processing still exist under zero-day retention.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping everything forever improves both investigation and privacy.
statements.explanation: It makes investigation easier and privacy risk worse.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A minimal, separated audit record can hold operation identity, policy decision, safe evidence references, error category, and responsible roles.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sensitive payloads should be stored in the audit record by default.
statements.explanation: Only when justified and protected.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about why consultation and consent cannot be handed to Claude.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The operational version of the argument needs no position on machine minds.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reply Claude generates in the voice of an affected student is not a statement by that student.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Consent is something a person gives.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You must accept the philosophical argument from Irreducibly Human to follow the chapter.
statements.explanation: The chapter says you do not need to.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If Claude writes a thorough enough reply, the consultation is complete.
statements.explanation: Someone still has to ask the actual person, hear the answer, and stay reachable.

questions.source: Design consultation that can change the project
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about designing consultation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Decide who is affected directly, who maintains the surrounding work, who has relevant domain knowledge, and who is routinely missing from design decisions.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: One convenient person can stand in for every stakeholder.
statements.explanation: Do not ask one convenient person to do so.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Participation should be voluntary where appropriate.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The team should explain what will be recorded, how it will be used, and whether declining has consequences.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Consultation counts only if the answer could have changed the purpose, boundaries, retention, or the decision to automate.
statements.explanation: Otherwise it is theater.

questions.source: Design consultation that can change the project
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about preparing and asking consultation questions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Does this helpful tool sound good?" solicits reassurance.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Better questions ask what outcome would be unacceptable and what would make the person withdraw support.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Promise each person that every request will be adopted.
statements.explanation: Do not promise that; explain how conflicts and decisions will be recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude's plain-language explanation can be shared without checking it against the real system.
statements.explanation: A human must check it first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the team asks only how to make a predetermined deployment more acceptable, participation becomes theater.
statements.explanation: Stated.

questions.source: Recourse is a system path, not an email address
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about recourse as a system path.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An incident contact field often becomes an inbox nobody owns.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reporter must supply complete private details so the team can investigate.
statements.explanation: A reporter should not be forced to expose more private data.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A triage owner and escalation route are unnecessary when the first contact is a named person.
statements.explanation: Escalation is needed when the first contact cannot resolve the issue.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An email address in the incident contact field is a complete recourse path.
statements.explanation: The whole path must be built.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Response times should be stated for every report regardless of the team's capacity.
statements.explanation: State them only when the team can meet them.

questions.source: Recourse is a system path, not an email address
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about remedies for different harms.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Correcting a displayed summary does not repair a decision already made from it.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing personal data from the active store does not recall a public copy.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Explaining a model's reasoning does not restore an opportunity denied to someone.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ask the affected person what meaningful correction looks like, while recognizing that institutional constraints may require additional decision makers.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A single remedy, correcting the record, serves every kind of harm.
statements.explanation: Different harms need different remedies.

questions.source: Recourse is a system path, not an email address
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the five-question test of a recourse route.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test asks whether a person can challenge a result.
statements.explanation: First question.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test asks whether a person can obtain an explanation appropriate to the decision.
statements.explanation: Second question.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The test asks whether a person can see downstream copies updated.
statements.explanation: Fourth question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The test asks whether a person can appeal beyond the original owner.
statements.explanation: Fifth question.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The test asks whether the affected person can debate the model until it changes its output.
statements.explanation: The affected person should not have to debate a model.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the worked incident rehearsal.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It uses a labeled fixture in which a course-note agent publishes a summary stating the wrong assignment deadline.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It is a simulated response sequence, not a claim that an actual incident occurred.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The harm mechanism is a privacy exposure of student work.
statements.explanation: The mechanism is reliance on a wrong deadline.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A successful rehearsal proves people trust the route.
statements.explanation: A rehearsal tests the route and does not prove trust.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rehearsal may include invented stakeholder testimony if it is realistic.
statements.explanation: Do not invent testimony, distress, permission, or repair.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about what the incident investigation found.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The citation audit checked whether a citation string existed.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The citation audit checked whether the cited passage entailed the deadline.
statements.explanation: It did not; that is the gap the investigation found.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mitigation did not address the harm.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The incident reopened the evaluation line of a register that was written before the system shipped.
statements.explanation: Design before implementation is not a freeze.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The register was structurally incomplete before the incident.
statements.explanation: It was structurally ready for review.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the before-to-after revisions in the incident table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Citation audit" became a support check for consequential claims.
statements.explanation: First row.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A generic project owner became a named content owner and backup.
statements.explanation: Second row.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An implicit external write remained implicit because the approver field already covered it.
statements.explanation: It became an explicit publication approval.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Correction means edit" became deleting every copy everywhere.
statements.explanation: It became a bounded copy inventory and limitation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Contact receives report" was kept because the response sequence was adequate.
statements.explanation: It became acknowledgment, triage, escalation, and recovery.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three variants that test the incident route further.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the student compared the summary with an outdated schedule, a respectful route still acknowledges, investigates, and explains the evidence.
statements.explanation: First variant.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Contestability means a person can trigger genuine reconsideration, not that every challenge decides the outcome.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the incident contact is unavailable, the backup pauses publication under delegated authority after the declared acknowledgment threshold and records why.
statements.explanation: Second variant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If no backup exists, the agent should nominate itself as the responsible party.
statements.explanation: That is an unresolved dependency; do not fill it that way.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A review of every deadline claim counts as a control if it reads well, even when the team cannot sustain it.
statements.explanation: A mitigation that cannot be maintained is not a control.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about deferral and narrowing scope.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Defer when the purpose is contested or no authorized owner will accept the decision.
statements.explanation: Two of the listed conditions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Narrowing scope, such as shortening retention, signals that the project failed.
statements.explanation: Narrowing is often productive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Automation is the default destination of every workflow.
statements.explanation: It is not the default.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a workflow is technically feasible, proceed even when the benefit is marginal and the cost falls on people who cannot contest it.
statements.explanation: Feasibility is not a reason to proceed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A register that can only say "go" is useful because it saves review time.
statements.explanation: It is a rubber stamp with a form attached.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: Check each statement that correctly pairs a situation with one of the chapter's governance failure patterns.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Every field holds a generic role and nobody has accepted operational ownership: complete form, absent responsibility.
statements.explanation: Stated pattern.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pilot has no end date and keeps accumulating data and effects: permanent pilot.
statements.explanation: Stated pattern.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A citation audit is offered for a privacy-retention harm: unobservable threshold.
statements.explanation: That is mitigation mismatch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Model-generated stakeholder reactions presented as feedback from people: compliance theater.
statements.explanation: That is consent by simulation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A threshold reading "when quality falls": consent by simulation.
statements.explanation: That is an unobservable threshold.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It step.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Write your own assess from the contract in the gate before opening the reference solution.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Trace one successful case by hand, marking the input boundary, the transformation, and the returned result.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For each of the lesson's six tests, write down which wrong program it exists to catch.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When comparing with the reference, name a difference in line count or style.
statements.explanation: Name a difference in behavior.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Build It happens after Claude has implemented the validator.
statements.explanation: It comes before Claude touches anything.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the first pass of Use It, the validator.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Give Claude the gate (the contract and your test list, including your two added tests), not your implementation.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Run your tests on what Claude returns, yourself.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in your gate, which Claude cannot see because it has only what you wrote.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ask Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version that still passes your tests, and check by hand whether it does.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the wrong version passes your tests, your tests were strong.
statements.explanation: Then your list was too weak.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the second pass of Use It, the register.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Read Claude's draft as the author of the gate, asking for each line which of the five decisions it answers and whether there is a person's name.
statements.explanation: Stated.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The challenger prompt tells Claude not to rewrite the entry.
statements.explanation: Withholding the rewrite is deliberate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The challenger prompt asks for thresholds with no observable signal and for mitigations that do not address the named harm.
statements.explanation: Stated items.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A finding you cannot locate in the text is still useful evidence of a weak line.
statements.explanation: It is a fluent guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking Claude to play an affected student tells you what a real student thinks.
statements.explanation: It only tests whether your explanation is clear.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It

questions.source: Chapter 15 opening (before "What you will be able to do")

questions.source: "In the wild" means bounded reality

questions.source: "In the wild" means bounded reality
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the owner and consent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The containment check runs first.

statements.label: E

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the containment check.

statements.label: E

statements.explanation: The second check.
