statements.explanation: Without links they remain ten islands.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The brief's success criterion maps to evidence.
statements.explanation: One of the chapter's example links.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the short-version gate you write before Claude implements anything.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The gate includes a wrong version of the run that your checks must catch: one that completes, reads well, and leaves the wrong state.
statements.explanation: For example a fluent draft whose citation does not support its claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The design section names the workflow, the owner, the approved data, and the one action that matters, and says whose choices they are.
statements.explanation: Claude can challenge each of them; it did not make any.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can write the gate for you without defeating its purpose.
statements.explanation: Claude can sharpen the gate but cannot write it for you.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The contract states what the workflow must refuse, such as counting a retrieved passage as support when it does not entail the claim.
statements.explanation: It also states the observable state that means done and the conditions that make the result unacceptable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If your checks cannot tell the wrong version from the right one, the gate is finished once the tests pass.
statements.explanation: Then the gate is not finished.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the failure sentence and what the build may claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The build may claim that the workflow is safe once the staged failure is rejected.
statements.explanation: It may claim only a bounded local result under recorded conditions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The failure sentence is added to the pre-mortem after the run as its closing entry.
statements.explanation: It is the lead entry, written before the run.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The failure sentence names the failure you will stage and what you expect each mechanism to do with it.
statements.explanation: That is its content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The build may claim that the owner consents to uses beyond the brief.
statements.explanation: Consent beyond the brief is outside what the build can claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The failure sentence is dated and written before the run.
statements.explanation: It is one dated sentence, written before the run.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about "Claude proposes, Python constrains."

statements.label: A
statements.text: Python holds whatever must be the same every time, such as which tools exist and whether a path stays inside the approved root.
statements.explanation: Plus whether a proposal matches approved content and what gets recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Telling Claude "do not publish" is a sufficient publication boundary.
statements.explanation: A prompt is a request, not a boundary; the boundary is an application that lacks or gates the capability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude does the language work: drafting, summarizing, and proposing a tool call.
statements.explanation: The division of labor.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Every boundary you code is a case you foresaw, so an unforeseen case passes straight through.
statements.explanation: This is why the gate also asks what a failure looks like.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A prompt-injected source should not be able to grant itself tools.
statements.explanation: Which tools exist is held in the application, not in the prompt.

questions.source: The gate: Claude proposes, Python constrains
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on building the controller and any live path.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The final claim is the record least likely to say more than the model request and application result support.
statements.explanation: It is the part most likely to say more.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A missing live run must never be replaced with invented output.
statements.explanation: Live behavior is evidence about a real run under recorded conditions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A live Messages path should be opt-in and should identify the model actually used.
statements.explanation: Along with bounded requests, protected credentials, and recorded cost-bearing behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Validate tool names and arguments in Python, and resolve paths before acting.
statements.explanation: These are Python's jobs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Inject a callable into the controller where possible so that tests do not need network access.
statements.explanation: Start offline.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the Build It baseline.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You write your own `validate_packet` before consulting the reference, from the ten names and the three conditions.
statements.explanation: Build first, then compare.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Your validator is the record of what you understood after Claude finished.
statements.explanation: It is the record of what you understood before Claude touched anything.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You add at least two tests of your own: a meaningful success outside the demo and a failure that would matter in your capstone.
statements.explanation: Beyond the Practice Lab cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: You need not state what remains untested when every test passes.
statements.explanation: The baseline includes stating what remains untested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You can audit a containment check you have never tried to break.
statements.explanation: The chapter says you cannot.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about conducting Claude Code against your gate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You preserve your prompt, the plan, the diff, the commands, and the outputs, with the date and displayed model label.
statements.explanation: If a session failed or did not run, record that rather than substituting a fixture.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A failing test is often a gap in the gate.
statements.explanation: Claude had only what you wrote.

statements.label: C
statements.text: You give Claude the gate (the six artifacts and the test list), not your implementation.
statements.explanation: Then you run your tests on what it returns, yourself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If Claude handled a boundary you missed, revising your gate violates design-first.
statements.explanation: That is a re-engagement; you log the reopening and its reason.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You ask Claude to propose a deliberately wrong version and test by hand whether it still passes your checks.
statements.explanation: If it does, your checks were too weak.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about a controlled failure.

statements.label: A
statements.text: You preserve only the reported outcome, since the independently observed outcome is redundant.
statements.explanation: Preserve the reported outcome, the independently observed outcome, and the gap between them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A gate you have never seen fail has not been tested.
statements.explanation: The chapter states this directly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A successful happy-path run shows the gate works, because every check passed.
statements.explanation: A polished happy-path demo proves very little.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Choose the most dramatic failure available, even if it cannot be reproduced safely.
statements.explanation: Choose one that matters and can be reproduced safely.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You predict the failure before running it.
statements.explanation: That prediction is the sentence you wrote in the gate.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the source-grounded report example and reviewed recovery.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan may narrow the claim, select a different approved source, add an abstention rule, or defer.
statements.explanation: The recovery options listed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A later success is compared with the original failure and checked independently.
statements.explanation: The changed proposal also goes through its gate again.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A changed proposal after recovery skips its gate because the failure already informed it.
statements.explanation: It goes through its gate again.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The chapter's trace of the deadline-claim failure is a recorded run from the course fixtures.
statements.explanation: The chapter calls it a constructed illustration, not a recorded run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recovery is not "ask Claude again until it passes."
statements.explanation: A human or declared policy reviews why the case failed.

questions.source: Controlled failure and reviewed recovery
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about independent routes to checking.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A demo edited to show only success is the strongest evidence of supervision.
statements.explanation: It hides the most valuable part of supervision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If Python calculates a total, running the same calculation again is an independent check.
statements.explanation: A separate derivation can check it; rerunning the same route shares its mistakes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If Claude drafts the claim, Python can validate source identifiers and structure while a person inspects semantic support.
statements.explanation: Different routes fail differently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Failed output should be discarded to keep the record clean.
statements.explanation: Preserve failed output when privacy and safety permit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Two Claude prompts that share the same context are independent checks of each other.
statements.explanation: They are not automatically independent.

questions.source: The miniature casebook
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the prediction-lock and the casebook entry.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Look at it and iterate" means re-prompting until the output looks right.
statements.explanation: The chapter says it never means that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The prediction is added to the entry after execution, once the result is known.
statements.explanation: Item one is the prediction recorded before execution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prediction-lock means writing what you expect, dated, before you observe, and never editing it afterward.
statements.explanation: The habit the chapter takes from Computational Skepticism for AI.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A casebook entry merges the system-reported and independently observed outcomes into one result field.
statements.explanation: They are separate items four and five of the eight-part entry.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The learning is the gap between the prediction and what happened.
statements.explanation: Hindsight is kept from smoothing the story.

questions.source: The miniature casebook
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on recording a casebook entry.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you expected the system to refuse and it accepted, record that.
statements.explanation: Honest recording of the miss.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If no failure occurs, manufacture a surprising error so the casebook is more convincing.
statements.explanation: Do not manufacture a surprising error for drama.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One observed miss proves a permanent limitation of every future model.
statements.explanation: It supports only a bounded claim about this workflow, case, and check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the checker correctly rejected, no explanation is needed because the rejection speaks for itself.
statements.explanation: Explain which mechanism did the work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One clean run establishes general reliability.
statements.explanation: It does not.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on predicting the reviewer's findings.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A prediction has to forbid something.
statements.explanation: Otherwise anything can match it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Record the displayed model label and the date.
statements.explanation: A later run of the reviewer may differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Predict three specific findings, each with an artifact location and a reason.
statements.explanation: Before asking for critique.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The review will find weak integration" is a good prediction because it will almost certainly be matched.
statements.explanation: It can be matched by anything, so it teaches nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Mark each prediction as a finding you expect to be genuine or a false positive.
statements.explanation: So the reviewer's judgment can be scored later.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on handling the reviewer's findings.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rejecting every finding shows independence.
statements.explanation: Rejecting every finding is the mirror-image failure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: To defend a finding away, it is enough to say the packet already covers it.
statements.explanation: Defend by citing the exact passage and explaining why the critique missed it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A finding without located evidence is not a finding.
statements.explanation: Locate the evidence for each row.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Accepting every finding is the safe default.
statements.explanation: Accepting every finding is a failure; a misreading you accept is someone else's error signed as yours.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Request the critique without allowing edits, and preserve the actual response.
statements.explanation: The review is one more output to evaluate.

questions.source: Audit the reviewer
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on evaluating the reviewer itself.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Credit the hit rate over the specificity of your reasoning.
statements.explanation: Credit specificity of reasoning over the hit rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Score each prediction as matched, partly matched, or missed.
statements.explanation: The scoring scheme.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A finding can be treated as established when the reviewer states it confidently.
statements.explanation: Treat every finding as a hypothesis to check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A clean review proves the packet is sound.
statements.explanation: A clean review is corroboration, not proof.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The course holds a measurement of how often such a review is wrong about a packet like yours.
statements.explanation: The course holds no such measurement.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about contingent misses and structural gaps.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A second pass by the same reviewer closes a gap that comes from sharing the draft's model and context.
statements.explanation: A same-model reviewer shares the blind spots.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A contingent miss is one that a better prompt, a second run, a differently built reviewer, or more evidence would close.
statements.explanation: The weak version of a Gap Account.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For a contingent miss, you record it as a permanent limit of the review rather than fixing it.
statements.explanation: You fix it, or run the better review, and say so.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Structural" means no reviewer could ever close the gap.
statements.explanation: It means owing to the reviewer's kind and access, not "for all time".

statements.label: E
statements.text: A structural gap for this review turns on the kind of reviewer, a model that reads only your packet.
statements.explanation: It is recorded as structural for this review.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the patterns of structural gap.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A consequence visible only from inside a relationship you answer to, such as an agreement that came with an unwritten condition.
statements.explanation: The first pattern.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reviewer that shares the draft's model and context shares its blind spots.
statements.explanation: So a second pass by the same reviewer does not close the gap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An asymmetry of stakes: you will bear the consequence and the reviewer will not.
statements.explanation: The third pattern.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A gap is permission to stop working on the final claim.
statements.explanation: A gap is a boundary on the final claim, not permission to give up.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A judgment grounded in domain experience the packet never stated, such as a number that is fine on paper and wrong for this site.
statements.explanation: The second pattern.

questions.source: The Gap Account
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the companion book's claim and your own Gap Account.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For each gap you should name the model that is expected to close it.
statements.explanation: Name the evidence or expertise that could help and the person accountable for the decision now.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The companion book argues that no reviewer of any capability can reach what depends on being situated, having a stake, and being accountable.
statements.explanation: It grounds this in philosophy and safety literature on correlated errors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The course treats that claim as an argued position and does not ask you to agree with it or prove it.
statements.explanation: The chapter says so directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Your Gap Account claims only that this review, on this packet, did not reach this item, that repeating it would not, and that this person can.
statements.explanation: A smaller claim you can check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One observed miss shows that no future model could find the issue.
statements.explanation: It sets a boundary for the decision now, nothing more.

questions.source: Independent verification and outcome state
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about mapping central claims to checks.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "The workflow is safe" is probably too broad and should be decomposed.
statements.explanation: Into smaller claims that can be checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The report is source-grounded" needs claim-to-passage inspection.
statements.explanation: File existence would not show it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The owner consented" can be supported by text Claude drafted in the owner's voice.
statements.explanation: It needs a real decision record, not model text.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The report was created" can map to file existence and read-back.
statements.explanation: A check suited to that claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: File existence is enough to show that a report is source-grounded.
statements.explanation: Source-grounding needs inspection of claims against passages.

questions.source: Independent verification and outcome state
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on inspecting outcome state.

statements.label: A
statements.text: State exactly what was observed.
statements.explanation: The standard for reporting outcomes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An agent can execute the planned calls while the destination remains wrong.
statements.explanation: The trajectory looks fine but the state is not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Inspect the resulting state, not only the trajectory.
statements.explanation: The planned calls may all run while the destination is wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A file write can succeed locally without being committed or published.
statements.explanation: So a write is not a publication.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A success code from a sent request shows that the intended person received it.
statements.explanation: The intended person may never receive it.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on building the claim-to-evidence graph.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once Claude has drafted the graph, its edges count as verified.
statements.explanation: Checking an edge means opening its target.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Claude can draft the first version quickly because it is an index-and-cross-reference task.
statements.explanation: Drafting is cheap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking an edge is as cheap as producing it.
statements.explanation: Output is cheap and verification is not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Start with the final recommendation and break it into smaller claims until each can be checked by one or more artifacts.
statements.explanation: The method.

statements.label: E
statements.text: You decide whether each edge is real, because an edge is a claim that this evidence bears on that claim.
statements.explanation: Edges must be verified.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the recommendation "Narrow the workflow to create a local source-grounded draft, retain only public fixtures for one day, and require a human before publication."

statements.label: A
statements.text: The claim that publication is gated needs no evidence because the recommendation states it.
statements.explanation: The graph maps it to a rejected no-decision fixture.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It contains at least six claims.
statements.explanation: The chapter lists six.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It is a single claim, so one check of the draft is enough.
statements.explanation: Each claim is mapped separately.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One of its claims is that deletion follows the stated day boundary.
statements.explanation: The fifth listed claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One of its claims is that the draft uses approved sources.
statements.explanation: The second listed claim.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the rows of the claim-to-evidence table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For "local draft exists" the evidence is the resolved path, read-back, and diff, and the residual gap is later mutation.
statements.explanation: Row one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An event trace can show no publish action inside the instrumented workflow but not every possible external channel.
statements.explanation: A limit that feeds the sign-off's "not checked" line.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The residual-gap column prevents the graph from becoming decorative certainty.
statements.explanation: Every evidence route has scope.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For "publication needs approval" the residual gap is interpretation disagreement.
statements.explanation: That row's gap is stolen credentials.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For "fixtures are public" the decision owner is the data owner and the residual gap is misclassification.
statements.explanation: Row four.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about orphan nodes and circular support.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A claim with no evidence should be removed, narrowed, or marked pending.
statements.explanation: An orphan claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The audit note can establish that the evidence is correct by summarizing `evidence.md`, even if `evidence.md` cites the audit note.
statements.explanation: That is circular support.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An artifact that supports no claim is harmless.
statements.explanation: It may be busywork.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evidence cited by many claims deserves less scrutiny, because it has been reused so often.
statements.explanation: It deserves extra scrutiny; one defect can collapse several conclusions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A decision with no named owner is unresolved.
statements.explanation: Another orphan.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on the contradiction pass and freezing the review candidate.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Resolve a contradiction by determining which artifact is authoritative, correcting dependent claims, and preserving the revision reason.
statements.explanation: Not by recency.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resolve a contradiction by choosing the newest document.
statements.explanation: The chapter says not to.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a consequential file changes after review, the old approval continues for the unchanged parts without new checks.
statements.explanation: It is a new review candidate; rerun the checks whose premises changed plus the integration checks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Compare the brief's declared purpose with the implemented tools, and the action map with the trace.
statements.explanation: Two of the comparisons.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Freeze the review candidate by revision or digest so that later edits cannot masquerade as reviewed work.
statements.explanation: The freeze.

questions.source: Handoff that survives the author
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on the handoff and on reproducing it as an experiment.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The participant should try live behavior first, since it is the most informative.
statements.explanation: They run the offline path first; live behavior comes later and only with explicit authorization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each question the participant must ask marks missing transfer evidence.
statements.explanation: Examples: an unstated working directory or a globally installed dependency.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After revising the documentation, you can assume the fix worked without rerunning.
statements.explanation: Rerun from a clean-enough context.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A handoff is a seam, and seams are where risk lives.
statements.explanation: A packet only its author can run has a gate with one person behind it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Give a bounded participant only the documented prerequisites and commands, in a sanitized environment.
statements.explanation: So hidden knowledge shows up.

questions.source: Reproduce the handoff as an experiment
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on recording the handoff attempt and stating exclusions.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A handover without answers to the maintenance questions is still a durable contribution if the tests pass.
statements.explanation: Without those answers it is a demo, not a durable contribution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If only local writes were authorized, the handoff may describe the work as published once the file is written.
statements.explanation: It must not imply publication.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reproduction is an observed property of a particular handoff, not an adjective awarded to documentation.
statements.explanation: The standard for claiming it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Packaging your API keys with the handoff lets the new person run the live path.
statements.explanation: Never package API keys; say who supplies which secret and how.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Record the attempt as evidence: environment, commands, failures, questions, and revisions.
statements.explanation: The record of the experiment.

questions.source: The sign-off: the last thing the evidence says
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude can write the sign-off's words fluently, so it can also supply the "not checked" content.
statements.explanation: What was not tested is the part a model has no record of.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sign-off is the last thing the audit-note says.
statements.explanation: It closes the audit-note.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chapter's template is a signature the author completes once the tests pass.
statements.explanation: It is the template and the standard, not a signature.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sign-off can be written from the packet's text alone, without your own record.
statements.explanation: Write it from your record.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The graph's residual-gap column, the Gap Account, and the handoff exclusions feed it.
statements.explanation: They supply its "not checked" content.

questions.source: The sign-off: the last thing the evidence says
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off template fields.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "How" says whether the check was by hand, by a test written before reading Claude's version, by recomputation, by a check that fails differently, or with Claude's help.
statements.explanation: And says which parts Claude helped with.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Not claiming" lists the claims the packet proves.
statements.explanation: It lists what is not claimed, such as that the workflow is safe.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Cleared by" can name "the team" when several people contributed.
statements.explanation: It needs a named person for each consequential decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Not checked" includes each residual gap in the graph and each Gap Account item.
statements.explanation: Plus live behavior if no live run was recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Checked" names which claims in the graph were checked against which evidence.
statements.explanation: Name them.

questions.source: The sign-off: the last thing the evidence says
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sign-off's verbs, withholding, and cost.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sign-off buys speed and deniability, at the cost of answerability.
statements.explanation: It buys legible answerability and pays in speed and deniability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A typed name authenticates the signer.
statements.explanation: A typed name does not authenticate anyone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Withholding is a legitimate outcome.
statements.explanation: A process whose only permitted result is "signed" is a rubber stamp.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing test supports the verb "safe".
statements.explanation: A passing test supports "tested", not "safe".

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Established" or "proven" are fine verbs whenever the checks passed.
statements.explanation: Only when a criterion supports them.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on deciding among ship, narrow, defer, and stop.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The criteria are neutral facts, so there is no need to say who chose them.
statements.explanation: The criteria express values, so say who chose them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Write the recommendation first and then assemble the supporting facts.
statements.explanation: Do not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing structure and tests does not oblige deployment.
statements.explanation: Evidence informs the decision; it does not make it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Put ship, narrow, defer, and stop into one comparison against the same criteria.
statements.explanation: One comparison, same criteria.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude can draft the comparison, including doing less, but it cannot supply the weights.
statements.explanation: The criteria express values.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on when to ship and when to narrow.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Narrow when a smaller action surface, data set, or audience preserves value while reducing unsupported claims.
statements.explanation: A design response to evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing automatic publication may keep most of the value and keep the artifact local.
statements.explanation: An example of narrowing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Narrowing is a failure to ship.
statements.explanation: It is not a failure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ship requires that owners accept their roles, consent and authority exist, and recovery is credible.
statements.explanation: Conditions for shipping.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Ship when the evidence supports the bounded use in the brief, not any future expansion.
statements.explanation: The scope of a ship decision.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on when to defer and when to stop.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Defer when the missing evidence, consultation, expertise, or capacity could realistically be obtained, and name the concrete condition and its owner.
statements.explanation: For example until the data owner classifies one source.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Stop when consent cannot be obtained.
statements.explanation: One of the stop conditions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Effort already spent is evidence for continuing.
statements.explanation: It is not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stop when a simpler non-AI process dominates.
statements.explanation: Another stop condition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An indefinite "more research is needed" is an acceptable defer.
statements.explanation: It evades the decision.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the sensitivity test.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It asks whether the recommendation would change if retention fell from a year to a day.
statements.explanation: Another counterfactual.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It asks whether the recommendation would change if the external-write capability were removed.
statements.explanation: One of the counterfactuals.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Its purpose is to confirm that the original recommendation was right.
statements.explanation: It reveals which assumptions actually drive the decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It also asks whether the recommendation would change if the reviewer backlog doubled.
statements.explanation: The last counterfactual listed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It asks whether the recommendation would change if the owner withdrew consent or the independent checker disagreed once.
statements.explanation: Further counterfactuals.

questions.source: Defend the four options against the same evidence
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the final recommendation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It includes the chosen option, rejected alternatives, evidence, affected interests, conditions, owner, review date, change triggers, and who may revisit it.
statements.explanation: The required contents.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It contains one sentence of epistemic restraint about what the packet does not establish.
statements.explanation: That sentence is often the strongest evidence the author understands the system.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The epistemic-restraint sentence weakens the recommendation, so it belongs in an appendix.
statements.explanation: It is often the strongest evidence of understanding.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once it is signed, the decision is closed to revisiting.
statements.explanation: A later source change, incident, or stakeholder objection can reopen the choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It names only the chosen option, because rejected alternatives clutter it.
statements.explanation: Rejected alternatives are part of the recommendation.

questions.source: Write the recommendation so the judgments are separable
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about Memo A and Memo B.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Memo B is Memo A with your name added.
statements.explanation: Memo B is not Memo A with your name added; it carries your own account.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The labeled parts include what you add that the packet could not show and why the evidence should be trusted, citing graph rows rather than Claude's confidence.
statements.explanation: Plus what Claude produced, why this is the right action here, and the recommendation you sign.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Memo A is the machine's analysis, here Claude's evidence assembly and option comparison.
statements.explanation: From Conducting AI.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The separation diminishes your work by showing how much Claude did.
statements.explanation: It makes your part defensible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A signature without the account behind it counterfeits accountability.
statements.explanation: The chapter's reason for keeping the judgments separable.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that matches the chapter's driver's-seat table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Claude can draft the comparison on your criteria and argue against your preferred row; you choose the criteria and weights.
statements.explanation: The criteria express values.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For the choice and the signature, Claude drafts and signs while you review.
statements.explanation: Claude does nothing beyond the draft.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claude can cross-reference, run `validate_packet`, and list contradictions; you decide which artifact is authoritative and recheck a sample by hand.
statements.explanation: A list of contradictions does not say which document to believe.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude can obtain a real decision from the owner on your behalf.
statements.explanation: Claude drafts the questions; you obtain a real decision from a real owner.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claude gives one read-only critique and also writes the Gap Account for you.
statements.explanation: Claude gives one critique; you predict first, judge each finding, and write the Gap Account.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the three verdicts from Irreducibly Human as applied to the table.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The last two rows of the table are supervise.
statements.explanation: They are protect: consent and authority, and the choice and signature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The first row (evidence trail and validator) is deprioritize with a spot-check.
statements.explanation: Recheck a sample by hand.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deprioritization is not deletion.
statements.explanation: You can hand Claude the claim-to-passage matrix only because you can still check a row.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The second and third rows of the table are supervise.
statements.explanation: Comparing the options and reviewing the packet.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The three verdicts are deprioritize, supervise, and protect.
statements.explanation: Hand over gladly, use and audit, keep.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on recording the split in the transfer reflection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The split is recorded in the Gap Account.
statements.explanation: It is recorded in the transfer reflection.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you cannot point to a transcript line or an edit that shows each, the split happened in your head and not in the record.
statements.explanation: Evidence of the split.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A transcript line, a diff, or an edit you made counts as evidence of the split.
statements.explanation: From the Irreducibly Human note.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Generic statements of lessons are enough if they are well written.
statements.explanation: That is the failure "reflection without evidence".

statements.label: E
statements.text: Record one task you delegated more readily, one capability you kept practicing, and one decision you retained.
statements.explanation: The three-part split.

questions.source: Ship It: submitting the packet
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on submitting the packet.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Include credentials so a reviewer can run the live path.
statements.explanation: Include no credentials or restricted source material.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The artifact brief checklist includes a Claude usage disclosure, source citations, a student-versus-external code estimate, the license, the style declaration, and one decision you revised after testing.
statements.explanation: The checklist.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Submit the ten files with exact commands, kept under learning-artifacts/week-15/.
statements.explanation: The submission location.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Acceptance is concrete: another student can reproduce the offline behavior and name what still needs human verification.
statements.explanation: The acceptance test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Progress Reel can substitute for reproducibility if it shows mechanism, failure, and recovery.
statements.explanation: It cannot substitute for reproducibility.

questions.source: Common capstone failures
questions.stem: Check each statement that correctly describes a common capstone failure.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Packet completeness theater is a failure of check: ten long files pass while no central claim is reproducible.
statements.explanation: The chapter's first failure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Demo-only evidence is a recording that shows success but omits commands, inputs, versions, and failed cases.
statements.explanation: A failure of check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Shared-check dependence is a failure of drive.
statements.explanation: It is a failure of check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Synthetic consent is a failure of conduct.
statements.explanation: Each failure is one of the three jobs left undone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Authority drift is Claude-generated stakeholder language presented as permission.
statements.explanation: That is synthetic consent; authority drift is a local-write approval described as permission to publish.

questions.source: Assessments - ungraded practice
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the chapter's Assessments.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Assessment 8 asks you to add cross-references and then trust them without opening the targets.
statements.explanation: You open every target and confirm it says what the pointer says.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Assessment 7 asks you to design a verifier that fails differently from the production route and name one assumption they still share.
statements.explanation: Independent check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The Assessments are ungraded practice that prepare the capstone evidence.
statements.explanation: They do not create a second capstone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assessment 9 asks you to accept every finding the reviewer returns as genuine.
statements.explanation: You judge each finding as genuine or a false positive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Assessment 4 asks you to select five central capstone claims, point to the artifact and evidence for each, and fill in the residual-gap column for the supported ones.
statements.explanation: Claim-to-artifact map.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance in the Anthropics section.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Demystifying evals for AI agents" can sharpen the distinction among tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, and outcomes.
statements.explanation: Compare it with your evidence packet.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The links were checked on 2026-09-06, so their guidance is guaranteed to stay current.
statements.explanation: Current product guidance may change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When you adapt one example, adopt the whole upstream stack.
statements.explanation: Do not adopt an entire stack merely because it is upstream.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For adapted code, record the specific source, URL, revision or date, license, changes, and evidence for those changes.
statements.explanation: The record to keep.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The Claude cookbooks provide Python examples you may adapt when the mechanism genuinely matches your project.
statements.explanation: Adapt, do not adopt wholesale.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the halt test.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you cannot find the person who can stop the workflow and the line where that authority is written down, the review was commentary.
statements.explanation: The result of applying the test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Borrowing this test validates the rest of the regime for your project and authenticates a signature.
statements.explanation: It borrows one test only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plain test is a named reviewer other than the builders, with authority to halt or revise.
statements.explanation: The test itself.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Claude's read-only critique can comment but cannot stop anything.
statements.explanation: So it fails the halt test on its own.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The companion's accountability chapter lists independent review among the requirements of a working accountability regime.
statements.explanation: The source of the test.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about aiming predictions at the seams.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The valuable finding names a relationship between two artifacts that each look fine alone.
statements.explanation: The seam.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A prediction rewritten to name two artifacts aims at the seams.
statements.explanation: The chapter asks you to rewrite one prediction so it names two artifacts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reviewer who confirms each artifact is thorough has confirmed what is cheap to confirm.
statements.explanation: Per-artifact thoroughness is the cheap check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The best predictions name a single artifact so they can be checked quickly.
statements.explanation: You are asked to rewrite one prediction so it names two artifacts.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One example is a data-boundary exclusion that the action map's read capability quietly reaches around.
statements.explanation: The chapter's illustration.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on the thin-sentence test for the transfer reflection.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The test is applied to the transfer reflection.
statements.explanation: That is where thin sentences restate the draft.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mark every sentence you could have written without knowing anything Claude's summary did not already state.
statements.explanation: The test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent, well-structured reflection passes the test.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not the criterion; knowledge beyond Claude's summary is.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Those marked sentences are the draft restated.
statements.explanation: The reflection must carry the others.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reflection is acceptable if every sentence could have been written from Claude's summary alone.
statements.explanation: Those sentences are the draft restated; the reflection has to carry others.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.stem: Check each statement that agrees with the chapter's guidance on the test for honest deprioritizing.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If you cannot tell whether a row you handed to Claude is right, the sign-off's "how" line claims a check you could not have performed.
statements.explanation: The consequence for the sign-off.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If you cannot tell whether a row is right, you surrendered the task rather than deprioritized it.
statements.explanation: The diagnosis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pick a task you handed to Claude, such as the first-draft claim-to-passage matrix, and redo three rows by hand.
statements.explanation: The test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The final division of labor is capable assistance joined to accountable human purpose and judgment.
statements.explanation: The chapter's statement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The final division of labor is "AI writes and a human signs."
statements.explanation: It is capable assistance joined to accountable human purpose and judgment.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about "AI should" and "Human should."

statements.label: A
statements.text: AI should assemble existing evidence, run the Python packet validator, identify contradictions, and compare bounded options including doing less.
statements.explanation: The AI responsibilities.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Human should own the ship, narrow, defer, or stop choice.
statements.explanation: And remain answerable for revision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The human's answerability ends once the AI drafts the revision.
statements.explanation: The human remains answerable for revision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Human should treat claims about irreducible human capacities as propositions the assignment requires you to prove.
statements.explanation: They are argued positions, not propositions to prove.

statements.label: E
statements.text: AI should not invent stakeholder consent, approvals, deployment decisions, or personal reflection.
statements.explanation: Nor confidence unsupported by the record.
